BY THE SEA. Tired with the struggle, With the ceaseless needs of life; Tired of the petty jar, Of the toil and strife; Of the doubt and of the fear, Of the care that haunts us here: Of the fever aud the fretting, Useless dreaming, vain regretting. Baffled aim, ungranted prayer. Chafe and turmoil everywhere— With a vague unseeing sight, She looked on the September night. Broad and vast before her, Spreading leagues away, Hushing in the hush of night, Gray beneath the gray, Light winds ruffling on her breast. Lay the sea in solemn rest. Bright and wide the pathway showed Where the harvest moonlight glowed. Beaching from the silent land. By the great horizon spanned, Where sky and sea together blend, Where our dim sweet fancies tend. To the golden glory Came a little bark, Shone in it for a moment, Then glided into dark. Bo in a dull life's hours and days, A child's fresh laugh, a word of praise, A flower, a smile, a gentle uty. Or a thought of peace and beauty, d O'er the arid waste may fling Where liegrhetaaisladpuhreeaad g rtninaisrteesntianng, d win New strength new conflicts to begin. S. K. Phillips in Tinsley's Magazine for August.

THE BABY'S TOLL-GATE, Knock at the door, Peep in; Lift up the latch, And walk in. What a funny door— A forehead fair; House with a roof Of golden hair, And tangled curls From ridge to base, Over the eaves— Queer little place. Two windows there, And baby peeps in; Finds the bright blue Where the sky went in, And a laughing elf Looks out to see Who raps so loud, And calls for me. A dainty nose Turned up—beware With thumb and fingers Lift it with care. The portals open; Don't walk in! Bow to the dimple On the chin. A kiss for toll Now you must pay Or not come in At all to-day.

open or shut as occasion requires. The mean height of an Englishman is five and a half inches above that of the Frenchman. "I find that with light meals my health improves," said an Esinimaux ; and down went another candle. More hearts pine away in secret anguish for the want of kindness from those who should be their comforters than for any other calamity in life. To do an evil action is base; to do a good one without incurring danger is common enough; but it is the part of a good man to do great and noble deeds though he risks everything. Justice and generosity are so intimately interwoven that neither can flourish healthfully without the presence of the other. No one can act fairly without acting sympatheti- cally; nor can anyone subserve his own best interest while

that is all he has it heart. Slimmish lady in the Highlands: "Farmer, could you let me have sixpennyworth of new milk ?"—Farmer (doubt- ingly) : " Saxpennyworth, did ye say P"—Slimmish lady tourist: " Yes. '—Farmer : " A'll gie ye a pennyworth; a think it's as much as ye'll haud." A Parisian who had been dining not wisely but too well "Went to a reception at a friend's house. He displayed an oppressive amount of gallantry. "What expressive eyes he has!" said a lady to the mistress of the house. "Yes," re- plied the hostess, "one of them expresses too much burgundy ane the o het 30 much champagne." A cheer! u .emper converts almost every day into a festi- val. It sings the psalm of life even while toiling with ad- versities. It gives thanks for all that divine providence may send. It finds cause for gratitude among broken hopes. It draws strength while under burdens from the great heart of Him who pities and helps His needy children. The home is the sunniest side of every great people. Without devotion to home there can be no devotion to country. The home is the cradle of good citizenship and patriotism; it is the fountain of happiness, not only to indi- viduals, but to nations as well; and it is the one spot on earth that should be guarded from needless shadows. It was his first appearance at church; and, in order that he might sit perfectly still and keep his little chatter be- tween his teeth, he was told that a little dog would bite him if he didn't keep silence. The little fellow cast several glances up and down the aisle, and at last, just at the most, interesting part of the sermon, startled the congregation by piping out," Mamma, where is the dog ?" WIT AND WISDOM OF BENJAMIN DISRAELI, EARL OF BEACONSFIELD.—One excellence, and a great one, of Lord, Beaconsfield as a novelist is his mastery of apt and forcible dialogue. The talk in Mr. Henry James's novels is charm- ingly level and appropriate, but it is also trivial and a little thin; the talk of Mr. Anthony Trollope is surprisingly, natural and abundant, but it is also commonplace and im- memorable ; the talk of Mr. George Meredith is wonder- fully eloquent and fanciful, but its eloquence is too of tea obstare, and its fancifulness too often abnormal and in- human. The conversation in Lord Beaconsfield's work is more satisfactory. What his personages have to say is not always distinguished either by originality or by profundity, but it is clearly and crisply phrased and happily uttered, it reads well and is easily remembered, and it seldom fails to produce a permanent impression. It is as a kind of Talker's Guide, or Handbook of Conversation, that we wish to re- commend the present volume. The compiler has done his work, which was evidently a labour of love, with judgment and discretion in the main; he has worked through his author's writings and speeches, from "Vivian Grey" to the discourse to the Lords in March of the present year; and his volume contains the most characteristic utterances of a great and successful artist in life, who was renowned for good and characteristic speech. Occasionally, it must be owned, there are disappointments. Now and then the writ- ing is bad, and the thought is stale. Lord Beaconsfield had many mannerisms, innate and acquired. His English was sometimes loose and inexpressive; he was apt to trip in his grammar, to stumble over "and which," and to be careless about the connexion between his nominatives and his verbs. Again, he could scarcely ever refrain in description from the use of gorgeous commonplaces of sentiment and diction. His taste was sometimes ornately and barbarically conven- tional • he wrote as an orator ; his phrases often read as if he had used them for the sake of their associations rather than their own. His works are a very mine of such ex- pressions as "Palladian structure," " Tusculan repose," "Gothic pile," " pellncid brow," "mossy cell," and " dew- spangled meads." He delighted in " hyacinthine curls" and "lustrous locks," in "smiling parterres" and "stately terraces." He seldom sat down, in print, to anything less than a"bangnet ;" he was capable of writing of "the iris pencil of Hope ;" he could not think nor speak of the beauties of woman otherwise than as "charms." Of ex- amples of this style of composition the "Wit and Wisdom" of Lord Beaconsfield is fall. Now and then, too, we light upon truths that are obviously venerable truisms in new clothes. Thus Lord Roehampton's statement, "I believe that absence is of ten a great element of charm," is clearly a variation on our old friend, " 'Tis absence makes the heart grow fonder ;" while the origin of the description in " Endy- mien " of a "common rumour" as "probably common falsehood" is more base, common, and popular still. On the other hand, we have plenty of good wit and unmistak- able wisdom. Sometimes they came upon us disguised as impertinent and whimsical boutades : as when the author of 4' The Young Duke" reflects concerning wedlock that "it destroys a man's nerves to be amiable every day to the same human being ;" when he confesses that he "always looks —upon a long-sighted man as a brute who, not being able to see with his mind, is obliged to see with his body ;" and when he describes jockeys as "those mysterious characters who, in their influence over their superiors, and their total want of sympathy with their species, are our only match f.m- the Oriental eunuch." Sometimes the sentence is oracu- lar, as, for instance, "Women are the priestesses of Predes- t,nation," and the famous "Youth is a blunder. Manhood a on of Wordsworth, "Gentlemanly stneaegle, Old Age a regret." Alhambra's delicious descrip- 's own poetry," is in its way as asretandes la goomdana— and b tuetlli onngly solemn and unsexual man " of "Peter Bell the Third." Here is a reflection in another strain, the strain fthe great Bidonia: " Man is only great when he acts from the pas- sions; never irresistible but when he appeals to the imagi- nation. Even Mormon counts more votaries than Bentham." Here, in a nutshell, is the author's own story: "It is the personal that interests mankind, that frees their imagination and wins their hearts. A came is a great abstraction, and fit only for students; embodied in a party it stirs men to action ; but place at the head of a party a leader who can inspire enthusiasm, he commands the world." Waldershare imme up Whitman's theology in a couple of sentences: "One should never think of death, one should think of life. That is real piety." There is a whole these reflections from " Tancred i" "How full of adventure Is life! It is monotonous only to the monotonous." There is a fine theory of morals in this extract from "Contarini Fleming :" "Instead of love being the occasion of all the misery of this world, as is sung by fantastic bards, I believe th it the misery of this world is occasioned by there not big love enough." And in this sentence from "Lothair," A' When the British nation is at once grateful and enthusias- tic, they always call you'My Lord,'" there is the whole '4 Book 9f Snobs," plug gaol temper and a oleasant face.— Atheneum.

Of all the products ot the soil, none are so prolific in seeds as weeds; 80,000 seeds have been counted upon one mullein

stalk. At a meeting of the Union Assessment Committee at Backinghara, it was decided to make a general reduction of 15 per cent. on the whole of the land in the Union. iThe value of farms in the United States is 11,000,000,000 &nail; and the annual product 43,000,000,000 dollars. in four years, therefore, the farm products equal the value

of the nftinilea few. sualiowers tor your poultry. They may be sown any time after the 10th of May. The mammoth Russian ißthe largest said most productive variety. A single flower will produce a large quantity of seed. Although it well repays care, it may be grown along fences where other plants are not WO cultivated. Leave one fences, on a hill. The seeds are otdcent for stock as well as for poultry; the leaves may be fed green to cattle, and the stalks will serve to light the kitchen fire.

The following is a good method of storing eggs: Having selected perfectly fresh eggs, put them, a dozen or more at a time, into a small willow basket, and immerse this for five seconds into boiling water containing about five pounds of common brown sugar per gallon of water. Place the eggs immediately after on trays to dry. The scalding water causes the formation of a thin skin of hard albumen next the inner surface of the shell, the sugar effectually closing all the pores of the latter. The cool eggs are then packed small end down, in an intimate mixture of one measure of good charcoal, finely powdered, and two measures of dry wan. Eggs thus stored have been found perfectly fresh and naltered after six months. THE TREATMENT OF SHORTHORNS.—"I see," says "R.," in the Agricultural Gazette," that Mr. Naden has got hold of the fallacy that shorthorns are daintily fed, and have extraordinary care taken of them. At Holker, Underley, and the many herds that have hitherto come under my knowledge, I have never seen anything beyond what a far- mer might bestow upon good dairy stock, if he but did his duty to them. They were all out at grass, the in-calf 4,300 guinea Duchess of Bathurst sth included, and they are not allowed even the luxury of a bed of straw when in the shippon. Duchess sth has bred a heifer calf (sold at the last sale for 2,000 gs.) and a bull calf, and is now three months of due to calve. I saw the heifer that was shown at the "Royal." Of course she had been prepared to show what could be done at eighteen months old. Had she been as good behind as she is before, she would have proved trou- blesome to the winners. The next process with her will be one of reduction, for breeding. That many heifers are irre- trievably ruined for breeding by show feeding I know; like the paint and tinsel of the showyard implements, it is the price we have to pay for knowledge and notoriety." THE MAYINO OF CONDENSED MILE.—The milk the , Aylesbury Company receives is supplied by eighty-two farmers, who live within an area of eight or nine miles. The price paid for the milk is 63. 6d. per 100 lbs. in summer and Bs. 4d., or id. per lb. in winter. The process of " con- densing " the milk is of the simplest possible character. It is merely that of exhausting by heat the water it contains. This is done by using what are termed "hooded vacuum pans." These are steam jacketted at the bottom, and coils of copper pipe are also placed in the bottom of the pans. Then there is a large pipe leading from the top of the "vacuum pan," applied to which is an air pump. This air pump is so effective in carrying off the steam which rises from the milk, and in lightening the pressure of the air in the "vacuum pans,",that the milk boils from 12in. to 15in. In height instead of the Gin, to 9in. that it would do under ordinary atmospheric pressure. Thus the water of the milk, in the form of vapour, is carried off twice or thrice as rapidly as it would be in an open boiler under ordinary at- mospheric pressure. So rapid is this exhaustion of vapour or steam that, in looking through the pane of glass, which is on one side of each "vacuum pan," the boiling milk is more distinctly visible than it would be in an open boiler. The milk is received by weight, as we have intimated. On its arrival it is raised from the carts or vans, then examined as regards its sweetness. If it be in the slightest degree sour it is rejected; then it is placed in warm water to raise its temperature to a given degree. Then the sugar is added, and subsequently it is placed in the " hooded vacuum pq.nsi," to have its superfluous water exhausted as described. Cows' MILK.—An interesting paper has lately been pub- lished by Professor C. A. Cameron, in the July number of the Scientific Proceedings of the Royal Dublin Society, on "The Composition of the Milk of Cows." Daring the winter quarter of 1880, analyses were made of the milk of 42 cows, which were kept at the Government agricultural institution known as the Albert Farm, at Glasnevin, in the county of Dublin. The morning's and the evening's milk of each cow were each analysed once, and an examination of the mixed milk of the 42 cows was also made on the 11th of December, 1880. The cows were, as might be expected, good animals, having from one to three crosses of the short- horn breed. They were in the house during the period Of the experiments ; their food consisted of a daily allowance of about nine stone of pulped mangolds and turnips, with exhausted brewery grains, together with about one stone of I hay. Their ages ranged from four to nine years inclusive. Dividing them into two groups—those aged four and five years, and those aged eight and nine years—a marked dif- ference in favour of the milk of the latter, both in quantity and quality, was noticed. This, however, might easily be accounted for by the process of artificial selection ; for, while it is only good [hitch cows that would be kept in the dairy for several years, the younger ones proved not to be good milkers, would be put into the fattening stalls. The belief that milk becomes deteriorated in quality towards the end of lactation was not supported by these experiments. The quantity naturally became scanty, but the quality im- proved. The average yield of milk was for each cow. la ,quarts:, In every instance the quantity of milk yielded in the morning exceeded the proportion furnished in the evening, eight hours intervening between the milking'. Thirty out of the 42 cows gave richer milk in the evening , than in the morning ; 11 gave richer milk in the morning I than in the evening, while the remaining cow's milk was equally good at both milkings. The increase in the amount ' Of solid matters in the evening's milk was chiefly due to , the larger amount of fats contained in the latter. The results ' of these analyses showed that the milk of well-fed cows in ' houses in the last quarter of the year contains, when poorest, I 13 90 per cent, of solid matter, including 4-20 per cent. of fats. The Society of Public Analysts of Great Britain and Ireland have adopted as a standard for the poorest pure milk 9 per cent, of solids, minus fats, and 2-5 per cent. of fats—a total of 11.5 per cent. of solids. While there is little doubt that milk containing less than this percentage of solids is watered or skimmed, still these analyses show that, ,so far as Ireland is concerned, the solids minus fats may be In pure milk less than 9 per cent. A more exact average would be 8.5 per cent. CATTLE Mar...ans.—Dr. Pasteur has been endeavouring to convince the world that nine-tenths of the diseases to which man and the lower animals are subject must be traced to the fructification of the microscopic spores of organisms floating in the air. To ascertain the cause of a disease is, however, only a step to its cure, or, still better, to its preveetion. To this aspect • of his researches Dr. Pasteur, aided—some say preceded—by M. Tottsiaint, of Toulouse, has been recently devoting his attention, with results the importance of which it is difficult to over-estimate. It has, of course, long been known that if a person has once suffered from certain dis- eases he is virtually proof against a second attack. Dr. Pasteur discovered that by inoculating fowls with the virus I of chicken cholera he could save the birds from an attack of that disease, which so generally proves fatal. But, com- pared with the ravages of Siberian fever among cattle, the loss by chicken cholera scarcely deserves notice. This ter- rible. animal plague, known in France as " charbon," in Russia as" Siberian pest," in Germany as " milzbrand," and in England as "splenic fever," is every year destructive of an. immense number pf oxen, sheep, horses, and even human beings. In one small Prussian district £9,000 was lost by the death of sheep from this disease. The country around Novgorod, in Russia, lost in three years 56,000 horses and cattle and 528 human beings, and in France alone the damage from its ravages is computed to average twenty million francs per annum. Hitherto, it has I been considered incurable and unpreventible. It is, however, invariably noticed that in the blood of animals buffering from this disease there are small transparent frods visible under the microscope, and ,known as the bacillus anthracis, and at a later date the round spores or propagating bodies of that organism. These constitute the I elements of contagion, and so virulent is the disease that they will preserve their vitality long after the carcase of the animal which they have destroyed has been buried under ground. Pasteur has utilised this knowledge in a most beneficial direction. Applying the facts known as to the chicken cholera to splenic fever, he inoculated healthy ani- mals with a prepared virus, containing the fatal bacillus, but capable of producing the disease in milder forms. The result was that while the animals which were not inoculated died, those which were inoculated resisted the infection. The immediate and practical bearing of this research is of course apparent. It will have the effect of saving to the world food supplies of which the money value is comparable to the cost of the most ruinous modern war. If Dr. Pasteur's method of preparing an artificial but "attenuated" virus of a disease is applicable to all the zymotic ills that flesh is heir to, a vista opens out before us the end of which it is impossible to see. To the grazier the researches of Pasteur are of the utmost immediate importance; for if by inocula- tion splenic fever can be prevented, there ought to be no- thing to prevent foot and mouth and the other zymotic .1 plagues being warded off in a similar manner.—Standard. pa-s-

The Louisville authorities have resolved to put down gambling and rowdyism, even if they had to arrest every policeman in the force. A boyish novice in smoking turned deadly pale, and threw away his cigar. Said he, "That's something in that air .cigar that's made me sick." "I know what it is," said his companion puffing away. "What ?" " Tobacker." "Don't waste your time in cutting off the branches," said the woodman to his son, " but lay your axe at the root of the tree." And the young man went out and laid his axe at the root of the tree, like a good and dutiful boy, and then went fishing. Truly, there is nothing like filial obedi- dience. How TO BATICE.—The mere fact of immersing the body in water, whether salt or fresh, has no magic power for good. As a matter of physical experience, bathing causes loss of bodily heat, which his rarely if ever desirable. People generally make great mistakes as to the use of baths 'and bathing. It seldom happens that an ordinary bath cleanses the skin, which should be the primary purpose. For the rest, no possible good can be done by merely bury- ing the surface of the body in water. As to the idea that ' the salt of the sea acts on the skin, that is a flimsy notion, resting on very insufficient premises ; and if it were true, a sponging with salt water would be better than bathing in the sea. The truth is, the value of a bath is in proportion to its effect as an agent producing reaction. There may be , cases in which the abstraction of heat by bathing in cold ' , water would do good. We know there are such cases, but they are not, as a rule, to be found among the multitudes who bathe. For the purpose of lowering the temperature of the body, cold bathing must be used under medical direc- tion, and it is improbable that a practitoner desiring to employ this remedy would order his patient to "bathe," in the ordinary sense of the term. It may therefore be repeated that the use of bathing is to produce reaction, and act as a stimulant to the circulation, especially at the sur- face of the body and in the skin. This should be borne in mind, and it will be at once perreived that there is nothing but evil in prolonging the bath beyond a very brief dura- tion. As soon as the surface is cooled, the bather should quit the water, and, rubbing the skin briskly with a rough towel, bring back the blood, and produce the redness and the glow of health. The actual length of time which a bather may remain in the water should be determined by the exercise he is able to take while in it. If he can throw his muscular system into vigorous action, so as to maintain his heat, the exercise will do him good, and in a few minutes he may secure as good a constitutional as he could get by a brisk walk, or a gallop, or a game of cricket ; but unless he I can thus work to make heat, he is simply throwing away heat, which he may not readily replace, every moment he remains in the bath. Many weakly but fairly healthy per- sons do themselves great harm by bathing frequently, and under the mistaken impression that remaining in the water is in itself healthfdl. This idea should be cast aside as erroneous and misleading. The only safe rule for the ordinary bather is to regard the bath as a means of pro- moting the circulation of his blood. If he finds that when he comes out of the water he is warmer than when he went in, he is benefited. If he is colder, the bath has done him no good. It may not perchance have done him serious harm, but it has certainly done no good, and a risk has been run by taking it, while the loss of heat entailed has been a waste of power. This power may be replaced ; but if it is, there will need to be an expenditure of strength in some subsequent exercise which had better have been turned to profitable account on land, instead of being simply devoted to the repair of an injury inflicted in the nursuit of health.

In the very highest grades of high society, men are wear- ing bracelets. It is thought that they go well with nice clean linen cuffs. An exalted personage sets the example, and he has already had a host of imitators. THE WEATHER AND THE ENGLISH HARVEST.—The Mark Lane Express says that evidence from all parts of the coun- try proves that the wet weather of the past week has brought disaster and ruin to the British harvest of 1881. The accouchment of Mrs. William Laird, of Birkenhead, during the mayoralty of her husband, is likely to result in the presentation of a silver cradle. This is the first event of the kind in Birkenhead. Three English ladies ascended Ben Nevis last Wednesday without a guide. They lost their way in returning, and were compelled to pass the night on the mountain in heavy rain and hail. They were found on Thursday morning at the top of a steep ravine by two guides sent out to search for them. The fair mountaineers were much exhausted. Thick snow fell on Ben Nevis on Tuesday. The Press Association is informed that the Government have decided to maintain the Irish garrison at its present present strength daring the winter. It is proposed that for the present the cavalry regiments shall remain at the Cape, and the 7th Hussars, in addition" to the Inniskilling , Dragoons, are likely to be told off to form part of the garri- son of Natal until further orders. A FATAL QUARREL—An inqsest was held on Tuesday at Birmingham on the body of Thomas Bodfish. A few days ago the deceased quarrelled with his lodger, named Smith. It was alleged that Smith, with some blut instrument, struck Bodfish several blows on the head, from the effects of which he died. A verdict of manslaughter was returned against Smith, who was committed to take his trial at the assizes. A large meeting of the burgesses of the borough of Newark was held' on Saturday night for the purpose of adopting the Free Libraries Acts in order to prepare the way for accepting the handsome offer of Mr. W. Gilstrop, of Fornham Park, to build a free public library, stock it with hooks, and provide for a custodian, as a gift to his native town. Resolutions determining to adopt the acts and tender- ing hearty thanks to the donor were passed. At a special meeting of the Watch Committee on Satur- day, Major Bond, chief of the police for Birmingham, who for some time has been in antagonism with the authorities of the town, in reply to a resolution passed at the last meet- ing of the council expressed his willingness to obey the instructions of the committee. Under the circumstances, the council will not press their resolution calling upon him to resign. ATTEMPT TO BLOW UP A HOUSE WITH DYNAMITE.—A carefully-prepared attempt was made early on Sunday morn- in, to destroy the house of John Ford, herb beer maker, of Broxwich, by means of dynamite. A quantity of this ex- plosive with fuse attached was thrown on the top of a porch at the front door. The explosion greatly damaged the premises and caused great alarm, the noise being heard for two miles around, but no one was injured. The motive of the outrage is a mystery. THE MACCLESFIELD COMMISSION: REMOVAL OF MAGlS- TRATES.—Considerable anxiety has been felt in Macclesfield as to the fate of the borough magistrates scheduled for bribery by the Royal Commissioners. The Lord Chancellor sent for the Commission of the Peace on the 11th of August, and on Monday the result was telegraphed. Four Conser- vatives and one Liberal are removed from the Bench, namely, Mr. W. C. Brocklehurst, Mr. George Godwin, Mr. John gtringer, Mr. Anthony Hordern, and Mr. Thomas Crew, SUDDEN DEATH OF A TOWN COUNCILLOR.—Mr. W. S. Spivey, member of the Carmarthen town council, died very suddenly on Tuesday morning. He was proceeding to the council meeting, then being held, when within the precincts of the Guildhall, he fell down and died within five minutes of heart disease, amidst the consternation of his colleagues, whose meeting terminated abruptly. The deceased, who came from the neighbourhood of Huddersfield, had resided in Carmarthen 25 years, and had been a councillor for three years. He was a widower with a large youeg family. SHOCKING OUTRAGE IN LIVERPOOL.—At the Liverpool police court, on Monday, a man named Thomas Hackett was charged with assaulting his wife. It was shown that the prisoner lived at No. 6, Solomon-street, Liverpool, and on Saturday night was illtreating his wife in their bedroom when the woman lifted up the window sash for the purpose of calling in the police. Whilst doing this Hackett went to her and gave her a push which caused her to fall through the window. She fell on the pavement a distance of 14ft. on her head. She was taken to the Royal Infirmary, where she lies in a critical condition, suffering from concussion of the brain. The prisoner was remanded for a week. A FORTUNE SUNK IN A ComEny.—One of the costliest colliery speculations in Durham was closed on Saturday by the sale of the loose plant of Mainsforth Colliery. For over six years sinking operations were carried on. A shaft was sunk eight years ago, which from the nature of the strata was given up, and another a few hundred yards to the north, and close to Ferry Hill Station, and for scores of fathoms sinking was proceeded with, several seams of coal being wen. But the treacherous strata—the colliery being on the magnesian limestone—and the heavy " feeders " of water met with made the cost enormous, and the dulness that set in in the coal trade compelled the closing of the colliery after a fortune had been spent in the sineing. NEW MARKETS FOR ENGLISH MANUFACTURERS. —Mr. Hibbert, M.P., having been written to by the secretary of the Oldham Trades Council on the subject of opening fresh markets for the products of the country, says With respect to the suggestion, I need not say that I shall be very pleased if the Government as well as Parliament is able to devote more of its time to the consideration of English and Scotch questions than has been possible during the present session, and, looking at the present state of the trade of the United Kingdom, I am sure that no question is of more pressing importance than that of finding new markets for our manufacturers. I am told by Mr. Chamberlain, to whom I have shown your letter, that the Government is quite alive to this necessity, and that, while not despairing of the re- newal of a satisfactory treaty with France, it is also hopeful of being able to enter upon better commercial relations with Italy, Spain, and Portugal." The delegates of the various branches of the National Land League of Great Britain met on Monday at Newcastle- on-Tyne for the first time in convention, under the presi- dency of Mr. Justin M‘Carthy, M.P. Upwards of 120 branches were represented. The whole of the sitting was devoted to revising the provisional constitution of the League, which had been drafted and was in force until the assembly of the convention. The rules adopted pledged those joining the League to pay such subscriptions annually as their branch might determine upon, one shilling at least per member to go the League, and any balance beyond local expenses to be under the eontrol of the executive. A reso- lution was passed expressing "love and admiration for Michael Devitt, the founder of the Land League movement." A resolution of sympathy with Mr. A. M. Sullivan, M.P., in his illness was also passed. A public meeting was held in the evening, at which Mr. Cowen, M.P., was the principal speaker. The hon. gentleman warmly denounced the "coer- cive policy" of the Government with regard to Ireland. Mr. BRADTAUGH.—Mr. Bradlangb is about to issue a mani- festo entitled "Right against Brute Force." He says 300 public meetings, attended by 350,000 persons, and 1,088 peti- tions with 175,000 signatures, have endorsed his claim. He contends that the house has no right to go behind the return of April 9, and that the Conservatives affirmed this in 1880. He charges Sir Stafford Northcote with having deliberately broken his word in blocking the bill introduced by the Government to extend the right of affirmation. He has never introduced his religious heresies into his political speeches. The Government has made no definite promise to see the law obeyed; it has only promised to consider what it will do. Its duty is to enforce the law, even for the meanest, the most unpopular, the most obnoxious. In the war against him, the Conservative party have broken through all rules of decency or honour, and of truth. Even his daughters are not safe from the as-ailment of a parliamentary coward like Sir Henry Tyler. Law proceedings have been multiplied to ruin him, and he can only ask justice from the people. Montwore Paosneamsar —That the Mormons are unceas- ing and untiring in their efforts to attract recruits to their agapemone at Salt Lake is pretty well known, and that they are tolerably successful is obvious to anyone who has crossed f rom San Francisco to New York and met the ' crowded trains of misguided creatures on their way to the Mormon Eden. Some of the modes practised by the elders to obtain proselytes are peculiar, as will be seen from the following letter recently addressed to a young married lady: --Dear Sister,—I have been informed by a brother and a Mormon elder that yon are willing to join the Church of Latter Day Saints, and to proceed to Salt Lake City. I shall be most happy to enter your name on our list as one of our fold. By the outgoing next San Francisco mail there will be a number of our brethren and sisters belonging to the Church of Latter Day Saints proceeding to the Tabernacle at Utah. If you will therefore hold yourself in readiness to proceed there with them, I will make arrangements with you to settle any little debts you may owe in Wellington, and likewise to make you an advance in money for what- ever you may require; so if you will please communicate with me at your earliest convenience, I shall be pleased to hear from you. I therefore, dear sister, subscribe myself, in the bonds of spiritual and brotherly love, your loving brother, George P. Sorensen, Chief of Council and Chief Elder of the Brigham Young Tabernacle, Salt Lake City, Utah, America, and may the blessing of the departed Joseph Smith be with you for ever and ever. IMPORTANT To MEMBERS OF FRIENDLY SOCIETIES.—At the Oswestry county court, on Saturday, beim% Mr. Arun- dale Rogers, two cases affecting the members of most friendly societies were heard. The defendants were the trustees of the Working Men's Lodge (Oswestry district) of the Grand United Order of Oddfellows and the secretary of the Philanthropic Lodge of Independent Order of Odd. fellows. The actions were brought to recover a funeral al- lowance and for sick pay, which the defendant lodges refused to pay, on the ground, in one case, that the member claiming had been expelled for misrepresenting his age when entering, and also because he had been convicted of a criminal offence; and in the second case, on the ground that the claimant Was not entitled to sick pay until he had paid certain fines standing in the books of the society against him, and aleo the expenses of an arbitration case between himself and the society. On behalf of the societies, it was contended that the judge had no jurisdiction in these cases, , the rules of the several lodges, the district rules, and the ! general rules of the order all providing that such disputes l should be settled by arbitration. After a lengthy argument, th ' his Honour held at he had jurisdiction in such cases, and expressed it as his opinion that the proper parties to initiate arbitration proceedings in these disputes were the societies and not the claimants, and that where this course was not pursued the claimants bad a perfect right to appeal to the law. A verdict was given for the plaintiff in each case. An ii plic for leave to appeal was made, and acceded to.

BARROW-IN-FrRNESS,MONDAY.—The meeting on 'Change this morning was poorly attended, and no business was transacted in iron or steel. During the week a steady in- quiry was experienced for all qualities of hematite, and particularly for Bessemer descriptions. There is no scarcity of orders, and makers have in every instance a large amount of work in hand. It is well known that there is a heavy tonnage of iron and steel, the latter in the shape of both blooms and railway material, to be shipped this year, but at the present moment very little shipping is being done. Prices of iron and steel remain as quoted last week, their being a margin of from 565. to 60s. for Bessemer and forge qualities. Shipbuilders are exceedingly well off for orders, and engineers are active. LANCASHIRE, Wednesday.—The exceptionally inclement weather lately experienced has naturally tended to produce activity in the house-fire coal trade, and to this extent a slight improvement is noticeable in the coal trade of this district. The increased demand for house-fire classes of fuel has enabled collieries to work rather more than of late; and in the Manchester district, where the pits have all along been kept fully employed, stocks have been going down in lessened quantities. There is, however, still an absence of any presure for supplies, which continued plentiful in the market. Common round coals also continued if anything in rather better demand, but manufacturing requirements gene- rally are still only limited as compared with the means of production throughout the district. Prices are without appreciableimprovement, and although there is not quite so much underselling as recently, coal lying in stock continues to be offered at very low figures. Quotations are without change from last week, and at the pit mouth may be given about as under : Best coal, Bs. to Bs. 6d. ; seconds, 6s. to 7s; and common coals for steam and ironmaking purposes, 55. to ss. 3d. per ton. A fair demand is maintained for engine classes of fuel, but in view of increasing requirements for screened coal, which will necessarily bring more slack into the market, prices are showing a tendency towards weakness. Although there has been no general giving way on the part of colliery proprietors, sellers are to be found here and there at under late rates, with lower quotations being made for September deliveries. Good burgy at the pit ranges from 4s. to 4s 6. per ton, and good slack can be bought at from I 3s. 3d., with the best sorts ranging up to 4s. per ton. There is still only a limited amount of businessdoing for shipment and 6s. 6d. to 7s. per ton remains about the average price for steam coal delivered at Liverpool and Garston. Coke is in fair demand at late prices. In the iron trade business has been dull during the past week, and pig iron especially still meets with very little inquiry. Makers, however, who are still mostly kept busy with deliveries on account of con- tracts which in some cases will see them over the next two or.three months, are not as a rule disposed to push sales at present; but to secure new business concessions upon late rates are generally necessary, and a few makers who are not so well supplied with orders are begining to quote lower prices. Lancashire makers of pig iron continue firm at 445. to 455. per ton, less 4. for forge and foundry qualities de- livered into the Manchester district; and although very little new business is being secured at these figures, offers made during the week at less money have been declined. In out- side brands there is still practically little or nothing doing except in Lincolnshire irons, and in some cases these are being offered at under late rates, but the average quotations for delivery equal to Manchester remain at 435. 6d. to 445. 6d, less 4, for forge and foundry numbers. In the finished iron trade makers continue very buisy, and are firm at fully late rates, bars delivered into the Manchester district being quoted at £6 2s. 6d., hoops £6 12s. 6d. to £6 155., and sheets £7 15s. to £8 per ton. The work in hand is, however, chiefly iu competing orders, the bulk of which are for shipment, fresh inquiries are now coming in but slowly, and the home demand shows but little sign of improvement. Tool makers generally are busy, and engineers are kept fairly going on low priced work. A fair quantity of fire-proof iron work is being given out for mill construction, partly in cast-iron columns and beams, which is giving moderate employment to some of the local foundries, and partly in rivetted plate girders and rolled iron joists.

div.head: TRADE NOTES
div.p: TRADE NOTES

At a conference of the Lancashire Miners' Federation,held in Wigan on Tuesday, it was resolved "That we commence at once to agitate for an advance in wages, and that the representatives report to their respective districts to be pre- pared to ask for an advance on the Ist October." On Wednesday, the Ruabon colliers working at the Wynn- stay Collieries, belonging to the New British Iron and Coal Company, resumed work, after a fortnight's strike, which issued from a dispute with the employers on account of the men having not only to load their coal but to convey it afterwards to the main roads. The men required that the masters should employ boys to convey the coals from the wickets after they had filled the tubs. This the masters objected to do, but have arranged to give them additional pay for bringing out the coal.

rHE QUEEN'S SPEECH. HOUSE OF LORDS.—SELTURDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at 25 minutes to two, when the only peers present were the Earl of Cork and Lord Carington and the Bishop of St. David's, who read prayers. Lord Milltown afterwards entered the House and took his seat on the Opposition benches. The Lord Chancellor retired after prayers, and soon after- wards returned with the Lords Commissioners, who were Earl Spencer, the Earl of Cork, Lord Kenmare, and Lord Monson. Their Lordships were habited in their scarlet and ermine robes. The Royal assent was given by Commission to the following bills : The Appropriation Act, the Leases for Schools (Ireland) Statute Law Revision and Civil Pro- cedure, Veterinary Surgeons, Expiring Law Continuance, Central Criminal Court (Pr;sons), Regulation of the Forces, India Office Auditors, the Newspaper Libel and Registration, Sunday Closing (Wales), Irish Church Act Amendment, Fugitive Offenders, Highways and Locomotives Act Amend- ment, Army, Pollen Fishing (Ireland), Supreme Court of Judicature, Petroleum Hawking,. Erne Lough and River, and Solent Navigation. The Commission having been read, The LORD CHANCELLOR read the Royal Speech, which , was as follows :
My LORDS and GENTLEMEN, The time has airived when lam at length enabled to release you from your unusually severe and protracted labours.

My relations with all foreign powers continue to be amicable and cordial. Progress has been made since I last addressed you in the territorial arrangements of the Levant. A treaty has been concluded with the sanction of all the great powers for the cession of Thessalis to the Greek Kingdom, and its peaceful execution has begun.

Recent events in Tunis have led to communications between my Government and the Government of France, and I have received satisfactory assurances from the Re- public as to the rights secured to me with the Bey,and as to the relations between the Regency and the neighbouring Ottoman territory of Tripoli. The Convention has been signed, which :secures the European population of the Transvaal, subject to important conditions therein set forth, a complete international self- government. It awaits ratification by a representative as- sembly of the people. I trust that when compared it will contribute effectually to the tranquility of South Africa and to stability in its affairs. The hopes in which I indulged on the last occasion of my addressing you, with respect to the war in Basutoland, have been fulfilled, and I have to notice with much satis- faction the cessation of hostilities in that country. In the month of April my troops were withdrawn from Candahar, and the Government of Southern Afghanistan assumed by the Ameer, Abdur Rahman. I have no reason to anticipate any disturbance of the peace on the north-western frontier of my Indian dominiohs from the contest with the Ameer, which Ayoub Khan has since entered into. It will be my , object, while respecting the independence of the Afghan people, to promote by my friendly offices, as opportunity I may arise, the restoration of peace. GENTLEMEN of the HOUSE of COMMONS. I thank you for the supplies which you have provided to meet public charges, and for the contribution you have liberally made towards the expenses of the recent war in Afghanistan. ' MY LORDS and GENTLEMEN,

There is no "royal road" to becoming a good mechanical engineer. The genius part of the business is for the most part a humbug. Being a genius generally means having the ability and the willingness to work hard. Let no young n who has an honest liking for his vocation be discouraged at not " seeing into things" as readily as he would like to. All this will come by application and perseverance.—Design and Work. The telephone, as is well known, will reveal currents of electricty which are so feeble as not to be discoverable by ordinary naeans. A French savant announces that the heat necessary to warm a kilogramme of water one degree would, If converted properly into the energy of electric currents, suffice to produce in a telephone an audible sound for ten thousand years continuously. Whe can prove that it would not ?—Design and Work. "It's all right to say that George Washington never told a lie," remarked a thoughtful American mining-superinten- dent. "I don't say he did; but he lived in a time when that wasn't hard for a man to accomplish. If George were alive now and running my mine, and had to write a weekly ' letter reporting progress, I'm inclined to think he'd wrap crape around his little hatchet and put it away where the i l historian of the future wouldn't be likely to.find t. i On one occasion, while still without the bar, the late Sir Alexander Cockburn had to examine a witness named Phinn, and asked, " Well, sir, how do they spell your name—with an For a Ph?" "Some spell it one way and some another, I believe," said the man. " Yes ; but I presume there is the right and wrong way, eh ?" "Oh, certainly," assented np,,,no,w, Ocher,tla_in the ehwisitcinueesrsy. . ' Very'"H owgdooGd" you, r esjpei int e idt Cy keo tic kr sbeut rf I—l don't spell it; I always make my mark !" Cockburn sat down defeated. MIXED.—Two babies were beim in the same house at Oak- land, Tenn. The mothers were sisters, closely resembling each other, and the infants wore both girls. In the excite- ment of the occasion the little ones got mixed, and this hap- pened before they had been dressed, or in any other way iked for identification. There seems to be no way out of , the uncertainty, for three months have passed without de- I veloping any resemblance to the father in either case; and if the children grow up, as they seem likely to, with no phy- sical characteristic of their mothers, nobody will ever know their exact parentage. The agreement is to decide the question by lot. THE WARMTH OF DIFFERENT COLOURS OF CLOTH.— Professor Elliot some time ago wrote :—As to the question whether a white dress or a black dress is the cooler, that has ' already been pretty well ascertained by experiment. If any one will take the trouble to cover the snow, during sunshine, with two pieces of cloth of the same kind, but one black, the other white, he will see that the snow melts first under the black. If he spread out the same two pieces under a clear sky by night, and place a thermometer under each, he will find that which is under the black cloth fall most rapidly, and sink lowest. Over the cold ground, therefore, the black cloth is warmer than the white in sunshine, but colder in frost. It would be different, however, if the ground were hot below the cloth, that is, different in sunshine, but not in frost. If we take two teapots, exactly alike, except in colour, one black, the other white, and fill both with boiling water, the water in the black teapot will cool more rapidly than that in the white, even in the sun- shine. The result, however, will depend on the temperature of the water.—Textile Manufacturer. The commercial obligations with France have been sus- pended, but I continue desirous on every ground to use my best efforts for the conclusion of a treaty on terms favourable to extend intercourse between the two nations to whose close amity I attach so great a value. The Act for the regulation of the forces gives full legis- lative effect to the plans approved by Parliament for connecting regiments with the districts in which they will be mainly raised, and for combining together more closely the several branches of my land forces. This completion of the series of arrangements adopted by a former Parliament cannot fail to render more efficient the military organisation of the country.

I warmly appreciate the zeal and assiduity with which you have devoted yourselves to the task of maturing a measure for improving the relations between the owners and occupiers of land in Ireland, and for otherwise bettering the condition of its agricultural population. It is my earnest hope that the new Land Law may be productive of benefit's commensurate with the care you have bestowed upon its enactments. I regret that it has been found impossible to proceed with many measures on subjects of importance which have been, or were prepared to be, submitted to .you, and that notwithstanding exertions almost unparallelled, you have been unable adequately to provide the country ' with legislation adapted to its growing wants. It has been my study to use the exceptional powers confided to me in Ireland by two Acts of this Session with vigilance and firm- ness, but with discrimination. I earnestly desire that the condition of that country may so improve as to enable me to dispense with or abate the use of temporary and excep- tional provisions. Finally, I ask you to join me in imploring the blessing of the Almighty on our unitel efforts for the peace, greatness and happiness of the Empire. The Royal Commission for the prorogation of Parliament having been read, The LORD CHANCELLOR, in Her Majesty's name and at her Royal command, declared Parliament prorogued until the 12th of November. Thus was brought to a close the second session of the 10th Parliament of Her Majesty the Queen. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—SATURDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at ten minutes before two o'clock. On the motion of 'Baron HENRY DE WORMS, a new writ was ordered to be issued for Cambridgeshire for the election of a member of Parliament in the room of Mr. Rodwell, who had accepted the stewardship of the Chil tern Hundreds. Eight questions stood on the notice paper, principally re- lating to Irish affairs, but before that part of the business had been reached, and while Sir Joseph M'Kenna was giving notice of a motion for next session, Black Rod appeared, and summoned the House to the House of Lords to hear the Royal assent given to several bills, and for the prorogation of the session. The Speaker,accompanied by 30 or 40 members, proceeded to the House of Lords. They returned about a quarter of an hour afterwards, and, the members present having shaken hands with the Speaker, the session was brought to a close.

div.head: CITESIIIRE SOCIETY'S AGRICULTURAL SHOW.
div.p: CITESIIIRE SOCIETY'S AGRICUL- TURAL SHOW.

The annual show of horses, live stock, butter, and the like, promoted by the Cheshire Agricultural Society, was held on Tuesday at Sandbach, under most unfavourable , climatic conditions, but was nevertheless attended by a fair number of persons. Sandbach was last visited by the Society in 1870, when the total number of entries was 375, made up as follows: Farms 6, cheese and butter 43, cattle 39, pigs 38, horses 77, sheep 88, seeds and vegetables 31, servants and labourers 34, cottage tenants 5, implements 7. This year the entries numbered 360, but a comparison of the figures generally makes it apparent that, though falling a little below that of 1870 in point of numbers, this year's show is really the more representative and interesting. One feature af the gathering of 1870 has now altogether ceased, viz., that of servants and labourers, so that a diminution of over 30 entries is at once accounted for. Then in the sheep and seeds and vegetable classes there is a falling off of some 70 exhibits, but as regards farms, cheese and butter, pigs, cottage tenants, implements, and notably cattle and horses, there are increases, the statistics being: ' : Farms, 9 • cheese and butter, 44; cattle, 91; pigs, 49; arses, 99; sheep, 37 ; seeds and vegetables, 10; farm produce, 2; cottage tenants, 6; implements, 13. Last year no independent show was held by the society, who joined with the Manchester and Liverpool Society in rendering successful their gathering at Crewe; but at the exhibition of the previous year the entries overtopped these of Tuesday by more than 150, numbering no less than 522. This is, however, pretty well accounted for by the two facts that the show of 1879 was held at the county town, Chester, and that it extended over two days. An interesting table has been issued with respect to the re- ceipts at the showyard since the establishment of the society. From this it appears that for the fourteen years from 1839 to 1852, inclusive, the receipts were £338 155., being an average of £24 3s. nid. per annum. The society's de- velopement is sufficiently evidenced by the succeeding figures in the tabular statement, which are to the effect that for the 25 years from 1853 to 1879—omitting 1866, when, owing to the cattle plague, no show was held, and 18691 when the Royal Society's show was held at Man chester—the receipts amounted to £6,326 13s. 5d., or an average per annum of £253 Is. 4d. Returning to yester- day's show, it may with truth be said that, though it might fall below some of its more immediate predecessors in point of numbers, it was above the average as regarded the merit of its exhibits. The cheese, a most interesting department to Cheshire people, was by those who were competent to form a judgment upon the matter said lobe most excellent; and we believe it is the first time in the history of the society that what may be termed home-made cheese has gone down before the superior merit of the entry of a factory. Amongst the heavy horses wee some animals of great excellence, including Young Champion. the property of the Stand Stud Company. The riding horses constituted an exceptionally good show, and of the cattle the judges spoke in terms of high praise. The bulls of all ages were pronounced to be far better than are usually seen at local or even county shows, and the dairy stock met with general commendation. The amount offered in prizes was about £5OO. At a luncheon provided in a large tent on the show ground Mr. Randal Wilbraham, Rode Hall, presided, and amongst the gentlemen present were the Hon. William Egerton and Mr. J. H. Toilernache, the members for Mid-Cheshire. Re- sponding to the toast of "The County Members," the Hon. W. EGERTON, M.P., alluded to the loss which the county had sustained in the death of Sir Philip Egerton, and, refer- ring to the labours of himself and his colleagues, said that during perhaps the moat arduous session of Parliament on record, they had endeavoured by their attendance and votes to do what they could to promote the welfare of the country and the interests of their constituents. One of the few occasions on which he lifted up his voice in the House was when he endeavoured to promote the interests of farmers by putting pressure on foreign countries to make them exercise greater caution in allowing diseased animals to leave their shores. He thought the action of the Government, which I was influenced no doubt by the feelings of the agriculturists and the county members, certainly had a great effect in stopping in the first instance the spread of the foot and mouth disease by the cessation of markets. That, no doubt, was a very severe remedy, and one which many agricul- turists felt to be a great hardship and grievance, but he be- lieved that the bitter experience they had had in the last Council. nweeozseuutin,nnhpt enyi egeych iahHartesnoeydorahfeahagoedrtpehgsttivatsaep‘s.acpeaostatrhtgttrlaerietndi cdgiu.tienhsl nteeutaaorsmier s neighbours pee: rrisgosuavhlor lebef dsoc turat ietrshedi npossibleCommittee i tateyats et .1 evttt way fbdceei hlseteenats that mrtewiopnasist f e toi pl nye ue rmyo pn ae vaanl de n fto, tb uatndhemobneltihevdeidseatsheathaidn addressing n entirelyot t. h e p(Applause.)resent He felt was very difficult indeed to say to them any words of com- fort. The gentleman who proposed the toast to which he was responding said that farmers were in a very had way at the present time. He quite admitted that the English farmers had suffered a great deal more than the Irish farmers had done, and he was not surprised that the former were thinking why it was that Parliament had done so much for the Irish farmers and nothing for them. (Hear.) He did not believe that that which Parliament had done for Irish farmers English farmers would wish to see introduced into this country. He was of opinion that whatever diffi- culties farmers laboured under at the present time would be met first of all by those cordial relations between landlord and tenant—(applause)—under which whenever a season of difficulty arose the landlord had due regard to the interests of his tenants and would not sufer them to go wrong. (Applause.) No doubt there were many points upon which the legislature could benefit farmers; and he gave all credit to English farmers for the great patience which they had exhibited during the past four or five years of distress—distress brought upon them not by any fault of their own, but principally by the very bad seasons which Providence had sent us. He did not recommend the farmers to trust to anything but their own right hands and skill in farming. He did not think they must ex- I peel that Parliament would do a very great deal for them These were things that be thought Parliament could do, but. I he though they must look for better seasons really to restore the farmers' prosperity to what it was in former times. No one cruld look at the agricultural statistics of the last ten years without being struck with the very serious dimi- nution in the crops of this country, not only in wheat, but also in the animals raised. There had been a large diminu- tion in the number of sheep; and although of late years there had been a little reaction in favour of both horses and cattle, yet the corn raised throughout the country had diminished to such an extent that instead of our being supplied by our corn crops at home with three-fourths of our food, we had now to get from the foreigner more than half of the corn we used. That, of course, was not a satis- factory stite of things either for farmers or for the general consumers, the latter of whom would no doubt much rather spend their money at home among the English farmers than let it go to enrich people on the other side of the water. Whether Parliament could do anything in this matter it was perhaps at the present time premature to say, but that to which agriculturists must really look for a return of their prosperity, together with good crops, was the prosper- ity of the manufacturing districts of England. (Applause.) —Mr. H. J. ToLLEMACRE, also responded.

div.head: RECOGNITION SERYEES AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: RECOGNITION SERYEES AT ST. HELENS.

At the close collections were made on behalf of the Trust Fund. On the following evening a tea meeting was held in the scheol-room, when about 101) persons partook of a good tea. MINISTERIAL CHANGES AT Sr. HELENs.—The Rev. J. A. B. Harry, for three years the respected superintendent Wesleyan minister, preached his farewell sermon on Sun- day evening in the Corporation-street Chapel, but made no Special reference to his departure from the town. The sub- ject of his discourse was "Christ walking on the sea." On Thursday morning Mr. Harry, with his family, departed for Cardiff; and in the afternoon the new minister, the Rev. John N. Walmsley, arrrived, and was welcomed by many of the members of the church and congregation. Mr. Walmiley 18 an elderly gentleman, and his last place was Leeds.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1881.
PRESCOT POLICE INTELLIGECE.
?loNDA.Y.—Before Mr. W. L. Evans.

N HARD AND COLD BED.—Patrick Kelly was charged with being drunk on the previous day.—P.C. Prior deposed that about two o'clock on Sunday morning he found the prisoner asleep in a cart in the farmyard of Mrs. Watkinson, Longview-lane, Huyton. He awoke him, and found he was very drunk and unable to take care of himself. He took prisoner into custody and locked him up.—Prisoner was fined ss. and costs, but as he was unable to pay he was sent to gaol for seven days. • WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. W. L. Evans.

A DESERTER IN TROUBLE: STRANGE STORY. John Cox was charged with deserting from the 60th Rifles (Army Reserve) stationed at Cork.—Mr. Superintendent Barker said the prisoner was taken into custody for being a deserter from the Rifle Brigade. Prisoner was passing through the town and he ordered him to be brought into the station, where he gave the name of John Cox and his regimental number, and stated that he had been discharged from the 60th Rifle Brigade. He asked prisoner the name of the colonel of the brigade, and he replied " Colonel Anley," and said there was a "Major Crowder" in the same brigade who knew him. Witness wired to "Colonel Anley," but received a reply that no such person was known. He afterwards wired to "Major Crowder,' and got an answer that no such officer was known in the Rifle Brigade Corps. He afterwards sent a telegram to the adjutant of the brigade, who replied that no man of the name of the prisoner had been discharged from the Rifle Brigade or Fusiliers (Lancashire.) The prisoner had since made another statement to the effect that the uniform he was wearing belonged to his brother, who was a deserter.— Mr. Spencely said the prisoner had told a lie somewhere. He said one moment he was a deserter and then that the uniform he wore belonged to his. brother who was a deserter. —The prisoner said he was very sorry he did not tell the truth at first. His brother, who was a soldier, had deserted, and he and prisoner changed clothing. He was wearing the uniform which belonged to his brother.—He was sent to Walton as a deserter, there to await as escort.

div.head: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A ST.
div.p: SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A ST.
HELENS GROCER.

At the St. Helens Police Court, on Wednesday, before Lieutenant-Colonel Gamble, Thomas Worsley, a man between 30 and 40 years of age, recently in a good position in a grocer's shop in St. Helens, was charged with having on Sunday night, the 25th inst., stolen from Joseph Brownbill a silver lever watch, value £4.—Superintendent Johnston said that Brownbill left home on Sunday afternoon between I three and four o'clock, and went to Pre'scot, where he visited several public-houses and got drunk. The last he remem- bered of Prescot was leaving the King's Arms, about ten o'clock, with the watch in his possession. He remembered nothing more until getting home at Ravenhead, Sutton. His wife remembered him coming home without watch, the guard of which was in his pocket. When at Prescot the guard I was not properly fastened to the watch, but was " thread " through the ring of the watch. Prisoner offered the watch on Tuesday afternoon to pawn at Mr. Moxon's shop, and Mr. Moxon' s assistant, having had a description of the watch from the police, detained the prisoner and sent for a policeman. Prisoner WO then taken into custody. In answer to the charge made by the policeman, prisoner said a man named Jackson, residing at Haydock, had given him half-a-crown to pawn the watch. Prisoner further stated that he was at the Prescot Hotel on Sunday night at eleven o'clock, and was at St. Helens at twelve—about the time the watch was stolen —Joseph Brown bill, glassmaker, working at Ravenhead glassworks, and residing in Factory-row, Sot- ten, said he left home on Sunday afternoon between three and four o'clock, and went to Prescot. The last thing he remembered at Prescot was his leaving the King's Arms a few minutes to ten o'clock. A few minutes later he saw a man who worked at the same place as himself. He then looked at his watch, it being then five minutes past ten, and went on his way home. That was all he remembered until some time after he got home, where, his wife said, he reached about midnight. He was then without his watch, but the guard was in his pocket. The watch produced was his property, and was worth £4.--Prisoner: Did you see use anywhere on the road ?—Witness: No—Prisoner: J was in Prescot at eleven o'clock.—Herbert Moxon said he was an assistant to his father, who was a pawnbroker in Claughton- street. On the previous evening (Tuesday), at about twenty minutes to six, prisoner entered the chop and offered to pledge the watch produced for £2 10s. He found that the watch answered to the description of one supplied by the police the same day, and he straightway sent for a police- man.—Prisort2r : If I had known it to be a stolen watch I should never have come in, because they know me. I was never in the place before to pawn anything. If I had known it to be a stolen watch I should not have taken it in. It was given to me by a man to pawn for him, and he gave me half-a-crown to take it in.—Colonel Gamble: Have you any reason why you should not be remanded until Friday? You admit that you pawned the watch—Prisoner: Yes; I pawned it certainly; and Mr. Moxon asked me whose it was, and I gave the party's name who gave it me. Prisoner was remanded until Friday, bail being accepted in one £4O and two £2O.

div.head: ST. HELENS BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: ST. HELENS BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Thurs- day, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presiding. There were also present Major Windus, Messrs. N. Lacey, Slater, Wood- ward, Lewis, Moxon, and Pennington.

FINANCE. The registrar's monthly statement showed that there was a balance in hand from last month of £2l 18s. 7d.; cash received during August, £24 15s. 4d. Wages and other pay- ments amounted to £25 17s. 7d., leaving a balance in hand of £2O 16s. 4d.—The CHAIRMAN stated that they had now a balance in the bank of £llO.
THE INTERMENTS. The REGISTRAR stated that the number, of interments during the year was 524, of which 68 were made during August, as against 91 in the corresponding month of last year.

div.head: AN ATTEMET TO MARE THE CEMETERY ATTRACTIVE..
div.p: AN ATTEMET TO MARE THE CEMETERY ATTRACTIVE..

Mr. SLATER said that Mr. Grant, the registrar, had selected a place in the cemetery as suitable for the rearing of plants. The place selected Was the small square at the extreme end of the Independent ground close to Mr. Barton's cottage. It was private enough and very suitable, being a place where plenty of sun could be obtained, and in full connection with every- thing that was necessary. He and Mr. Grant went to Man- chester and they were very much pleased with the frames they saw there. He never saw such a collection of plants and flowers brought together.. It was worth the journey. That was not the object of their journey so much as look- ing out for the various designs of conservatory frames. They saw many excellent designs, but none which met en- tirely with the views of Mr. Grant. The prices went up as far as £BO independent of the heating apparatus, so that on the whole to put up a very efficient structure it would in his opinion be considerably over £lOO. That might be diminished by putting up the basement with the stones they had on the premises. They could build as high as they pleased to save the depth of glass. It was for the Board to say whether they were willing to have* the proposed conservatory or whatever they wished to call it. The brickwork could be done by the men they were now employing. Finding that there was nothing which especi- ally met the views of Mr. Grant, he suggested to Mr. Grant that it might be as well to get a sketch made of what he thought to be desirable, and this Mr. Grant had done.—Mr. LACEy : What would be the expense altogether P—Mr. GRANT: I have not ascertained anything about the heating apparatus.—Mr. SLATER thought about .-ClOO would be the amount.—Mr. LACEY and Mr. LEWIS thought it was too much.—Major WINDUS, after examining the design, asked if they could not have one half the size and have it lengthened out afterwards if they thought fit.— Mr. impression was that 40 feet was a little too long at present —Mr. GRANT said if they did it I all at once they would obviate the necessity of pulling down one end of the house, when they thought fit to ' lengthen.—ln answer to Mr. Lacey, Mr. SLATER said they I would manage with their present staff of men for some time to come.—Mr. LEWIS: Should we be much of a gainer by it 2—Mr. SLATER: It was thought that by making the floral appearance of the entrance much more attractive to the eye than it is at present, and one or two members of the Board having said they would be much better pleased if the cuttance could be made pleasanter, Mr. Grant intimated that he could do that if he were only provided with the means.—Major WINDL'S : I don't think it reqeires a house of 40 feet long to cl 9 that. (Laughter.)—Mr. PENNINGTON : I think we ought to get the cost as nearly as we possibly can with respect to the heating apparatus. I think it will not be done under £2OO altegether.—A MEMBER: It is a great deal of money there is no doubt about that.- -Mr. PENNINGTON: You may have a turkey to dinner, but if it isn't trimmed properly it is not very good. (Laughter.) —Mr. SEATER: This is to propogate colonial plants that wont leaf here altogether. Hitherto there has not been that floral display which there ought to have been, and as the idea of a public park has been given ep the public places we possess—and the cemetery is one—ought to be made as attractive as possible. Mr. Grant has been trying to make it more pleasant to the eye, and the question is will you have him to do it still further.—Mr. GRANT: What I have al- ready done has been done under difficulties simply to make a beginning. Mr. Grant went on to say that he lied three conservatories there which were his own property, and he ahnayd ngurorswenrv._pl;nirt.spEthNastaicooruoldNnthoot be thought tgtoht nneyredgeuri£reldssofrmome. thing else before a conservatory ; and the subject dropped.
