CONSECRATION OV A NEW M LODGN AT FRODSIIAM.

The picturesque village of Frolsharn was on Saturday the scene of a most interesting masonic event, which attracted a large gathering cf the leaders of the fraternity in this part of the province, over which Bro. Lord de Tabley rules with so much acceptance. The occasion of the assembly was the consecration of the Cholmondeley Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons, No. 1,908, which has been started under the most favourable auspices and with every prospect of success. By direction of the Provincial Grand Master of Cheshire (Bro. Lord de Tabley), the ceremony of conse- cration was performed by Bro. the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, M.P., Deputy P.G.M., and the Provincial Grand Lodge of Cheshire was very numerously and influentially represented. The consecration took place in the well-appointed lodge- room at the Commercial Hotel, Frodsham' and amongst those present beside the acting P.G.M. were Bros. Horatio Lloyd, P.P.G.W. (Cheshire), Past G.D , Eng.; Rev. W. Spencer Stanhope, grand chaplain; Rev. R. Hodgson, P.G.C.; W. D. Finney, P.G.D.C. (West Lancashire), E. Smith, P.P.D.G.C., N. Wales and Salop; H. Holbrook, P.P.G.S. of NV., and P.D.P.G.M. of British Columbia; H. Finch, P.G.D.C. -, H. Collins P.P.G.D.; H. Jackson, P.G.P., J. Bowes, P.P.G.J.W.; T. M. Lockwood, P.P.G.S. of W.; J. K. Diggs, P.G.A.D.C.; G. Moss, P.G.S.-' F. Dickson, P.P.G.J.W.; E. Wood, P.P.G.S.W.•, F. K. Stevenson, P.P.G.S.B. ; Stanhope Bull, P.G.S. of W.; J. Hocken, P.M. 673.; W. T. May, P.M., 673; J. P. Platt, P.P.G.J.W.; J. Salmon, P.P.G.S.W.; A. S. Collins S.W., 1375; J. C. Robinson, P.M., 249; J. White, LP:M. 1384; J. Yapp, 594; T. T. Redford, 721; J. D. Wainwright, 1182; T. Wil- kinson, P.M., 1126; R. Stutter, 32; W. Booth, S.W., 104 G. &He, 104; H. F. Lloyd, W.M., 724; G. F. Heywood,/ 1357; F. Field, 1756; G. F. Adams, 721; H. Baynes, 425 S M. Jones, 721; T. Brown, 823; J. Benson, 721; S. W. Ramsden, S.D., 425, die. There were altogether about Co brethren present. The assembly took place in the lodge-rosin about two o'clock, and shortly after that hour an especial P.G. Lodge was opened by Bro. the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, D.P.G.M. assisted by the chief P.G. officers present. During the cere- mony, which was of an impressive nature and most admi- •rably performed, an oration was delivered by the Rev. R. Hodgson, P.G. chaplain. He said the origin of their order was lost in antiquity—not that they owed very much to that nationality many of whose members were at the present time suffering so cruelly in a neighbouring country. Mang of the Mosaic customs—much of the ritual ol the Temple-- were still practised in all the lodges. The consecration of a new lodge was a most important matter, because it meant that a number of old and zealous masons were anxious to spread the tenets and enrol new members to follow in their places in their ancient brotherhood. It also meant that they were so convinced of the benefits of the craft that they heartily desired to communicate its blessings and advantages to others; and, further, that they had the well-being of their fellow creatures so closely at heart as to be willing to undergo great expense and much mental and bodily labour in order to impart to them the moral, religious, and tem- poral benefits which masonry undoubtedly conferred. He trusted the Cholmondeley Lodge might prove a great suc- cess, and that it might nobly fulfil all the purposes for which it was consecrated that day. From the lodge all envious, uncharitable, unforgiving tempers and feelings were to be banished, ant within it were to be exhibited in their fulness, brotherly love, relief, and truth. He counselled the brethren to be courteous and loving one to another, knowing no difference of rank or wealsh. Let them hide each other's faults, bear with each other's infirmities, and strive to be brethren in heart as well as in name. He would, further, remind the brethren that if there was any reality in masonry and its glorious ritual, the one thing far above and beyond all others was charity or relief, and he asked the brethren of the new lodge to give cordial support both to the Cheshire and the London masonic institutions. In conclu- sion, the P. G. Chaplain exhorted the brethren to show themselves good men and true, so that the charges lately brought against their craft by a certain archbishop as being a fosterer of revolution, Nihilism, and all that was bad might be plainly refuted by their peaceable, law-abiding, and loving conduct and behaviour. He trusted that masons would set such a noble example of every moral and soclel virtue that the words of Bro. Scott might be found increas- ingly true, when he said—" Masonry does not have to depend on its great men of the past, nor on its connection with religious reformations, to justify its existence; neither does it rely upon its great antiquity for its future success. It possesses the inherent principle that will command respect. It needs no apologist ; its acts of kindness and deeds of benevolence have spoken to the ages, and to all the nations of the earth." The musical portion of the consecration was performed by a choir under the direction of Bro. H. Collier P.G.0., who presided at the harmony. At the close of this part of the afterpoon's proceedings,t the ceremony of installation of W.M. and officers of the new lodge was conducted by Brother Councillor Birch, of Man- chester, whose working was remarkably effective. Brother Joseph Kertland Digges, P.G.A.D.C., was installed the first W.M. of the Cholmondeley Lodge, No. 1908; and he subse- quently invested the following as his officers :—Brothers J. Salmon, 1.P.M., and Master of Ceremonies; George 11. Danby, S.W. and Secretary; John J. Yapp, J.W. and Treasurer; Henry E. Heywood, S.D. ; Matthew Rodgers, jun., J.D. (by proxy); John R. Lamb, I.G. ; and D. Baynes waS unanimously elected Tyler. Votes of thanks were passed, and ordered to be recorded, to Brother the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton for his services as the acting E.G.M. that afternoon, and also Brother Councillor Birch f w the admirable manner in whicii be had performed the installa- tion ceremony. "Hearty good wishes" were given to the W.M. from the representatives of about 20 lodges in East and West Lancashire and Cheshire'; and after several initia- tion propositions had been made, the business portion of the proceedings was brought to a close. The majority of the brethren subsequently banqueted at the Town-hall, under the presidency of the W.M. (Bro. J. K. Digges), who was supported by the P.G. lodge officers already named. The banquet was provided by Bro. Baker, of Chester. After the toast of "The Queen," given hy the W.M., Bro. Horatio Lloyd proposed the toast of "The M.W.G.111. and the Princess of Wales and the rest of the Royal Family." In doing so, Bro. Lloyd said they had never possessed a grand master who had so endeared him- self to the brethren as the Prince of Wales; but in connec- tion with his approaching visit to Liverpool, he (Bro. Lloyd) trusted that no masonic demonstration such as that which had been suggested by one or two correspondents in the newspapers would be carried out, as the prince's time was so limited. Besides, he (Bro. Lloyd) thought the less they made a parade of masonry the better for the order. (Hear, hear.) Bro. J. Salmon proposed "The Pro. G.M. (the Earl of Carnarvon), the D.G.M. (the Earl of Lathom), and the Officers of Grand Lodge, Past and Present," which was acknowledged by Bro. H. Lloyd, Past G.D. The S.W. (Bro. Hanby) gave the health of Bro. Lord de Tabley, P.G.M., which was cordially received; and Bro. W. T. May, P.M. 673, in proposing the health of Bro. the Hon. Wilbraham Egerton, M.P., D.P.G.M., also spoke of the un- desirability of any masonic demonstration in connection with the royal visit to Liverpool. The D.P.G.M., in ack- nowleging the toast, said he was glad to find so many P.G. officers present that afternoon, and hoped the new lodge would enjoy a prosperous existence. "The Worshipful Master," proposed by the D.P.G.M., and other toasts fol- lowed, and the brethren separared at an early hour.

MAIIIIIAGE OF' Miss lIALSA-LL, OF MIESCOT. On Tuesday forenoon, the marriage of Miss Mary Catherine Halsall, eldest daughter of Mr. Wm. Halsall, of Church- street, and Mr. William Barlow, took place at the Parish Church, in the presence of a fair assemblage of the inhabi- tants of the town. The ceremony was performed by the Rev. F. R. Lee, curate of Prescot ; and the bride was given away by her father. The bridesmaids were Miss Louisa Halsall and Miss Agnes Halsall (sisters of the bride), Miss A. Barlow' and Miss Vidiano ; Mr. Wm. Watkin, of Huvton, acted as "best" man. As the bridal party arrived at the church selections of music were played upon the organ by Mr. Ewart, the organist, and at the conclusion of the ser- vice the "Wedding March" was rendered. The bride was tastefully attired in a brown satin dress, trimmed with white lace, and a tulle fall fastened with orange blossom. The presents to the bride were numerous and valuable. After partaking of breakfast at the residence of the bride's father, the happy couple left the town en route for Whitby, York- shire, where they purpose spending their honeymoon.

ST. THOMAS'S (ST. HELENS) SUNDAY SCHOOL TEACHERS' Astwx.kr. xecusloN.—The teachers connected with St. Thomas's Sunday school, and the teachers of the day 'school, numbering altogether thirty five, had their annual excursion on Saturday. The place fixed upon to be visited this year was the ancient city of Chester, and at twenty minutes past six in the morning, the party started for that place by train. Arriving in the city early, the excur- sionists had ample time for sight-seeing, and they availed themselves of the numerous opportunities afforded them of inspecting the quaint old buildings, the cathedral, and the various other sights including the picturesque old galleries that are built on the roofs of the ground-row of Shops and cellars; and as no stranger who goes to Chester would dream of walking along an ordinary pavement, so long as he could patrol the long line of galleries, these passages were well frequented by the excursionists. While some of archieologi- cal and antiquarian tendencies, visited and enjoyed a few minutes stay in the noble cathedral, others more amphibious indulged in their aquatic taqtes by bathing in the river, a floating bath having been engaged for the purpose. A slow walk round the city walls awakened thoughts of olden times; of what was perpetrated on the very spot, when crowns sat uneasily on the heads of kings, and when the times were more turbulent than they are at present. After dinner had been disposed of in a manner which excursionists know how to accomplish, the teachers engaged a covered boat, and they were propelled pleasantly down the river Dee to near Eaton Hall. The Hall was not visited, but enjoyment was found to be had, and it was obtained, in grounds specially set apart for entertaining visitors. Here games were indulged, and afterwards tea was partaken of in one of the teats there. A most enjoyable day was spent, and the weather remained fine, the only shower of rain being one of about five minutes duration. At Warrington a train was missed which necessi- tated their waiting an hour. They arrived in St. Helens at a quarter past eleven. The Rev. J. C. Pigot, the vicar, and the Rev. S. Jegg, the new curate, accompanied the excur- sionists.

OBTAINING GOODS BY FALSE PRE- TENCES AT PRESCOT.

COMMITrAL OF THE PRISONER. At the Prescot Police Court, on Wednesday, before Mr. W. L. Evans, Wm. Ryan, a young man, was brought up on re- mand charged with having, on the 23rd instant, obtained a dust overcoat, hat, and silk pocket handkerchief, value £l. 'Ts. 6d., from Mr. Henry Park, tailor and draper, Eccleston- street, Prescot, by false pretences.—Mr. Superintendent Bar- ker prosecuted, and said the pretence was that the prisoner by his dress, manner, and conversation led Mr. Park to be- lieve that he was in Mr. Spencely's employ, he ordering the articles mentioned to be set down to Mr. Spencely's ac- count, whereas he had been discharged and was no longer in that gentleman's service.—Mr. Henry Park said he was a tailor and draper, in Ecclesten-street, Prescot. About eleven o'clock on Tuesday, the 23rd August, the prisoner came to his shop and asked to look at some drawers and shirts. Some were shown to him, and be selected two under shirts and two pair of drawers. He also selected four pairs of socks and an umbrella. Prisoner asked him if he kept hat brushes, and he replied that he did not. Prisoner then said that their hat brush had been lost and they required another, but that a pocket-handkerchief would do instead. He selected the handkerchief produced, and ordered it to be set down to Mr. Spencely's account; also a dust overcoat and a felt hat, which he afterwards chose. Prisoner said the horse had trod on his hat and spoiled it, and he required another in its place. He also ordered a cap for the stable boy, which was also to go down to Mr. Spencely's account. He had known prisoner for about twelve months. He understood that he was still in Mr. Spencely's employ when he got the goods. Prisoner said Mr. Spencely had not settled with him for the last twelve months, but was about settling with him. In the course of conversaticn prisoner said he had been to St. Helens that moraing to look at a horse. Within the last twelve months he had supplied the prisoner with a stable suit on Mr. Spencely's account. Had witness known that prisoner had been discharged he would not have let him have the goods. Shortly after the prisoner had left his shop he heard that prisoner was not in Mr. Spencely's service, and he at once gave information to the police.— Mr. Evans (to prisoner) : Have you any question to ask Mr. Park? Prisoner: I don't know anything about it. I was drunk, and had been three or four days. I did not do it with any bad intention.—Mr. Castle Spencelv (magis- trates' clerk), Prescot, said the prisoner was in his employ as groom up to Monday, the 22nd ult., and on that evening he discharged him for misconduct, and he ceased to be in his employ from that time. Prisoner had been in his employ about two years. Witness did not send him to Mr. Park to obtain the goods in question, and he had no authority to get them on his account. Prisoner had got into the hands of the police the night previous, and witness's clerk settled up with him at the police station on the following morning.—P.S. Crawford deposed that on Monday night, the 22nd inst , be found the prisoner in the stable yard attached to Mr. Spencely's house, near to the kitchen door, lying on the ground helplessly drunk. Witness took him to the police station where he was detained till the follow- ing morning for safety.—P.C. Morgan stated that on Tues- day morning, the 23rd inst., he found the prisoner was being detained in the station. A little after ten o'clock he was in the office when Mr. Blackwell (Mr. Spencely's clerk) settled with the prisoner, who left the station about a quarter-past ten o'clock. Prisoner left the station in a cab. About five o'clock in the evening of the same day, he saw the prisoner in the same cab in a helpless state of drunkenness. Prisoner was perfectly sober when he left the station in the morning. Witness took him into custody and locked him up. He had since charged him with obtaining the goods in question by false pretences, and the prisoner replied "I was very foolish; it serves me right."—Prisoner was then formally charged, and Mr. Evars asked him if he had anything to say why he should not be committed to take his trial at Kirkdale Sessions.—Prisoner replied : Nothing at all. lam guilty of the crime. I was drunk, and did not know what I was doing for two or three days. That's all I have to say. I had no intention of doing such a think. I had no intent to do wrong. If your worship will be lenient I will pay for the articles.—Mr. Evans: I have no alternative but to com- mit you to take your trial at the next court of quarter Sessions at Kirkdale.—Prisoner : Can you send me from here ?-1)1r. Evans: No, I cannot commit you from here. We cannot deal with the case here at all. All we can do is to send you for trial. I will take bail for your appearance if you can find it.—Prisoner: I could find bail ; but, of course, you would not let one look for it.—Mr. Superinten- dent Baker: We will allow you to communicate with your friends.—Mr. Evans (to prisoner) : I will allow bail, your- self in £2O and two suries of £lO each, to answer for your appearance when called upon.—Prisoner, who seemed to feel his position rather more acutely, was then removed.

div.head: SAD FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: SAD FATALITY AT ST. HELENS.
THE CORONER ON THE USE OF CLOGS.

On Monday an inquest was held at the Griffin Inn, Peasley Cross, on the body of George Bibby, 19 years of age, who died on Thursday night from injuries received at the Ravenhead Glass Works Yard.—James Bibby said de- ceased was his son, and worked with him at the Ravenhead Glass Works. On Thursday afternoon they were drawing a glass wagon out of the road in order that they might get some salt cake in, for the mixing room. Witness was at the horses' head, and deceased was at the booking-on chain. They had not gone more than a dozen yards when witness heard deceased shout. He turned round, saw deceased under the wagon, and stopped as quickly as he could. Wit- ness, and Wm. Leyland, who was working near, ran to de- ceased, who held out his arms to witness. Deceased's right leg was on the rail, and was cut right through, just above the knee; the foot of the other leg was injured. Deceased was lying within the rails. Leyland then took him to Twyford's in a. van kept at the works for the purpose of ready conveyance in case of acc:dent. The doctor ordered deceased to be taken to the Cottage Hospital, where they arrived at half-past four. Witness added that there was some lime in the road, and deceased was trying to get out of the way when he got one of his feet fast on the points, and fell. In answer to the coroner witness said that de- ceased had a pair of lace-np clogs on shod with irons.— Sarah Eliza Ransford, matron of the Cottage Hospital, said deceased was brought to the hospital at half-past four. Mr. Galton arrived soon after : Dr. Reid came some time after, followed by Dr. Twyford. Deceased's injuries were a compound fracture of the right thigh just above the knee, and a wound on the left foot. Deceased lost a great deal of blood, and began to sink about an hour after his arrival. At ten o'clock he died. Witness believed the immediate cause of death was shock. The doctors in- tended to amputate the limb, but deceased was not in a con- dition to allow the operation to be performed.—Coroner: He attached no blame to anyone P—Witness : No—Coroner: Did he say how he did it : Yes. I believe he said he got his foot in the points.—The Coroner: And you have no reason to doubt it 7—Witness: No, I have not.— Deceased's father was re-called, and he said the foot that was fast in the points was the one that was hurt —The Coroner : Do you wear those sort of clogs yourself ?—Witness : No, I don't; strongish boots.—The Coroner: Well, why did you let him 7—Witness: Well, he had been used to working in the pit, and always wore clogs. I did not want him to wear them.—The Coroner: But they are dangerous in the pit, and very bad on the railway. They are the cause of all sort of accidents on the railway.—Witness: I don't think there was hardly a morning passed without my telling him to be careful.—The Coroner But you should not have let him wear those clogs. I wonder at the managers allowing these things en the premises at all ; they are very danger- nus.—William Leyland, Thatto Heath, corroborated the statement of last witness—The Coroner: What had he on his feet 7—Witness: He wore clogs—Coroner: With irons 7—Witness: Yee—Coroner: Don't you think that less been the cause of it 7—Witness: I can't say what the cause was.--The Coroner: He slipped between the points, didn't he ?—Witness: Yes; be must have.—The Coroner : , If they would only wear proper things on their feet it would be a great deal better for them. There is no question as to Iwhat he has died from, and there is no question as to what has been the cause of his death. It is one of the cases that happen frequently in St. Helens and elsewhere from wearing clogs with irons.—A Juryman . Yes; they are particularly dangerous in frosty weather.—Coroner: Yes, in frost and in other circumstances, amongst metals and moving wagons, but they ought not to be allowed.—:The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

The property was mentioned as belonging to Mr. Dromgoole. but it was in the occupation of a lady named Scott. On the 14th inst., directly after Mrs. Scott and her family returned from church at night, they were told that some boys had been in the vinery, and had stolen some grapes. Mrs. Scott and her daughters went to look, and found that a great deal of damage had been done, and many grapes taken away. The girl who gave the in- formation to Mrs. Scott was, he believed, a relative of the defendant, and she had since altered her story. That was the reason why he was obliged to get the case adjourned, and after bearing the witness he should call before them, they would have no doubt whatever that the defendant, with two brothers who were younger than defendant, had on that Sunday night gone into the vinery, and committed the damage complained of. The garden adjoined a field the gate of which was in Schole's-lane. div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
Nolan LINCOLNSHIRE ELECTION. The polling took plate on Thursday and the result will be declared to-night.
BERWICK.'

Mr. Jerningbam, the Liberal candidate for Berwick, has issued his address. He gives a staunch support to Mr. Gladstone. He favours the assimilation of the borough and county franchise and a revision of the present system of lecal taxation. He believes that the best guarantee for the policy of peace is a jealous care of the national honour. It is not yet known whether Mr. Cargill will be accepted as the Conservative candidate. Nearly 400 Liberals were added to the register at the last revision.

div.head: TYRONE.
div.p: TYRONE.

The nomination of candidates took place on Thursday morning in the following order :—Mr. Thomas Alexander Dickson (Liberal), proposed by Mr. Jas. Brown, J.P, seconded by Mr. Robert Sproul, J.P.; the Rev. Harold Rylett (Land Leaguer), proposed by Mr. Daniel Elliott, peconded by Mr. Patrick Donnelly; Colonel the Hon. Stuart Knox (Conservative), proposed by Major Hamilton J.P., seconded by Mr. James Holmes. The proceedings were quiet. Mr. Parnell is stopping to-day in Omagh.

div.head: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.
div.p: ST. HELENS POLICE COURT.

FRlDAY.—Before His Worship the Mayor, and Colonel Gamble. A DISCORDANT MUSICAL FAMlLY.—Charles Rhoden Skel- ton, described as a travelling musician, who sometime lived in Arthur-street, St. Helens, was brought up on warrant, charged with assaulting his wife on the 11th September, 1880.—Mary Skelton said that she had been to the market, and returned home. Prisoner was lying on the sofa, and when she showed him some vegetable marrows she had bought he came out with a vulgar expression before the Children. She threw one of the vegetable marrows at him. He got up, threw her down in the passage, and violently kicked and assaulted her. When she took out a summons he went away, and did not return until Wednesday morning, when he was apprehended by Police-constable Sheriff. In reply to questions complainant said they had been married thirty-one years. She had travelled about with him from town to town, and taken the little children with her, until she was weary, and had stayed in St. Helens because her sister had been kind to her. Since he went away the guardians had for some time allowed her 3s. a week for the children. Her daughter had left home through him; he having given her a black eye and led her a wretched life. For some timelier daughter acted at the St. Helens theatre, and "she was a very nice girl."—The Magistrates. Is there any possibility of your living together peaceably P—Com- plainant sad there was none. He brought female singers past the house, and said they were better than she was.— Prisoner said they had not lived comfortably together since Le death of his wife's mother. His wife had been an imbecile, the least thing excited her, and she imagined all sorts of things.—Complainant fNow, Charles, I don't want to expose you any more.—Prisoner: No, you have done quite enough.—Complainant (in a sorrowful tone): My hus- band says that a woman of 50 years ought to be pole axed. —After some consultation the magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for three days. A FOREIGNER DEFRAUDING THE RAILWAY COMPANY.— Benjamin Blumberry, of Parr, a Pole, apparently about 50 years of age, was charged with riding on the railway with- out ticket, on the 18th.—Mr. Ferrand, of the solicitors' department at the Lime-street railway station, Liverpool, called James Wilkinson, who said he was posted as a detec- tive on the railway, St. Helens, on the day in question. The prisoner arrived by the 12-10 train from Liverpool, and after walking about the station for a quarter of an hour, made to- wards the door, and told the ticket collector that he had not come by train. Witness followed and apprehended him. Ills son, who was with him, said his father had got a ticket at Liverpool.—ln answer to the Bench, witness said he had been on duty on the railway for some time, as the company had been imposed upon by passengers acting in a similar manner to the defendant.—Defendant was fined £2 and costs.

FOUL-MOUTIIETI WOMEN.—Bridget Gahgan, Eccleston, was tined 2s. 6d. and costa, for using profane language; and Ellen Vardy, Parr, was mulcted in a similar penalty, for using obscene language. THE CHARGE OF STEALING BEER.—David Platt, Eccles- ton, was again charged with stealing two bottles and two pints of beer from William James Rigby, a lad who was taking the liquor to Messrs. Carrington and Shaw's works.— This case was remanded on Wednesday, when it was stated that Rigby was unwilling to prosecute.—After the case had been heard prisoner was discharged. ASSAULT.—Stephen McGrory, a young man, was charged on remand with assaulting Henry Sod, on Monday night, in the Hesketh Arms, Churcb-street.—Comnlainant, who is the father of Mrs. Cruise, the landlady at the Hesketh Arms, told the defendant, who was drunk, to leave the house, when defendant struck him a blow on the breast, and knocked him down.—Fined ss. and costs. AN OLD OFFENDER SENT TO GAOL FOR ASSAULTING THE POLICE.—John Ormsher was charged with being drank and disorderly, and also with assaulting P.C. James Cottam on Sunday afternoon in Liverpool-road, Eccleston.—?.C. Cottam said the prisoner was challenging people on the foot- path to tight. Witness too: prisoner into custody when he became very violent, and kicked witness on the legs, and continued doing so for about twenty minutes. With assist- ance he got the prisoner to the office where he was locked up.—Prisoner: I never was guilty of hurting an officer be- fore, not as I know of.—lnspector Wood: I think you will be told different, your worships.—William Quince, a youth, dressed as a sailor, deposed to seeing prisoner kicking the officer. He assisted the officer.—Mr. Thompson : That is quite right, you did very well.—Superintendent Johnston said the prisoner had been 31 times convicted before this, and one of those offences was for assaulting the police. Prisoner had always been committed, never having paid a fine.—Prisoner was fined 108. and costs for being drunk, and 20s. and costs for the attack on the constable, or in default, six week's imprisonment. A NEWTON MAN IN TROUBLE.—James Gloster, respec- tably dressed, who said he came from Newtolt, was charged with being drunk at the railway station.—A railway detec-' tive officer named Wilkinson, said that at half past eleven on Saturday night he was on duty in the waiting rem. The defendant was drunk, and leaning over the bar at the book- ing place, preventing passengers from booking. Defendant would not go away, and when he was told to go away he struck the station master a blow on the face.—Defendant: I am very sorry; I was going to Newton, and must have been very stupid. I would rather assist than Impede anyone.—Mr. Thompson: Public officers must be protected.—Defendant: I never was in a police court in my life before, and I cannot account for it. I was wanting to get home, and I had lost my friends.—Superintendent John- ston : That is so, as far as I know. I an: told he is a very respectable man.—Mr. Thompson (to Mr. Johnston) : After that explanation, are you willing to withdraw the charge ? —Mr.Johnston : lam not the prosecutor, sir.—Mr. Ferrand (of the solicitors' department, Lime-street, Liverpool) : Oh no, I don't withdraw the charge. This is done for the protection of the company.—Prisoner was fined ss. and costs.

MAINTENANCE ORDER AGAINST A BUILDER. - John Prescott, master builder, of Huvton, was summoned to show cause why he should not be ordered to contribute to the maintenance of his mother, Ellen Halsall, who is now chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union.—Mr. Stuart, relieving officer for No. 1 St. Helens District, said defendant's mother was a very old woman, and had been receiving relief from the Guardians for upwards of three years. Defendant was a man in good position, and although ,he had six children two of them were working. Ellen Hal- sail had been receiving 3s. 6d. per week; Is. 6d. a week was paid by another son, and he asked that the defendant be ordered to pay 2s. a week.—The magistrates made that order.

husband had threatened to kill her if be went into him house again. On the Monday night previously he dragged her up and down the yard by the hair of her bead. He had - ill-.used her very much lately. but she had looked over it. . lie sent his little boy t. pawn a blanket, and because he could not pawn it, he ill-used the boy. One of the children was quite bald on the top of his head through the prisoner plucking it.—Prisoner was bound over to keep the peace, and succeeded in getting sureties on Tuesday. MONDAY.--Before Messrs. S. H. Thompson and A. It. Gladstone.

A NOTED CHANACTEE.—EIizabeth Lawrence, a young woman, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Windle, on Satnrday.—Prisoner pleaded guilty, and an •officer stated that the prisoner was conducting herself in a disorderly fashion in Naylor-street, at ten minutes p.rst eleven on Saturday night. —Superintendent Johnston said the prisoner had been up 32 times. She had ben nine times before the court this present year. The last penalty I imposed upon her was on the 23rd April, and for beings 'disorderly prostitute she was sent to pribon for two month', and for assaulting the police on the same occasion she was I sent to prison for two months, one term of imprisontnent te I follow the other.—Mr. Thompson: How long have you been out? Prisoner : Last Wednesday, sir.—Mr. Johnston: Since the 14th March she has spent four months in gaol.— Mr. Thompson: You evidently want to go back again; you must go for one month.—The prisoner, after delivering her.. self of her usual execration against the officer interested in the case, was taken downstairs. MAKING THE ACQUAINTANCE OF THE NEW BOBBY AT Rernvonn.--Joseph Hall, a pugnastic-looking fellow, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at'Rainford, on Saturday, and also with assaulting P.C. George Pickup. Whilst in the execution of his duty.—The officer stated that he found prisoner drffnk, shouting, and swearing in Chapel. lane, Rainford. He went up to prisoner and requested him to be quiet. Prisoner said, "You are the new bobby are you," and struck him on the neck. He handcuffed the pi isoner and took him to the station in Rainford, where pri. saner again struck him in the face.—Prisoner, who made' his tenth appearance, was fined 55. and costs for being drunk and disorderly, and for the assault on the officer 20s. and costs.

ROBBING HIS BENEFACTORS. Michael Colvin, (20), who resided at Sutton, WU charged with having, on Satur- day night, stolen a silver watch, value 205., and 355. In money from his lodgings, the property of John Pickavance, Sutton-road.—Margaret Picicavance, wife of prosecutor, said 1 the prisoner had lodged with her and her husband since he was twelve years old. At four o'clock on Saturday after- noon she saw the money safe in a bag in a box, upstairs. The box was locked and stood on a table in her bedroom. Her husband's watch was safe on the table. She missed the property at half-past nine the same evening. She gave in- formation to the police—Prisoner pleaded guilty and was sentenced to six weeks' imprisonment with hard labour. A MODEL WlFE.—George Glover summoned his wife, for using threatening language towards him. Mr. Swift appeared on behalf of complainant, and said the parties were husband and wife, and were living separate from each other. Defendant had had her husband before the guardians about her maintainance, and, after bearing both sides, the guardians decided not to interfere. On one occasion de- fendant had gone to the house where complainant lodged, and some disturbance took place in consequence of which defendant summoned complainant, and the case was heard last Monday' but was dismissed. After the case had been dismissed, the husband was going down the stairs from the court room when his wife got hold of him by the arm and said, "I will swing for you." The husband then turned back and complainei to the magistrates who granted a sum. I mons against her.—Complainant said they had lived apart since last New Year's Day, when his wife broke up the home and went to live with another man in Wales. On Monday last defendant followed him from the court, and used very bad language towards him, so that he was obliged to take refuge in a house in Claughton-street, occupied by a man named Wood. She stayed outside the door four hours, and said she would be hung for him.—Defendant said she had assisted her husband for many years' and it was "a great sorrow" to her that she should be done by in that manner.—Defendant was - bound over in her own recog- nizance, of £5, and one surety of £5 to keep the peace for two months.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Pilkington. IF HE HAD ONLY HAD SOME "CHECIC."—ThOMSS WiIHAMS'S middle-aged man, was charged with having, on the previous afternoon, stolen 51135, of ham, the property of Mrs. Lancas- ter, of Park-road. It appeared that prisoner entered prose- cutor's shop about seven o'clock, and finding no one there ran away with a piece of ham, which was on a bench near the door. He was observed to leave the shop and informa- tion was given to the owner of the ham. A man named Smith then went in pursuit of prisoner and captured him on the top of Primrose Hill.—Prisoner had the ham in his possession, and asked not to be locked up, but he was taken back to Mrs. Lancaster's, who handed him over to P.C. Rhymer. On being charged with the theft prisoner replied, "I did so; I was hungry, and it would have made a good supper if I had had some chuck to it."—Prisoner was re- manded until Friday, and will, in the meantime, subsist on prison "chuck."

div.head: WEATHER AND THE HARVEST.'
div.p: THE WEATHER AND THE HARVEST.'

Throughout the country the heavy rains of Monday and Tuesday have made the agricultural outlook more gloomy than ever. In Sussex the cern crops, whether standing or in stooks, had withstood the weather pretty successfully until a week ago' but the last week's rain has proved too much for them. Barley, which promised to be "the crop of the year," is mostly spoilt, or all but spoilt, for malting pur- poses. Oats, never a good crop, aie soaked or beaten out by the wind, and the valuable straw is spoilt. Peas and tares are shedding or else rotting. Some wheat and barley has been carried lately "between the showers," hat torefer-fit condition. Throughout Kent generally the loss to the farmer is expected to be very great. On Monday night the rain for some hours fell in torrents, completely submerging all the lowlands of the county, and doing irreparable in- jury to the outstanding grain, of which there is a large area still unsecured. Wheat cut reveral weeks ago may still be seen standing in the fields, where it is now sprouting in many instances. The barley crop, too, has b.on much injured by the heavy rains. Taking the whole of Kent, the present has been as .1 sis'toua a season as the farmers have known for several years past. A violent storm, which unfortunately occa- stoned loss of life and considerable destruction of roperty,, broke over North-East Lancashire late on Monday night. In some districts rain fell very heavily, and several places were flooded, the rain being accompanied by thunder end lightning. In every district the crops have suffered im- mense damage. Many fields are covered with water, and much hay has been destroyed. At Canterbury, on Tues- day, a heavy thunderstorm, with frequent flashes of lightning, broke over the city and neighbourhood. Rain fell in-torrents for at least an hour, and the streets were at one time deluged. The weather near Chester. on Tuesday, was, if possible, more disheartening than on Monday. Rain fell more or less heavily from seven o'clock in the morning. Corn, and especially oats, is sprouting, and a great deal .a the wheat and oats is now only available for cattle. The season was very late in Cheshire, and it is no exaggera- tion to say that not a hundred acres of any sort of grain have yet been carried. Around Windsor an immense acreage of wheat, barley, and oats (mostly cut about three weeks ago) still remains unharvested. Upon many farms in East Berke, West Surrey, South Beds, and West Middle- sex, the groups of sheaves out in the fields are completely soddened, a gteat deal of the grain where most exposed to the elements having been washed out of the ears, while the straw has the appearance of old thatch. On Tuesday morn- in rain continued to fall in South Durham, and at Billing- ham and other low-lying points there are large areas of • land flooded. In the afternoon rain ceased, and throughout the day a fine drying wind succeeded. The damage done to corn crops is not so great as further south, but in the west hay not yet carted is spoiled. A tremendous thunderstorm occurred at Hartlepool early on Tuesday morning, accom- panied by a heavy rainfall, which flooded the Belle Vue district to Bach an extent that the roadways were only pass- able by means of carts. Many cellars were flooded, and considerable damage done to the grain crops standing or in stock. A severe thunderstorm broke over Southport on Tuesday, washing away the ballast on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, and suspending traffic for some hours. There was a slight improvement in the weather at Salisbury on Tuesday, but the dretthing and persistent rain of Mon- day, thoroughly saturating everything, has rendered the harvest prospects in that neighbourhood still more gloomy, and wheat, which is in a very damp condition, has gone up to 565. to 60s, per imperial quarter, bread having been raised per 41b. loaf. A large quantity of ntandirg corn in North Wilts has been beaten down, and around peviies the cereals will apparently be roined by a few more days' rain. In some instances ears have grown out three inches, but barley seems to have sustained comparatively little damage. Similar reports have been received from the Potteries and Warminster. Of barley and oats in the latter district not much has yet been cut. The agricultural prospects through- out Shropshire at the present time are most gloomy. Very littlecorn has lean garnered, but a great deal has been cut, and is lying in the fields blackened by exposure to the con- stant rains. In some parts sprouting is general. It is feared a great p ,rt of the harvest is new practically lost. On the North-we -'ern side of Lancashire, the presentefloods . have not been •Inalled for twelve years. About Thornton , and Bispham tue .'ad a are in some places four feet deep, and some farmhouses are surrounded. Many farm houses cannot be approached, the roads being flooded too deeply for the passag of traps. Geese and ducks are in some parts swim- ming in the wheatfields. From Weeton to Poulton, the railway was flooded, and a goods train was delayed several hours in a cutting through the embankment giving way. At Canton, the damage is irreparable for a great length, only the tops of the hedges being visible. At Pilling and Cocker- ham the roads are submerged for miles—for a censiderable distance several feet deep-cutting off communication between villages. In some cases farmyards and haystacks are inundated half a yard deep; in others, people are obliged to leave their houses for safety. The crops are ntterll, ruined in many places, and the greatest depressieu prevails. Potato bEr;ht is rapidly extending.

PROPOSED INCREASE OF LINCASPIRE PoLic-..—Tatio Chief Constable of the county of Lancaster has bubmitted to the Constabulary Committee 4 •roposal to increase the police force of the county to the extent of two inspectors, 14 sergeants, and 102 constables, which will give one constable to every 1,264 of the population. The present strength of the force is 1,188, or one Constable to 1,389 inhabitants. The increased cost of the proposed additions will be £10,178. 18s. 61.

liam Bostock : LOT I.—This lot consists of a commodious and well-built DWELLING-HOUSE, containing 3 entertaining rooms, kitchen, scullery, pantry, 8 bedrooms, w.c , and 5 cellars, also coal- house and outside offices. This lot is in the occupation of the said William Bostock, and has a good garden and yard, and contains altogether 686 supei ficial square yards of land, or there- abouts, and will be sold subject to the apportioned yearly rent _ _

Of £4ss 9d. LOTS 2,3, 4,5, AND 6.—These lots consist of the Five MES- I KLUGES or Dwelling-houses adjoining Lot 1, and facing the Stockton Heath-road. Each house contains 2 entertaining rooms, kitchen, scullery, pantry, 6 bedrooms, we., and 3 cel- lars; also coal and wash-house and outside offices. Each house has a garden facing the road, and a yard at the back. Lot 2 contains 211 superficial square yards of land or there- abouts, and will be sold subjects to a ground rent of £1 6s to.. Lot 3, whirls is in the occupation of Mrs. Taylor, contains 228 , superficial square yards of land or thereabouts, and will be sold , subject to a ground rent of £1 8s 6d. Lot 4, which is in the , occupation of Captain Knott, contains 234 superficial square yards of land or thereabouts, and will be sold subje2t to a ground rent of £1 9s 34. This house also contains a bath. Lot ' 5, which is in the occupation of Mr. Fletcher, contains 228 superficial square yards of land or thereabouts, and will be sold subject to a ground rent of £l. 8s 6d ; and Lot 6, which is in the occupation of Mrs. Oakden, contains 235 superficial square , yards of land or thereabouts, and will be sold subject to a . ground rent of £1 9s 41-d. LOT 7.—This lot consists of the DWELLING-HOUSE adjoin- ing Lot 6, and containing 2 entertaining rooms, large kitchen and scullery, 6 bedrooms, bathroom and we.. 3 cellars and coal cellar. This lot, which Is in the occupation of Mrs. Seward, with the garden in front and yard behind the house, contains in the whole 331 superficial square yards of land or there- abouts, and will be sold subject to a ground rent of £2 ls 41d. LOT B.—This lot consists of a HOUSE, containing one enter- taming room, kitchen and large scullery, and five bedrooms, coal house and outside officrs, and with the yard contains in the whole 189 superficial square yards of land or thereabouts, and will be sold subject to aground rent of £l3s 71d. This lot is in the occupation of Mr. Spenceley as tenant thereof. LOT 9.—This lot consists of all that large DWELLING-HOUSE, situate facing the Old Quay Canal. The house contains two large entertaining rooms, large kitchen, pantry, small back kit- chen, and four bedrooms, bathroom and we.; also three cellars, outside coal house and offices. This lot, with the garden and yard, contains in the whole 579 superficial square yards of land or thereabouts, and will be sold subject to a ground rent of £3 12s 4lcl. LOT 10.—This lot, which adjoins Lot 9, consists' fa DWELL- ING-HOUSE,containing two entertaining rooms, kitchen, scul- lery, three large bedrooms,w.c. and one cellar; also coal house, washhouse, and outside offices. This lot, with the garden and yard, contains in the whole 187 superficial square yards of land or th reabouts, and will be sold subject to a ground rent of £1 3s 40. LOT IL—This lot, which adjoins Lot 10, consists of a DWELL- ING-HOUSE, containing two entertaining rooms, kitchen, scullery, three large bedrooms and one cellar; also coal house, washhouss, and outside offices. This lot, which is in the occu- pation of Mr. Chadwick, with garden and yard, contains in the whole 150 superficial square yards of land or thereabouts, and will Ise sold subject to a ground rent of 18s 9d. The whole of the lots are held for the residue of a term of 999 years from the 24th day of June, 1874. For further particulars, or to view the premises, apply to Mr. W. BOSTOCK; to the AUCTIONEER, at his Offices, Bewsey-street, Warrington ; or of Messrs. R/DGWAY & WORSLEY, Solicitors, 2, Cairo-street, Warrington.

Valuable LEASEHOLD PROPERTY, LATMIFORn, and WAR- • NINGTON.—To be SOLD BY AUCTION, by MR. THOMAS SUTTON, on WEDNBSDAY, the 21st day of rEPTEMBER, 1881, at 4 for 5 o'clock in the After- noon, at the BLUE BELL INN, HORSEMAMEET-STREET, WAR- RINGTON, subject to certain conditions then and there to be produced ; LOT 1,-4.11 that Valuable Leasehold SHOP and DWEL- LING-HOUSE, situate opposite to "The Chesh:re Chesse," in Latchford, and now in the occupation of Mr. Thomas Norman, joiner, with the outbuildings, worksh p, and garden thereto belonging. Ths House contains on the gi ound floor; Shop, par- lour, kitchen, and scullery; and on the Ist floor three bed- rooms. There is a large encicood yard at the back of the premises The Workshop, a large and substantial building, is situate at the rear of the premises, and is now used as a joiner's workshop. Theist contains 468 1-9th square yards or thereabouts, and has a frontage to Knutsford-road of 36 feet or thereabouts, and is held for the residue of a term of 984 years, from the 25th day of March, 1879, subject to the yearly ground rent of £4 17s 6d. These premises are entirely new, and are well and substantially built, and excellently adapted for business pur poses. To anyone desirous of commencing in the provision trade or about to establish a milk-selling business, a cc al depot, or any similar business, an opportunity is offered rarely to be met with. LOT 2.—A1l those two leasehold semi-detached VILLAS, situate and being Nos. 5 and 7, in Museum-street, Warrington, with the yards, gardens, and outbuildings belonging thereto, and now or lately in the respective occupations of Messrs. G. Y. Bolton and J. R. Tomlinson. These villas each contain on the ground floor, entrance hall, two large entertaining rooms, kitchen, scullery, and larder. On the first floor there are 5 good bedrooms, w c., lavatory and bath, and in the basement 2 capital cellars. This lot contains (including one halt of and to the centre of Museum-street, and co-exten- sive therewith) 491 superficial square yards of land or there- abouts, and is held for the residue of a term of 995 years from the 25th day of March, 1878, subject to the yearly ground rent of £l2. The houses are new, and substantially built and beau- tifully finished and decorated, and situated in the pleasantest and most fashionable part of Warrington, and as they will always command a good rent and readily let, this would prove a sound investment. LOT 3.—A1l tiaat Valuable and Commodious SHOP, situate and being No. 79, in Bridge.street, Warrington, and formerly in the occupation of Mr. Richard Dowd, saddler; together with the house, yard, and outbuildings belonging thereto, and con- taining on the ground floor Shop (34 feet by 17 feet), sitting- room, kitchen, pantry, scullery, and wash-house; on the first floor a large dining-room and 5 bedrooms, and on the second floor 4 bedrooms and a workroom. The shop, dwelling-house, yard. and outbuildings occupy an area of (including one-half of Boss and Crown-street, so far a.s the same Is co-extensive there- with) 348 square yards or thereabouts. Also all those five Cottages, situate and being Nos. 6,8, 10., and 12, in Rose and Crown-street, off Bridge-street, aforesaid, and now in the respective occupations of Esther Taylor, W. Naughton, W. Caldwell, and others; and also all that Smithy and the stables adjoining. The site of the cottages, smithy, and stables (in- cluding one-half of Rose and Crown-street, so far as the same is co-extensive therewith) contains by admeasurement 398 square yards or thereabout. The whole premises are held for the residue of a term of 999 years, commencing from the 24th day of December. 1840, subject to a chief rent of £9 14s. The Shop is large and commodious and has a frontage of 20 feet to Bridge street, which is the hugest thoroughfare of Warrington, and is the principal entrance into the town from Cheshire. The tenant's fixtures to be taken by the purchaser at' the valuation of the Auctioneer. The Smithy is now in the occupation of Mrs. Hewitt, and a good business is being carried on thereat. The Stables are well built and have accomodation for six horses, and are now in the occupation of Mr. Broadhurst as tenant thereof. For further particulars as to Lot 1, apply to Messrs. JOSEPH DAVIES, VOISEY & DAVIES, Bewsey Chambers, Warrington; as to Lot 3, to Mr. HENRY THORNTON, Insurance Buildings, Mill- street; and as to all the lots, to the AUCTIONER, at his Otlice, In Bewsey-street, or to PERCY DAVIES. Solicitor, 1, Market Place, Warrington.
For the Largest Single Sheet -Fosters in the district go to The Exaracner Steam Vrinting Works, Bewseratreec, War- rington.

be restricted to the owners and cultivators of the soil. We all understand the simple process by which con- sumers are dragged into the mesh, and have to stand the rack .of bad harvests along with producers. We, who have to buy farm produce, must expect to pay more dearly for it all through the ensuing autumn, winter, and spring; and more than that, when much of the wheat is damaged, the average quality of the flour sold is deteriorated accordingly. Already, too, we begin to know what a blight of the potato crop in- volves. Diseased potatoes are making their appear- ance in the markets; if the weather does not take lip at once, few fields of potatoes will escape the invasion of the rot, and a sound sample of this favourite esculent will before Christmas be the excep- tion. An abundant and excellent yield of potatoes was reported before these latter rains fell to drown our harvests and our hopes together; and there may yet be a bare possibility of the rescue of a portion of this particular crop. The general descrip • tion of the state of the fields and the ungathered crops at the middle of this week will apply, with but slight differenees, to nearly any district of this country that sould be named. The seaward flats of West-Lanca- shire, the valleys of the Wyre,tho Ribble,the Douglas, the Mersey, and the Weaver, in Lancashire and Cheshire, seldom miss an exceptional discharge of rain, and in this instance have fared as badly as most districts. Those farmers have the least cause to ' lament who have their fields chiefly in grass, as is the common practice on the eastern side of Lancashire and in some parts of Cheshire, and who fix their hay- time before the end of July or beginning of August. A good many tenants of grass farms are able to say that the late rains have cost them but little. Let such be duly thankful. They have got their hay safe and dry within the barns; and there is plenty of grass in the pastures which lie above the reach of the floods. Even in these cases, cattle are suffering from the humid atmosphere, and foot and mouth and lung diseases have decimated the stock upon quite a large number of farms. The recital of all these dishearten- ing circumstances is a pain to us; but if the news- paper press of the country took no special notice of the incidents of the disaster which has befallen the harvest, our farmers might imagine that the com• munity at large had little or no concern for them in their tribulations and that would be a most mistaken impression.

THE QUEEN'S SPEECH having been published in our second edition last Saturday, may be regarded by some of our readers as already stale. But after such a session as we have witnessed, it would be singular if we allowed the closing scene to pass away without any comment. We commend that speech to the care- ful consideration of the opponents of Her Majesty's Government, if only that they might recall some of their predictions, and especially their lamentations over the rapid decay of that glorious empire on which " the sun never sets." They say that England stands unbefriended and alone in the wide world, isolated or insulated, we scarcely know which, from all the nations of the earth, whereas Her Majesty asserts that her "relations with all foreign Powers continue to be amicable and cordial." But says some wise- acre, is not the general break down of the foreign policy of the present Government a fact? It seems not, for "a treaty has been concluded with the sanction of all the Great Powers, for the cession of Thessaly ter the Greek Kingdom; and its peaceful execution has begun." This does not appear like failure. But affairs in North Africa must surely be allowed on all hands to be in a most unsatisfactory condition so far as we are concerned? Not so, says Her Majesty :—" I have received satisfactory as- surances from the Republic as to the rights secured to me by the treaty with the Bey, and as to the re- lations between the Regency and the neighbour- ing Ottoman territory ot Tripoli." In fact, the whole speech belies the accusations and predic- tions of those who nursed the hope that Mr. Glad- stone's Ministry would prove a failure. The strong hand which he has shown both at home and abroad, has secured for us advantages from which we seemed to be at an almost infinite distance eighteen months ago. It is true we cannot boast of many things in the way of legislation, for the measures of importance which have become law are not numerous. But when we consider the value of the work done, it must be admitted that the one principal measure of the last session is one of the wonders of legislation. Therefore to call the past session barren would be to pronounce oneself a fool. There may be many who care very little what becomes of Ireland, and would as soon see the powerful restraints of law put into full operation to subdue the people, as witness any- thing in the shape of the removal of wrongs. But even selfish persons like these must remember that new principles have been laid down affecting the relationship between landlord and tenant. It is something to be able to say that the fact that tenants have rights which have not previously been recog- nised, has been brought out into full relief. The Irish Land Law Act is only a foundation stone on which the Governments of the future will have to build. That Act is the mould in which other bills will be cast, and every one may expect it as a certainty about which there can be no dispute, that this Parlia- ment, or one not far removed from it in order of succession, will have to do for England, Wales, and Scotland what has been so far accomplished for Ireland. There may be a sore struggle before the full measure of justice can be wrested from the reluctant grasp of the more selfish land-owning classes, but the battle will have to be fought. Necessity will bring the conflict on. Those who are crying out lustily for protection and for something like are-enactment of the Corn Laws are hastening it on. The Irish Church Act did not famish a model for future measures of its own kind, but it has led the way to something creeping nearer and nearer towards us every day. The Land Act, on the other hand, is more radical in its provisions, and its opera. tion in Ireland, once it has had the welcome and the trial to which it is fairly entitled, will inevitably sug- gest what may be and what ought to be done else- where. The laws affecting landlord and tenant lean to the one side, :re mandates of might, and are among the most intolerant and unjust pieces of legis- lation ever framed. These must be modified; many of them must be repealed; entirely new provisions must be introduced; and the legislature of this country will have to supply us with a reason for rejoicing that we live in a land in which justice means r find ebut u l s na in thereiturexpressing landlord the same thing for rich and poor. We like to say that such is the case now, and to some extent it is true; ajulittle enough of truth in it to justify the teahnoapnt treatedethatwe shwialltheraenlionang . partial hand, and the poorest citizen enabled not merely to demand, but to obtain, justice without being reduced to absolute beggary.

div.head: LOCAL NOTES.
div.p: LOCAL NOTES.

All manner of rumours are afloat as to what course the relatives of Mr. Treacy, of Church-street, Runcorn, who was drowned last week under such melancholy circum- stances, will adopt. Some say that a very large sum will be claimed from the London and North-Western Railway Company on behalf of his wife and Children; but there is.no doubt that if any heavy demand be made, it will be stoutly contested. I understand that the friends of Mr. Treacy have placed the matter in the hands of Messrs. Robert Davies, Sharp, and Kirkconnel, of Warrington, who are carefully considering what will be the best course to take under the circumstances. Many people in Runcorn seem to have come to the conclusion that the man Cox will be dismissed by the railway company, but this is a somewhat absurd thing to expect, as if he were sent about hisZbusiness, it would be as good as admitting that they were guilty of negligence, and therefore , bound to make reasonable compensation. Cox admitted, at the inquest, that his eyesight was not good, but he also stuck firmly to his

text that the captain of the flat was to blame for the acci- dent. Supposing the case went for trial it is scarcely to be supposed that a clevar counsel would neglect to place pro- minently before the jury at Nisi Prins the fact that it was exceedingly probable, and, indeed, almost certain, that in such circumstances the captain of the ferry boat would, for the sake of saving his own skin, take good care that every thing was done that would, to the best of his belief, tend to the safety of the vessel and its living freight. It might also reasonably be argued that it is not common sense to suppose Cox would, for the sake of obstinacy, pursue a course which involved the greatest risk to himself personally. If it be said that the man's eye-sight is failing, according to his own admission, it might be urged against this plea that a water- man cannot need very strong eyes to see a flat a consider- able distance at about two o'clock in the afternoon. No one can help deeply sympathising with the bereaved family in 11 their great loss, which was referred to in touching terms by the vicar of Widnes in his sermons on Sunday; but it will not do for the friends of Mr. Treacy to follow their sympathies entirely, and altogether ignore what may be said on behalf of the company. By-the-bye, a rather sad slip was made at the inquest by one of the com- pany's inspectors—a Mr. Peters, who was formerly station- master at Wrdnes, and has been promoted to the position of traffic inspector. Mr. Ferrand, from the solicitors' depart- ment, Lime-street, who should have been present at the opening of the inquest, was detained owing to being engaged in an important police case, and before he arrived, Cox was examined. I suppose that Mr. Peters must have become a little excited, mentally, on hearing the evidence offered by the man Cox, and he interpolated a remark to the effect that the witness did not know what he was talkingabout and had only had charge of the boat whilst the regular captain was ill ! The County Coroner (Mr. C. E. Driffield) then made the observation : "This is a very ugly speech on behalf of your company :" This would seem to intimate that though Mr. Peters may be a very good traffic inspector, he has not got a legal cast of mind There is still truth in the old proverb about the shoemaker sticking to his last. I understand that the Frodsham Volunteer Corps have been invited to form part of a guard of honour for H.R.11. the Prince of Wales on the occasion of the opening of the new docks at Liverpool on Thursday next, and to a man have loyally accepted the invitation. _

The Rev. Canon Barclay, vicar of Runcorn, has just issued his annual letter to his congregation and the parishioners, detailing the work of the religious and chari- tbe associations connected with that edidce. It will, no doubt, interest many of his Nonconformist brethren to know that the canon, who is considered to be pretty wise in his generation, though one of the children of light," and not belonging to that large body denominated " the children of this world," is of opinion the time is coming when the stipends of the ministers of the Church of England will have to be provided wholly by the voluntary contributions of the Church's members.

In is a pleasing thing to know that "the good time com- ing," of which Mackay sings, when right, not m4ght shall rule the day, is advancing, for it makes the pulses of a citizen who boasts that he "comes of fathers brave and free," to throb rather violently when he thinks of the proceedings of a dignitary of the church, as by law established, lately re- ported in the South of England, in selling by auction the fruits of the earth belonging.to another, in order that he may put the profits into his own pocket on account of tithes. In the times of James and King Charles, anything appeared to be thought good enough for English citizens who did not see fit to attend to a Parish Church, according to Lord Macauley's wonderful history of those stirring times. Noncon- formists have, however, now got rid of church rates, and the day is not very far off when tithes and all such prodnctions of an age of bigotry and intolerance will be consigned to the limbo of almost forgotten th;ngs. Lord Beaconsfield gave household suffrages to the workingmen of this country,—in all probability, merely on the ground of political expediency, and not from any love of right, for he. during a long course of years, was a violent opponent of the ex- tension of the suffrage—and when the School Boards of the country have done their work, and given the rising genera- tion an education free from the control of the vicar of the parish and his particular clique, the men of the future will sweep away from the statute book the iniquitous laws by which such seizures can for a moment be tolerated by free- men. It is amusing to read such sentences as the follow- ing, from the pen of a clergyman who professes to have faith in the assertion of sacerdotalists that the Church of Eng- land is expected to deal with the entire spiritual wants of every parish:—" How long this state of things may last it is difficult to say; for although the Liberation Society, which is avowedly hostile to the principle of state endow- ment by religion, or the alliance between Church and State, has not made any considerable progress of late years, yet the result of the general election has sent many avowed enemies of the Church into the House of Commons, who are already clamouring for their reward, and avow that they will be sati.fied with nothing less than the disestablish- ment and disendowment of the Church. And although the strength of the Church, considered as a spiritual society, would not be impaired by any such legislation, but would survive the shock, as she had already survived many, yet one cannot but tremble for the effect of such a proceeding upon both the temporal and spiritual interests of the mass of our people, especially in the rural districts, where the in- habitants are too sparse or too poor to pay the stipend of a minister. At present we have handed down to us an institu‘ tion coneoerated by ages, with all the machinery adapted to the state of society in which we live, a machinery wonder- fully well suited to our parochial life and ideas of local government." It is enough to raise the risible faculties of a constant reader of newspapers, to be told that the Liberation Society has not made any considerable progress of late. Such statements remind one of the saying that when the blind lead the blind they will both fall into the ditch.

A few weeks ago I referred to a very amusing instance of high life in the kitchen when a domestic servant installed her mother in the drawing-room during the absence of her master and mistress. This wcek I have come across a case which demonstrates the necessity of being very careful as to who we leave in charge of our residences during tem- porary absence. Last week a lady and gentleman. residing in a very respectable part of this town, went away for a few weeks change of air, leaving two servants in charge of some little boys and the family residence. On Sunday morning the younger servant went to chapel and on returning to dinner was astonished to find that two gentlemen (?) had been invited to spend the day there. These worthies made them- selves quite at home with their generous hostess, remaining until late, causing no small stir amongst a number of young ladies whose attention was called to the high life going on there the same evening. No doubt the " master " and "missis " will be more particular than ever in future as to whom they leave in charge of the " larder " when they go from home, and I rather fancy that the domestic referred to will not be so indiscreet as not to draw the blinds when she next allows her guests to ramble at will over the upper por- tion of the house.

Apparently the youth of Widnes are getting tired of the poor quality of the milk they obtain at home, for of late many cases have come under the notice of the police of youngsters climbing over fences and taking their fill from the cows' udders, to the intense disgust of the owners of the animals. Some of these youths were brought up before Mr. F. H. Gossaae, and warned what evil consequences they would meet with if they did not quit milk and take to some- thing more substantial.

The Rev. Mr. Collier, a rising young Wesleyan Methodist preacher, occupied the pulpit at Bethesda Congregational Chapel on Sunday evening, and during some telling remarks on the brevity of life, in illustration of the text, " So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom," took as his illustration the sad fate of the late Mr. Treacy, who was recently drowned. Mr. Collier, whilst making his appeal, described the deceased as a capital swimmer. Unfortunately, the poor fellow could not swim at all! I suppose the young preacher had not seen the last issue of the Examiner.

At the trial of Mr. Clough, a country traveller to Mr. Randle, of Bridge-street, Runcorn, for embezzlement, at the Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, an incident was wit- nessed which has given rise to much comment in the town. This was the exhibition of interest in Mr. Clough, shown by his master, which was cartied so far that at the close of the proceedings the two shook hands very heartily. It is certainly rather strange to see a prosecutor walk up to a prisoner, who has upon his own evidence, been sent to gaol a month, and give him a hearty shake of the hand. Perhaps this is A new version of the story of Damon and Pythias, the two Syracusian youths who carried their friend- ship to such a length as to win the admiration of Dionysius the tyrant. Perhaps the poor prisoner was grateful for his employer's request to the Bench that he should be leniently dealt with; but the mere prosecution is enough to injure dough's reputation for life. Mr. Henry Johnson, clerk to Mr Marwood, ship broker, Runcorn, is the winner of the appropriation of £2OO in con- nection with the Runcorn Starr-Bowkett Society. This en- titles him to the loan of the sum for 12.12- years, free of interest. There is a saying tolhe effect that it is better to be born lucky than rich, and this is in sometmeasure illustrated in the case of Mr. Johnson, who only entered the society on the same day as the appropriation took place. The wind of popular favour is at times, something like the trade winds met with in certain parts of the glope, and blows gaily in one direction for a considerable time. But the love of the populace is very similar to that of the male flirt, on that coquette—it is given to change. lam led into this train of thought by a consideration of the election of Runcorn Commissioners which has taken place this week, and resulted in the complete downfall of what an humourist might be inclined to style The Marshall-Dobson Ministry. Both these gentlemen had apparently been " wanting" on being weighed in'the so des of public opinion. The bare contemplation of a return which puts down the late chairman of the Board as only polling 43 votes, against Mr. W. Whittaker. 724, aud a young gentlemen so new to public life as Mr. Lake solicitor, 651, completely staggers one. What is it that has brought about this sudden change? Perhaps the remarks of Mr. Marshall and Mr. Dobson in regard to Sunday funerals; perhaps the fierce disputes of the former gentleman with Dr. Steele and Dr. McDougall complete the Vyrnwy invitation tickets. Certainly such a collapse has not been known iu Runcorn for a long time. FLACCUS.

A WIDNES MAN KILLED IN CALIFORNIA.—The follow- ing is from the Daily Examiner, San Francisco, July 9th, 1881 :—" A Journalist's Death. Richard Ileyes falls through the S.P.C.R.R. Trestle-Work.—Richard Heyes, a well-known San Francisco journalist, was killed while crossing the narrow-guage trestle-work at Alameda, between MT. Haight's residence and the oil works. He was found by the pas.en- gers of the 6 p.m. train dead from the effects of a fractured skull and dislocated shoulder. It is supposed that he fell through the trestle-work and was injured by striking against the cross-beams. lie was a native of England, aged 43. Mr. Heyes was one of the founders of the Sand Lot, and ars° started the Weekly Union, a campaign paper. For the past year he has written sporting articles and reports of pigeon 'matches for the Gall, Chronicle, and Examiner. He resided with Mr. Bird, at Bird's Point, Alameda. He was much liked and trusted by all who knew him, and his loss is deeply felt by all of his many friends. The coroner's in- quest on the body of the late Richard Heyes resulted in a verdict that death was mimed by falling oil the cars while under the influence of a fit of .apoplexy." The deceased gentleman was born at Crow-wood, Whines, and educated by Mr. Moss at the Crow-wood School, and was son of the late Mr. Wm. Heyes, file manufacturer, of Appleton, and brother of Mr. Joseph Heyes, Halton View.

RUNCORN AND DISTRICT 406 m STARR-BOWRETT SOCIETY.—This society, which consists of 131 members, and has upwards of £23,000 worth of shares already issued, held its first appropriation meeting on Wednesday evening, in the Lecture Room of the Public Hall. Mr. T. B. Jones, of Liverpool, presided, and Mr. W. J. Davies, was also present. The room was crowded. Mr. J. Barcroft, of Ramsbottom, delivered a very interesting'and telling address in explana- tion of the society's principles. The first business which followed was the election of five arbitrators for the purpose of deciding any dispute which might arise amongst the members. The following names were submitted and received the number of votes appended :—Rev. Canon Barclay 34, Messrs. John Simpson 38, G. S. Hazlehurst 37, Roht. Shaw 34, Richard Lea 26, John Brundrit, J.P., 13, Wm. Whittaker 13, Thomas Povey 11. The first five were accordingly declared elected. The next business before the meeting was the election of scrutineers, and Messrs. Albert Povey and Thomas Povey were selected, after which Mr. Barcroft gave a very lucid explanation of the manner in which the ballot was conducted. The balloting was then proceeded with amidst considerable excitement. It was conducted with much ability, and a lad was appointed to draw the numbers. Mr. Henry Johnson, shipbrokers' clerk, Ashridge-street, who had only joined the society that day, was declared the win- ner of an appropriation of £2OO, amidst considerable ap- plause.

RUNCORN, WESTON, AND HALTON WATEDIVOLICS COMPANY.—HALF-YEARLY MEETING.—The shareholders of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company held their half-yearly meeting on Monday afternoon, at the Public Hall, Mr. Jobs Brundrit, chairman of directors, pre- siding. Amongst those present were Messrs. John Simpson and Wm. Whittaker (directors), J. Rigby, James Shaw, Peter Smith, R. Collier, and W. F. Saikeld (secretary). It was agreed that the report, which has already appeared in The Examiner, should be taken as read.—The secretary next laid before the meeting the report of Messrs. Ralph Forester and R. B. Toft, the auditors.—The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the report, expressed his regret that it was not of quite so favourable a character as the one for the preceding six months. The causes which had led to their having to present it, were circumstances over which the directorate had no control. One of the great causes was the severity of last winter, which necessarily forced a con- siderably increased expenditure upon them. One item was that of fuel, which during the preceding winter had been very difficult to obtain, owing to the stoppage of the canal, the blocking of the railways by the severe storms, and the strike of colliers. Although they had made a very good contract for coal at the rate of ss. 11d. per ton, the strike clause, as in all contracts of such a nature, was inserted, and they had to make the best purchases they possibly could elsewhere, and in some cases they had to pay nearly double the ordinary price. Again, avast quantity of water was wilfully wasted by the public. Many people, to prevent their taps being frozen, left them running at full bore, and the consequence was that much valuable water was wasted. The company found this to be so by sending inspectors round, and it was very diffi- cult to keep up the supply when it was wasted by such means. They therefore had to pump night and day, which caused a very heavy expeuse, and their expenditure instead of being less owing to a lesser quantity of water being used at the works was very much increased. The depression in trade, not only in small matters but in their large works, also was a very serious matter. One large works which paid them something like £250 was completely stopped, and this was almost the 2-1- per cent. with which they paid the dividend last half-year. In addition to this they had also had to repair both their boilers. They were.very large, and having been in use for ten or eleven years, needed very extensive overhauling. They had been put in thorough repair with the best iron. The decrease in the expenditure had not been through any negiect on the part of the employes, nor through any in-attention of the directors. There had been no diminution in the supply of water to the pumps, but the waste, as he had pointed out, had been very damaging. They had now every reason for hoping, now trade was better, that a better balance sheet would be shown next half-year, and that they would be able to show what they called a proper dividend of five per cent. They had extended their mains to Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele's Nvorks, and to the new works on the Sprinch, which he understood would require a large quantity of water.—Mr. Simpson seconded the motion, and it was unanimously carried.—Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. W. Whittaker, who retired from the directorate, were ' unanimously re-elected, en the motion of Mr. Smith, I seconded by Mr. Shaw.—Mr. R. Forester was unanimously re- elected one of the auditors of the company, on the motion of Mr. Whittaker, seconded by Mr. Collier.—On the pro- position of Mr. Shaw, seconded by Mr. Collier, a vote of thanks was unanimously accorded to the chairman for pre- siding.—A similar compliment having been paid to the secretary for his services in connection with the company, the proceedings terminated.

THE SOUTHPORT BANK. At ten o'clock on Monday morning the doors of the Southport and West Lancashire Banking Company (Limited) were reopened, after having been doled since the 17th of January last. All depositc,rs in the old bank who presented cheques on the new company (after having signed a transfer of their accounts) were promptly paid. Many of the creditors having signed agree- ments to allow their accounts to remain in the new bank, there is now plenty of money in the coffers for any emer- gency. One of the first accounts which was withdrawn was that of the Southport Corporation, which amounts to £27,000. Mr. Currie. late of the Preston Bank (Southport branch), has been appointed manager.
