I THE IMPRISONED RITIIII,IST.—According to a letter 1 by Mr. Belcher, of Stoke Newington, the Rev. F. S. Green, of Miles Platting, has not a very good time of it in Lancas- ter Gaol. He says his health has broken down, and he will probably die if he is not liberated. As Mr. Dillon, M.P., has recently received his unconditional release by the Gov- ernment on the score of ill health, Mr. Belcher suggests that the same clemency should be extended to Mr. Green. Speak- ing of the rev, gentleman's quarters, the correspondent adds :—" He is confined in a large whitewashed room.which formerly was used as a hospital ward, the hospital furniture being pushed hither and thither in various directions, so as to make an area for the prisoner in the centre, before the fireplace. At one end, very high up, like the east window in a church, is a large window, secured with double or treble bars inside. The whole aspect is dreary and lonesome in the extreme."

LANcasunan FrxaxcE.— On Thureday the Treasurer for the county of Lancaster issued his repart for the year which terminated on the 31st of T.laj last. The report shows that the total sum expended during the year on lunatic asylums and the matetenanCo of lunatics was £143,771, as compared with £104,438 for the previous twelve months. The sum of £17,419 has been spent during the year on the administration of justice in the county, ex- clusive of the salaries paid to a large number of officials. The police force of the county has cost £131,524 during the year, from which must be deducted the amount received in aid of the rates from the Treasury, namely, £69,227. Fees and fines received in the various police divisions amount to £16,177, as compared with £10,071 in the pre- ceding year. Prosecutions at assizes and sessions have cost the shire £13,697, as against £15,312 for the previous twelve months. The report of the County Finance Committee, which was also issued on Thursday, states that the extra expenditure incurred in consequence of the riots which oc- curred in the colliery districts in the early part of this year amounted to £3,056. It also explains that owing to the brief interval which has elapsed since the passing of the Lancashire County Justices Act, 1881, the Committee have have not been able to prepare any plan for the issue of county stock.

EDDISBURY LICENSING BUSINESS.—The annual licen- sing sessions of this division were held on Monday at the Court House, Oakmere, before Messrs. S. Woodhouse, E. A. Wright, and IV. Forster. Superintendent Naylor presented the following report:—" My Lord and Gentlemen,—l have the honour to present to you my annual report with refer- ence to the conduct of the licensed victuallers and beersellers in this division. The number of licensed victuallers is 86; beersellers, 41; others who sell off the premises, 14; total, 141; giving an average of 226 of the population to each license. The number of licensed victuallers proceeded against last year was 15, and 11 convicted, including one license endorsed; this year four, and three convicted, and one to be heard to-day. Beesellers proceeded against last year three, and one convicted; this year none proceeded against. Persons convicted of drunkenness last year, 159: this year, 114; decrelse, 45. Several samples have been submitted to the county analyst during the past year. In two cases the articles were returned as adulterated, and pro- ceedings were taken against the persons for selling same. Each person was fined 20s. and costs. I have also much pleasure in stating that drunkenness is decreasing in this division."—Mr. E. A. Wright asked where the superinten- dent was stationed before he came to Oakmere.—Superinten- dent Naylor said he had previously been at Crewe; and, in reply to t urther questions, said drunisellileBb V.aa on the de- crease in Crewe last year, but it was a very fluctuating place; it would be very quiet for a few weeks, and then there would be a "general hurricane." (Laughter.)—The existing licenses were renewed, there being no opposition.

STRANGE DISAPPEARANCE OF Two GIRLS ruom CitESTlnt —For several days past the Chester police have been try- ing to trace the whereabouts of two girls tvho disappeared mysteriously from the city on Friday, the 3.9 th inst. They are both very respectably connected, and bad for a few months been learning the millinery business at a leading establishment in Chester. It has been discovered that two or three weeks ago they answered in assumed names an advertisement which appeared in a Liverpool paper for two young women to learn the profession of actresses. On ' the morning of the 19th inst., they received a telegram ask- ing them to proceed to Mrnchcster to meet a man. Later in the day they received a second telegram, appointing Liverpool instead of Manchester for the interview, and they left for the former place by the 8 o'clock train that evening. Inquiries have disclosed tht they arrived and met some man, and the next morning proceeded, it is believed to Man- chester. Here all trace has for the present been lost. The friends of the girls, bearing in mind recent disclosures re- specting the exportation of English girls to the Continent, are naturally much alarmed. The elder of the two is 19 and the other 15 years old. Searching inquiries subsequently made resulted in the police being enabled to give informa- tion as to the whereabouts of the young women who were discovered at a house in Manchester, and their friends were at once communicated with. After some demur the young women consented to accompany their friends, and were brought back to Chester. The matter will, we understand, be thoroughly investigated. The mother of one of the girls writing to a Manchester contemporary says :—"I feel it my duty, as well as pleasure, to ask you to allow me to say that through the persevering tact and zeal of the detective force of Manchester, Chester' and Liverpool the girls have been discovered and returned to their homes. I will also take this public opportunity of giving expression to the strongest feel- ings of gratitude to the aforementioned officers for their energy, and also to yourself and the press generally for their kindness in giving publicity to the matter, and so assisting in effecting their rescue from what otherwise would have been their utter ruin: I would say that with respect to the future of the girls no doubt remains but that ultimately they would have been exported to those continental miseries of which we have heard so much of late. As your report stated, they were allured by the promise of an engagement for the stage. and being simple and unsuspecting, were easily laid hold of; but, as we have become convinced by their ten days' experience, they were being led, not to the stage of the drama but to the horrible stage of real continental tragedy." MR. BRIGGS'S MARRIAGE REGISTRATION 13/IL.—The following is the text of this bill, which was brought into the House of Commons in the last days of the session now closed, and which was in the usual:. way ordered to be printed : A Bill to render unnecessary the presence of civil registrars at Nonconformist and other marriages, and to make provision in lieu thereof. Be it enacted by the Queen's most Excellent Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Lords Spiritual and Temporal, and Commons, in this present Parliament assembled, and by the authority of the same, as follows :
- 1. This Act may be cited for all purposes as the Marriage Registration (England) Act, 1881. 2. This Act shall ot extend to Scotland or Ireland.

3. This Act shall come into--fOrce on the first day of January, one thousand eight hundred and eighty-two. 4. The presence of a registrar shall not be necessary at a mar- riage in a building registered for solemnising marriages the em, any law to the contrary notwithstanding. 5. On the ,cession of a marriage solemnised in any such registered building the certificates or licenses required by law shall be delivered to the priest, minister, or person pfficlitting, who shall, immediately after the marriage ceremony is com- pleted, fill up the certificate according to the form 'D in the schedule hereto, and cause the same to be signed by the parties contracting the marriage and by the witnesses, not being less than two, and shall himself sign and deliver, or send by regis- tered post letter, the same to the superintendent registrar of the union, parish, or place, tohe kept by him as the Registrar- General shall direct, with others of the like kind, in the form and as part of the marriage register. Any person who shall refuse or omit without reasonable excuse so to deliver or send or to regi,ter the said certificate shall forfeit a sum not exceed- ing fifty pounds for every such offence. f 3. The form D in the schedule hereto shall be printed in such manner and type as the Registrar-General shall direct and furnish to the superintendent registrars of unions, parishes, or places, and all persons who have given the notices and obtained the certificates or licenses by law required shall be entitled to receive and have the same form D from the superintendent registrar on payment, of the fee of one shilling. 7. This Act shall be read together and as part of the Marriage and Registration Acts pas•ed in the sixth and seventh years of the reign of King William the Fourth, chapter eighty-five, intituled "An Act for Marriages in England. 7 and chapter eighty-six, intituled "An Act for registering Births, Deaths, and Marriages in England," and in the nineteenth and twen- tieth years of the reign of Her Majesty, intituled "An Act to amend the provisions of the Marriage and Registration Acts," and together with all Acts amending the same or incorporated therewith. The bill is backed by Mr. Briggs, Mr. Hopwood, Mr. Borlass, Mr. B. and Mr. D. O'Connor.

- THE 'VICAR OF RUNCORN AND THE FRIENDLY. EOCIETIES. On Sunday afternoon, the Rev. Canon Barclay, M.A., vicar of Runcorn, preached a sermon to the members of the various Friendly Societies in that town, in the Public Hall, from I Cor. 12 C. 27 v.: "Now are ye the body of Christ, and members in particular." The rev, gentleman remarked that he saw before him a large assembly of persons who had very great differences one with another. There were members of very different shades in polities and certainly very different shades of religion, but there was one principle which he thought animated them all, and that was a desire for unity, concord, and charity; a desire to provide for themselves against a rainy day; and if, by God's blessing, they should never want help them- selves, that they might like Christian men and brothers help those who were in necessity and need. It was hardly necessary, he thought, to remind them of the conditions of a Friendly Society. 3.'4/ a workiugman who bad to earn his bread by toil, and who might be prevented by accident or sickness from earning the wages upon which he and his family depended for subsistence, it was absolutely necessary that he should be a member of a Friendly Society or Benefit Club. This principle was not overlooked or less acted upon by those in a higher rank in life. No matter what a man's • income might be, if he had only a life-interest in that in- come he considered it to be a Christian and a social duty to make some provision during his lifetime for the members of his family when he himself should be no more. This he usually did by what was called insurance, which secured some provision against sickness, old age, and death. In fact there was no person exempted from liability, except perhaps the highest in the land. The principle was the same however the provision was made, through whatever channel the contributions were paid. It was laudable to guard against the sickness and accidents to which flesh was heir; and the principle was to be commended both OR worldly and religious grounds. It was universally acknow- ledged that nothing kept down the working classes so much as living from hand to mouth, and that nothing would better their condition so much as the possession of a little capital. A man saw an opening for commencing a little business on his own account, but was only prevented by the lack of a little capital, and thus he remained the same as before. If sickness came upon him or an interruption of work, such as occurred at Runcorn last winter, or a difficulty arose between masters and employers, the workingman way dependent upon the precarious charities of the public or upon the funds of the Trades' Union ; and these were some- times utterly inadequate to keep the bulk of their property from the pawnshop or prevent their getting into debt with their tradesmen. Sunday clothes were worn out, and ne money to replace them, and they had to pay 25 per cent. more for them by weekly payments than they would if they paid for them atet-lee. He did not consider it at all incone sistent with his position as a minister of Christianity to urge them to save their money, not merely for the sake of having money, but for the sake of providing against adverse times. Upon social grounds he might use the command of St. Paul to the Thessalonians to study, to be quiet, and to do their own business, to work with their hands that they might walk honesty toward them that were without, and that they might lack nothing. When he spoke of making this provision on religious grounds he did so as a minister of Christianity. Could they tell him which of the two men the drunkard and the spendthrift, or the steady and sober man, was most accessible to the influence of religion? Was it not a fact that the wastrels formed a class of men who were the heart-breaks of the minister of religion, the scrip- ture reader and the visitor? He would earnestly recommeed every man, whatever his position in life may be, and especi- ally the workingman, to enrol himself as a member of a Friendly Society or Benefit Club, so that when the rainy day came suddenly upon him he would be prepared for it. As he was speaking in a secular and not a sacred building he thought he might fairly say a word as to the principles which should regulate their clubs. He was not a member of any club himself, having adopted that principle of insurance which he mentioned at the outset, therefore he was not commending any particular club to their notice. There where certain rules which ought to regulate their Societies, and the non-observance of which was sure ta bring them to insolvency and ruin. First he would recommend them to be careful about having good tables. By this he meant so that every member might pay in proportion to his age. He did not think it was a fair thing that a young man of 18 or 20shou1d have to pay as muchasa man of 40 or 45. The latter was twenty years nearer the time when he was cer- tain to meet with a certain amount of sickness. The average sickness of a man at 45 was two weeks in the year, while from 18 to 35 it only averaged two or three days. The Manchester Unity was the first to take up this matter, ' and the result of their labours had been yery satisfactory. I Good management WRS indispensable and should be divided between active and honorary members. The former because they had the greatest interest in the club, and the latter because they generally belonged to a business class and knew where to place the funds to derive the greatest benefit. Persons when pining a Society make sure that it is tegis- tered according to law, for if not there was not the slightest remedy against anyone who chose to swindle them. He knew that most most clubs adopted the principles he had mentioned but perhaps there was no harm in mentioning them. They had provided against their worldly necessities, but he now came to speak of their spiritual wants, and he might now speak about that great organization founded 1850 years ago. This great Friendly Club was the Catholic Church, which, regularly hold its club days and feast. This Society had been originated for the salvation of the soul, and heasked them to avail themselves of all the opportunities which the Great Benefit Society offered them. They thought it their bounden duty to provide against the wants .of the perishmg bud; , bec o eea I.l,Thar duty th... this to their Creator, and as well as providing for the wants of the body he impressed upon Vim tho iroossity of pro- viding for the wants of their never-dying souls. A collection was made at the close to defray expenses. I Before the service a procession numbering about 170 mem- bers of Friendly Societies formed in Devonshire-square and marched to the Public Hall.

div.head: STATE OF THF, CROPS,
div.p: THE STATE OF THF, CROPS,

FBODS HAM AND DISTRICT.—Root crops: Early potatoes I have been a complete failure. We think one-half of those in the district will not be paid for seed, labour, and railway freight, and those that were left to grow for seed for another year have now got the disease in them very bad in damp fields. Second mlaps, such as mangolds and turnips, those that were planted late in June or early in July, are getting on very nicely in fields that are in good condition; but the later planted ones will be a failure unless we have a very fine open back end of the year. Hay and grass pastures very light; a few early pieces of clover got pretty good. Hay crops, all on the marshes, about 12 cwt. per acre; a deal under that. There is a large quantity out yet, which has been much damaged by the weather. After-grass is grow- ing very badly. Corn crops: Wheat is very thin on the ground, but very fairly fed in places. Oats very short and very thin in places. Barley not much grown here. Beans only half podded, and blighted in a many places. Our cor- respondent adds—"! have been in the farming class for over 20 years, and don't recollect a time equal to this, taking bad seasons, bad prices, bad crops, nay, I may say, everything bad alike. I honestly believe this year to be the most unsuccessful and the worst year farmers in this district ever experienced."

INVEST AT WARRINGTON.—The county coroner, Mr. Driffield, held an inquest at the Woolpack Inn, Sankey- street, on Monday, as to the cause of death of John Powell, 61 years of age, sexton of St. John's Baptist Church, Chester. The circumstances of the case were fully re- ported in the last issue of The Examiner. The son of the deceased, John Powell, plumber and painter, Mount Pleasant, Liverpool, where deceased had been paving a visit, said his father enjoyed health when with him and had not been under the doctor's hands for some time.—Dr. Fox, who was called in, stated that the cause of death ITU heart disease. The jury returned a verdict of "death from natural causes."

FOUND DEAD IN TUE MERSEY AT WARRIN GTON.— On Tuesday, at the Bridge Inn, Latchford, the coroner, Mr. Yates, held an inquest on the body of a female child, found on the bank of the river Mersey, near Latchford Weir, on Monday morning by a labourer named James Phillips. The child was wrapped up in a piece of the lining of a dress and jacket, and appeared as if left by the receding tide. Dr. T. Starkey Smith, who had made a post-mortem examination of the body, said the child was not fully grown. There were no marks of violence on the body, and he was of opinion that the child died either before or immediately after birth, and that the cause of death was premature birth. If it had been born alive it could not certainly have lived many minutes. The coroner remarked that this was the second case within six weeks of finding a dead body in the Mersey. It seemed to be a receptacle for that sort of thing. The jury returned a verdict of "Found dead." Sotrm-WitsT Lexcesrung GOOD TEXPLLII3. —On Saturday the District Lodge of the South-West Lancashire Good Templars held their quarterly session in the Wesleyan schook-room, Dicconson-et., Wigan. There was .a numerous attendance of representatives, members, and Visitors. Mr. Robert Williams presided until the arrival of Mr. Malins, of Birmingham, when be vacated the chair in the latter's faveur.—The District Secretary reported that ninety-five lodges were working, with 4,722 members.—Mr. Stephen Pugh, the treasurer, reported that he had received from all sources the sum of £47 Os. 2d., and expended £46 12s. 4d., leaving a balance in hand of 163. 10d.—The District Secre- tary also presented the report of the Executive, which con- tained the following clause, and to which exception was taken, but the whole of the reports were adopted "Several meetings and special sessions have been held—one an intended united conference of the West Cheshire, Welsh, and the English South-West Lancashire District Lodge Executives ; supposed armour bearers valiant in their several spheres. The result did not warrant the outlay of cost, and we propose being more careful in accepting SUR- gestions in a similar direction. 'The sugar was wasted? " The following motions were carried :—" That district lodges have the privilege of electing orrefusing to appoint electoral deputies ;" "that when an executive officer neglects to attend four consecutive meetings of the committee, his office shall be declared vacant ;" "that the next place of meeting be left with the executive ;" and "that a procession of the members present be formed to walk to the Public Hall, King-street," where a public temperance meeting was subse- quently held, under the presidency of the Rev. E. Franks. The district lodge closed in the usual manner.

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

The Democratic Federation 'will hold & convention ite London on the I.sth instant. Gazer Corrow STRIKE:A strike has commenced among the cotton handlers of New'Orleans, by which 10,000 more or less skilled labourers are affected, and the movement of cotton is checked. Intelligence from Galveston and Mobile reports the existence of similar strikes at those places.

Mr. William Lee Howard, who was sent in April last by the United States Geographical Society to Ireland to ex- plore the less known parts of that island, returned to London on Thursday, and leaves to-day for New York. Mr. Howard, states that the icebergs will be from one to two months later in becoming detached this year from the shores of that island, and hence will be met with much out of the usual time by vessels crossing the Atlantic.

TYPBOLD FEYER IN Onntasrecur.—A serious outbreak of typhoid fever in one of the Rev. Mr. Muller's orphanage houses, at Ashley Down, near Bristol, was officially reported on Thursday by the medical officer, who said that 60 of the children are down in the disease, and that some deaths must occur. In the five houses there are 2,000 children, but the epidemic has been confined to one of the buildings. It is supposed that impure wed water is the cause of the out- break.

It is asyet uncertain how many have perished by the wreck of the Teuton on the treacherous coast off Quoin Point. The• Directors of the Union Company have telegraphed to their agent for the fullest information, but at present-nothing is known beyond the scanty information contained in a few brief telegrams. The Directors, of course, hope that the sad loss of life may prove to be somewhat less than announced on Thursday, and indeed they have been advised that another beat containing nine persons reached Cape Town a ' midnight on Wednesday. They believed that another boat with about thirty women and children may turn up. Mr. Osborne Morgan, M.P., speaking at Lieu rWst, yester- day, said that the church of the future, whether it was to be the Church of England or of any other denomination, must depend more or less upon the voluntary principle which in Wales had been carried out with such excellent re- sults, there being a chapel in every hamlet and upon almost every green hillock, lie believed the Sunday Closing Act for Wales, and the recent commission for higher education in the Principality would be attended with beneficial results, and pointed out that the Buria/s Act, despite the prophecies to the contrary, was operating quietly.

Mr. Henry Richard, M.P., presided at Thursday's pro- ceedings in connection with the National Eisteddfod at Merthyr. In the course of a pithy defence of the institution he showed that Wales had produced a fair proportion of highly distinguished men, and that vrhile the Welsh had been heavily handicapped in the race of life, in point of original faculty they were equal to any other nation, and only required fairplay, for the means of education were afforded them.

Sir Stafford Northcote was one of the guests at the Shef- field Cutlers' Feast on Thursday, and responded to the toast of the House of Commons. Speaking of the suggested reform of the mode of procedure in the House, he said it would be very easy to upset what was good, and perhaps to root up a great deal of wheat with the tares. He warned the reformer not to confuse mere symptoms with the disease, ant to take care not to destroy that which was a valuable preserver of our liberties. The House of Commons was the guardian of our privileges, and at the same time it furnished us with the opportunity of grumbling which was the dearest of all things to the hearts of Englishmen. The Earl of Wharscliffe and the Duke of Norfolk spoke to other toasts. In a characteristic speech the Duke of Rutland denounced "one-sided Free Trade," and aslind where we were to seek a remedy for the present depressed condition of commerce and agriculture.

PRESIDENT GARFIELD'S CONDITION. The following telegram was received yesterday, at the American Legation, in London :—" The President continues to do wel! in his eating and digestion, and the swollen gland steadily improves; but in the past twenty-four hours he has made no substantial progress in his general condi- tion. In the judgment of his physicians, however, he still bolds the ground gained on Saturday and Monday. His pulse and temperature yesterday have shown marked in- crease over the record of Thursday. The weather has been exceedingly warm and sultry, and this may account in part for the adverse changes noted. Even in the September climate of Washington such an oppressive day as this has been is rare.—(Signed) BLAINE, Secretary." NORTH LINCOLNSHIRE ELECTION. The following is the result of the Werth Lincolnshire election:— Lowther (C) 4,200 Tomline (L)

Majority 471 NORTH DURHAIVI ELECTION. The poll opened yesterday at eight o'clock. and during the morning one constant stream of electors poured into the balloting stations. In the afternoon there was a perceptible ailing off, but neither side Telma :efforts until the puma ,Ivacal •T polled heavily, but so far as could be ascertained the Irish vote was given for the Conservative in accordance with Mr. Parnell's advice. Mr. Lowther's victory for North Lincoln was the occasion for much jubilation among; Conserva- tives, and the figures were posted throughout the ceastitv- ency. The result will be declared to-day.

THOMAS COOPER, POET AND EE-CHARTIST.—One of the last remains of the actors in the Chartist agitation about 1840 Is Thomas Cooper, a fervid patriot and an honest man, who was driven by the sufferings of the people 40 years ago to dream of desperate remedies. He suffered imprisonment, but his genius blazed out in his "Purgatory of Suicides." In his old age this gifted man is very poor, and to befriend him Mr. Mundella and Mr. Forster, with more than 70 other members of Parliament, have signed a memorial to the Government on his behalf. By the grace of the Queen, a gift of £3OO has been conferred on him from the royal bounty, and this, aided by donations from Mr. Mundella, Mr. Forster, Mr. Morley, Mr. Seely, and Mr. Cowen, has secured to Mr. Cooper an annuity for life of £lOO. The Right Hons. W. E. Forster and A. J. Mundella are the trustees. Mr. Gladstone has warmly sympathised with the effort. During his last short illness he read Cooper's autobiography with great pleasure.

THE PROPOSED VOLTINTER REVIEW la PRESTON.—It iS stated on good authority that the tenant under the Preston Corporation has refused the use of Moor Park for the pro- posed volunteer review at Preston, to be held during the present month. This will render it impossible to hold the review on the extensive scale originally planned, which con- templated a muster of 10,000 men. It is understood that, in consequence of this unforeseen difficulty, a plan of the Marsh has been prepared and forwarded to General Cameron, C. 8., commanding the Northern District, with a view to the review being held there. The troops of Fnlwood Garrison and local and other volunteer corps will take part in the review, which we are given to understand is fixed for the 17th instant. The character of the ground at the Marsh will, however, render any military manoeuvres impossible except the march past, which, it is expected, will be of a very imposing character.
WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. (Continued from Page 6.)

FRlDAY.—Before Captain Reynolds, Mr. John White, and Mr. Ziba Armitage. CAUGHT IN THE TR.AP.—An old woman named Ann Phillips was charged with begging.—On the previous after- noon, prisoner stopped P.C. Cokeley, who was in plain clothes, in Bold-atreet, and asked him for a penny. He afterwards saw her stop four ether persons, and he took her into custody.—She was committed to gaol for seven days.

Vaanewcy.—Elizabeth Agnes Darcy and Margaret Ann Webb, two young girls, who stated they came from Liver- pool, were charged with being vagrants.—At about three o'clock that morning, the prisoners were found sleeping in the porch of a house in Liverpool-road, and taken into custody. They stated they were in search of work.—The prisoners were remanded until Monday, for inquiries to be made about their parents. WOMEN AT VARIANCE.—Mary Woods was summoned for assaulting Mary Walsh, on the 27th ult., and Mary Woods had issued a cross-summons against Mrs. Walsh.—The latter stated that she went into Mr. Jolly's house, on School- ' brow, on.Saturdav night. Mrs. Woods was "sitting on old Mr. Jolly's knee," and commenced at once to call witness bad names. Witness then struck her.—The Bench bound both parties over to keep the peace for six months, in one surety of £5. THE MAINTENANCE OF GRAN'D-CHILDREN.--Geo. Hil- lidge, a flatman, was summoned to show cause why be should not contribute towards the support of his five grand-children, who were inmates of the Warrington Workhouse. The Board of Guardians asked for an order for 5s per week. An order for that amount was made upon the defendant, who did not appear.

COUNTY Pols= CasEs.—Lt the Occasional Court House, Bank-street, on Thursday, before Mr. Robert Pier- point, John Earle was charged with assaulting a woman named Mary Caldwell, at Antrobus, on the 31st August. The proseeutrix did not wish to press the charge, and the prisoner was bound over to keep the peace for six months.— Yesterday, at the Court House in Horsemarket-street, a woman named Sarah Ellen Wilkinson was charged with sleeping in an outhouse at Sankey on the let September. She was remanded to the Petty Sessions on the 7th el- tember.

MONARCHY IN RELATION TO THE EMPIRE, &c, "Put not your trust in Princes."—Psl. cxlvi. 3. Sir,—Neglecting the sound piece of advice which I gave to him and his co-thinkers in my last communication, to be quiet and not to burden the shaky old institution he is defending by piling more reasons upon it than it can bear, to shield it from the winds of argument, and above all to keep away the earthquake of popular investigation from its rotten foundations, Mr. A. Bennett has been trying to show me, what he is pleased to call, reasons in favour of our monarchical system. Neglecting the first, upon which he I evidently places great value, 'the thousand leaping swords," ac., as being too childish to be worth a moment's thought. (for does even Arthur Bennett seriously think that the people of England would brook the interference of any out- siders if they had once determined to make their govern- ment the free government of a free people?) neglecting this, let us see if we can pick some more plums out of this rather overdone monarchical pudding. Mr. Bennett allows his imagination to outrun his judgment in supposing thatth e British Empire is sapported by such a broken reed as : Royalty; if it has no better prop than that then indeed is its disintegration at hand. But here is one of the plums turned up—" eclat is lent to great and important national gatherings by it,"—that is to say it is a kind of regal fire. work that feces and cracks, at a cost of a thousand pounds a day, for the delectation of the upper ten. Another—" its members work (sic) hard' for the good of the country," Yes, but I have never • heard of any of them dying through over-exertion, although I will admit that the pursuit of pleasure is the hardest work a man can follow. And here is another, a bouncer, "its soldiers can -fight and die for a common sovereign as they could not for a republican section." I would not give much for the man, be he soldier or civilian, who would not defend his country in preference to a name. I think the civil war in the United States was rather a big thing in its way, and it needed not the stimulus of hereditary irrespon- sibility to make these republicans fight for their cherished institution. Bat, sir, the whole question lies in a nut-shell. Suppose that we awoke some fine morning and found that some political earthquake had swallowed this institution; would there be found ten sane men in the country to advo- cate its restitution? I think not. And an institution not worth restoring is certainly not worth retaining. By a curious coincidence your last impression contained two articles, the one a strong commentary on the other—Mr. Bennett's letter and your Parliamentary column—in which it was stated that the Royal assent was given by commission to thirty-one public and private bills (including the Irish Land Law Bill). Now if the onerous duties of royalty can be thus summarily shuffled off by commission—that is, by proxy—could they not be done without altogether? Again, the power of assenting implies also the power of veto—the forbidding of some bill agreed upon by the country through their representatives in Parliament. Now just try toimagine this veto to be put on such a bill as the Irish Land Law Bill! The very idea of such a conflict between the Crown and its so-called subjects the people, is pre-eminently absurd, and could only end in the defeat and removal of this semblance of sovereignty. The thing, as it is, is an acted lie, a hollow sham, and therefore cannot long stand the questioning it will get. To be compelled to pay any sum, however small, for which nothing is given in return,is a robbery; and in this case there is the added sting of seeing the money spent in maintaining a lot of useless people in a state of gilded idle- ness. Can any human being make himself worth the nation spending a thousand pounds a day in keeping him? The enormous sums of money annually spent in keeping up this show were voted away when the greet majority of the people of this country had no voice in the legislature. Since then Parliament has seen fit to bestow the franchise upon this outlying majority. Now that they have a voice in the legislature, it is only right and proper to give them the opportunity of saying whether this office shall be filled again by an over-paid smecurist. Mr. Bennett talks of a millennial democracy. Why, the Government:of England is democratic in all but name. The House of Commons, as representing the people, is the sole and ultimate director of national affairs. Where they are determined the other two anomalies—the hereditary and irresponsible branches— the Crown and House of Lords, must either give way or succumb. These are nineteenth century facts, and not millennial fancies. Then, if we are democratic in all but name, why not let the name drop, and with it this enormous and useless waste of public money? Vox populi may not be vox dei, and, indeed, sometimes may have a lower and darker origin; but, as we have lost faith in the Divine right of kings to rule wrung, the will of the majority of our fellow citizens must determine the policy of the country, and this without let or hindrance from any born or self- elected obstructor. And this will come about by course of law, despite that splendid bit of colonial braggiclocia "the thousand leaping swords," &c.—l am, &c., Aug, 29th, 1581. JOHN PEERS.

NEWTON AND EARLESTOWN. NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.—These sessions were held on Saturday, before Messrs. Birley, Pearson, and Houghton:— Extraordinary Scene at Winwick : Frank Hewitt, a labourer, was charged with assaulting and beating a bailiff, George Iledgecock, whilst in the execution of his duty at Winwick. Hedgecock appeared to have gone to Hewitt's house to execute a distress warrant, and while there endea- veured to get him to pay the amount owing by instalments to avoid distress. Defendant refused to pay anything, and Hedgecock obtained the use of a cart and carried away most of his furniture. The cart had only .proceeded a short dis- tance when a large crowd of the neighbours gathered and followed it. Defendant was amongst them, and jumped into it, and struck Hedgecock several blows on the face, and in- flicted a severe wound upon the forehead of the carter. The crowd rescued the furniture, and the bailiff and his assissant .2her Cu.- navin, incited toe crowd to do so. The Bench fined him £2 anecosts, or, in default, one month's imprisonment.—Dantage to Railings: George Chadwick was charged with damaging certain rail- ings the property of George Hill, of Newton, on the 21st instant, and was fined ss. and costs.—Cruelty to a Horse: Robert Edwards was charged with cruelly ill-treating a mare at Earlestown, on the 22nd June, by working it whilst in an unfit state. Inspector Coleman, of Wigan, found defendant driving a mare attached to a cab at the Newton races. It was in a very unfit state for work, and was lame on both hind legs. Fined 20s. and costs, or, in default, a month's imprisonment. Breach of the Peace, -c.:j Matthew Littler was bound over in the sum of £lO to keep the peace for six months, he having created a disturbance at Haydock, on the evening of the IsCinstant. Ann Wright was charged with assaulting an agent named Alfred Cannes at Golborne, on the 15th instant. Defendant was in a state of intoxica- tion when complainant went to her house for rent. She struck him and called him bad names, and caused a crowd of people to assemble. She was bound over in the sum of £5 to keep the peace for six months.

div.head: NEWTON LICENSING SESSIONS.
div.p: NEWTON LICENSING SESSIONS.

The general annual licensing meeting of the magistrates of Newton portion of the Wigan and Warrington police divisions of the county was held at the Court House, New- ton-le-Willows, on Saturday morning. Mr. E. H. Birley presided, and the other magistrates present were Messrs. John Pearson and Robert licughton.—Mr. Superintendent Weir, of the Wigan division, reported that the number of licensed victuallers in his district was 12, beersellers 14, grocers to sell wine and beer off the premises 1, beersellers 7, and wine to be sold off the premises 5. Ninety persons had been summoned for drunkenness' and of these 83 were fined, two paid costs, and five were dismissed. Of the 11 apprehended for drunkenness, nine were fined, and two dis- missed. The number of persons summoned for all classes of offence in his division had been 230, and 35 had been appre- hended.—Mr. :Superintendent Jackson reported that in the Warrington petty sessional division there were 48 licensed victuallers, 15 beerhouse keepers, 12 persons licensed to sell beer to be consumed off the premises, one billiard and baga- telle license, and two sweet wine licenses. 167 persons had been summoned and 34 apprehended for drunkenness in the year ended July 31st last, as against 118 summoned and 46 apprehended in the previous twelve months. In the War- rington division, in which there were 133 licensed victu- allers, 164 beerhouses, and 95 persons licensed to sell beer off the premises. There had been 554 persons summoned for drunkenness during the year ended 31st of July, 1881, an increase of 62 over the previous year, and there had been 221 apprehensions for the same offence, a decrease of nine, or a total increase of 35 over the previous year.—Thomas Foster, Ram's Head, Newton, and David Bromley and James Hulme, Poulton, were cautioned as to the manner in which their houses had been kept prior to the last licensing day.—Mr. Superintendent Jackson stated that the pro- visional grant of a license for the Glazebrook Hotel, Rixton, was again applied for. The original grant was made in 1875, and had been renewed ever since. Last licensing day, however, the Bench intimated that unless the house was built by the present date the grant would not be renewed. No steps had been taken to erect a house, and he wished to have the opinion of the magistrates with regard to renew- inn the grant. Mr. Birley : The applicant must apply again when the house is built. The grant will withheld.

WINSFORD. EIsITERTATNITENT AT WINSFORTO.—An entertainment was given in the Board school, High-street, on Wednesday even- ing by the choir of the Primitive Methodist Chapel, assisted by friends, the proceeds of which were in aid of the liquida- tion of the circuit debt. The chair was taken by Mr. G. Okell, Mayor of Over, who after a brief introductory speech called on the Volunteer Band to play a fantasia entitled "The pirates of penzance." The choir followed with the glee "Awake 2Eolian Lyre," and they also sang "The charm of the mill" and "The return of the revel." Some good recitations were given by Mr. J. 0. Gleave, of Northwich, and Mr. W. Shaw; a dialogue "An Irish stratagem for I bacon" by Messrs. Kitchen, Kennerly, and Hallmack, and another "The fortune teller" in two pat ts by the Misses , Boswell, Bailey, Hulse, and Weedall took well. A comic duet "Very suspicious" by Miss E. and Mr. J. Rav,riscroft, accompanied by Miss Buckley, was a deci,aed success, as were also the songs by Mr. Timperley, Mr. T. T. Thompson, and Mr. J. 0. Gleave. Mr. Kennerley played a cornet solo with great precision and taste, and Miss E. Ravenscroft gave an excellent pianoforte solo. The latter Toung lady accompanied the songs on the piano, and Mr. T. Kitchen, the choir, on the harmonium.

Prisoner mediatel He had only just been liberated, after being imprisoned 84 I days for desertion.—Prisoner said he had only been absent' without leave.—He was remanded to Walton Gaol to await I a military escort. The Bench recommended that the reward of £1 be paid to P.S. Spinks for the capture. ALLEGED ROBBERY FROM THE PERSON. Mary Ellen Duffy was charged with stealing from the person of Wm. Chatterton, a purse containing 19s. 7d.1 and Peter Duffy was charged with receiving th, k • • WARRINGTON POLICE COURT. DESERTION.—James Travis, alias Joseph Wild, was ySinsauvrattiVt.w—aßsetfilt3-epArldoenreMr,atltßounirgehses. charged with deserting from the 22nd Regiment of Foot, stationed at Chester, on Tuesday last.—P.S. Spinks said that at ten minutes to eleven last night he was walking through the new market place when he heard the sound of footsteps knew very in Barley Mow entry, and he waited to see who it was. Im- said he had none, and that he left Chester on Tuesday last. I L, same, knowing it to have I been stolen.—From the statement of Mr. Hunt it appeared

that the complainant, who is 19 years of age, is a tabourer on the permanent way from the London and North-Western Railway Company, at Birdswood Junction, near Preston Brook. The prisoners stated themselves to be man and wife, and had been living as such at a common lodging- house in the town, but he (Mr. Hunt) doubted the statement. The complainant, on Thursday night, came to Warrington, and missing his train home, took lodgings at the British Workman Coffee House. During Friday morning he and a 'mate " were drinking at several beerhouses with a number of women, and in the afternoon when intoxicited he met the prisoners at the Fox Jim, treating the female prisoner and a number of others to beer. Whilst here Peter Duffy held the complainant whilst his wife rifled his pockets. He, however, got away from them and made his way to Bank Quay station. He went in the Patten Arms tap, where the prisoner and three young women followed him, and he or- dered a quart of beer, giving in payment a sovereign. He received 19s. 7d. change, which he placed ha a leather purse in a pocket in the lining of his waigtcoat. The female pri- soner went up to him, and tearing open his waistcoat ran off with the purse, followed by her husband. They were fol- lowed by the complainant and the other women, and the female prisoner was seen to band the purse to her husband. Subsequently the prisoners were apprehended, but the purse and money had not been found.—Plisoners were remanded until Monday. MONDAY.—Before the Mayor, Ex-Mayor, and Councillor Crosfield.

A "GOOD HUSBAND" STRIKES HIS WlFE.—William May Weber was charged with being drunk in Buttermarket- street, on Saturday, and assaulting his wife by striking her. —The wife did not wish to press the charge as he was a "good husband," and he was fined 55. including costs. His 66TH APPEARANCE—John Bohan was charged with being drunk and disorderly by fighting in Dolman's-lane, on Saturday night.—P.C. Bruen proved the case, and priso- ner promised "to give over drinking."—He was fined 103. and costs or 14 days, the Mayor remarking that he hoped the prisoner would reform as that was his 66th appearance. DRUNK AT THE POLICE STATION.—A man named John Taylor was charged with being drunk at the police station. I Prisoner went to the police office to see if a friend was locked up, and as he was drunk he was put out of the office, accord- ing to P.C. Powell's statement, three times. He, however, went in again, and as he became very disorderly he was locked up.—The Mayor: It is a very remarkable thing how some men get drunk and come to the police station. (Laughter.)—Prisoner was fined 10s. and costs or fourteen days. PUNISHING A POLICEMAN—EXEMPLARY SENTENCE.—A young man named Thomas Higgins was charged with violently assaulting P.C. Monaghan, whilst acting in the execution of his duty in Fennell-street, on Saturday night. —P.C. Monaghan said at a quarter to 9 o'clock on Saturday night he was in Fennell-street, 3nd saw a man who was drunk walking before him. A man struck him and knocked him down in the middle of the street. Witness lifted the man up and found he was helpless. He put the man against a wall, and told a young man to stand by him to prevent him falling. He went up Robinson's Yard to look for the man who had struck the drunken man, and he put his light on but could not see anyone. He was coming down the entry when he heard footsteps behind him, and while turning round he was struck with a stick or poker on the side of the head, which was cut and bled very much, and knocked down. He caught prisoner by the leg, and was getting up when he was pushed down again. He managed to get up and get prisoner into the street. A woman came and struck him several times on the arm and once on the head with a poker. Prisoner got loose and struck him with a stick. There was a large crowd, and witness was knocked down and "struck and kicked awful" on the legs, and he could scarcely bend his arms he had been struck so badly. He drew his staff, which was taken from him, and he was kicked about the head in such a manner that he had had to get it dressed by a doctor.—Ellen Roach said she saw the prisoner rue up the entry with a poker in his hands.—Wm. Sutton saw the prisoner "up with a poker and down with the constable on the floor," where be was "punished."—For the defence a woman was called, who made a loaig statement which had little bearing on the case, and a girl called by prisoner created some amusement by asserting that P.C. Monaghan was drunk, a statement that was disproved by P.C. Jones.—The Mayor said this was a continuation of assaults on the police, and they must be stopped.—Prisoner would be sent to prison for three months' hard labour. ON THE ROAD.—William Batten and Andrew Fielding, boys, were charged with wandering about the streets of the borough without having any visible means of subsistence, and being in possession of industrial school clothing.—ln- spector Singleton found the prisoners in Church-street, and noticing they wore uniform, questioned them. They statpd they were nicking their way from Cadishead, where they had been working, to Liverpool, as the master they worked for haft thrashed them.—The prisoners were ordered to be taken to the school. THE ROBBERY FROM THE PERSON.—Mary Alice Duffy and Peter Duffy were charged with stealing from the person of William Chatterton, whilst in the Patten Arms bar, a purse and 19s 7d, his money.—The particulars of the case I have been previously reported.--The Bench said the priso- ners had been put into temptation by the prosecutor's bad conduct in paying for them 80 much drink. Prosecutor had placed himself entirely in their hands and the Bench did not feel the slightest sympathy for him.—The prisoners were each cttnmitted for two months' hard labour. CRUELTY TO ANIMALS—WiIIiam Highcock was sum- moned for having on the 24th August cruelly illtreated a mare by working the stoic whilst in an unfit state. Inspec- tor Harper, R S7P.C.A., proved the case and stated the animal was totally unfit even to walk, add was very much distressed by coming from Parr Moss' St. Helens to War- rington. The defendant said he had had the mare destroyed, and under these circumstances he was discharged on pay- ment of costs.—Thomas Norman was summoned for a similar offence. Inspector Osmond described the animal as being simply skin and bone. The animal had since been destroyed, and at the request of the inspector, the defendant was simply ordered to pay the costs. STREET OBSTRUCTION.--eJohn Bagguley was summoned for obstructing Cheshyre's-lane, by allowing a horse and cart to re.nain there nearly an hour. On the evidence of P.C. Monaghan, defendant was tined 2s. 6d. AN. UNREGISTERED LODGING HOUSE. —Thomas Hen- naghan was summoned for having, on the 24th ult., kept lodgers without having his house registered. Inspector Church, having given evidence, the case was adjourned for a Month. OVERCROWDING A LODGING HOUSE.—Catherine Buttress was summoned for over-crowding her lodging house, and on the evidence of Inspector Church, was ordered to pay the costs 3s. 6d. BREACHES OF THE ELEMENTARY EDUCATION ACT—Mr. G. Riley, school attendance officer, appeared to prosecute the following persons viho were each fined ss.—Patrick Wall, Old-road; William Johnson, Keen-street ; William Hart, Fountain-street; John Mannion Ashton's-yard ; Thos. Burns, Latchford; Bartholomew McKenna, Bewsey ; John Morgan, Ellesmere-street, and William Cork, Dial-street. TUESDAY.—Before Alderman Davies and Alderman Burgess. BEGGING.—John Tobian, a middle-aged man, was charged with begging in Bold-street on the previous afternoon.— 1 P.C. Cokely proved the charge, and the prisoner was sent to gaol for seven days with hard labour. A CANNIE SCOTCH3SAN SENT To GAoL.—A "Scotch tramp" named James Thompson was charged with stealing Bibs. of cheese, valued at 35., from the pantry of John Evans, Bull's Head public-house.—On the previous after- noon Mrs. Evans was employed in the kitchen when she heard the cellar door creak, and looking round saw the prisoner making his exit from the house. From his hand small pieces of cheese were falling, and on making an ex- aminttion Mrs. Evans found that Bibs. of cbeese had been stolen from a shelf in the pantry. She took no action in the matter further than telling a manservant, but an hour afterwards the prisoner again made his appearance; this time to beg some bread. He was recognised by Mrs. Evans as the thief, and he decamped. Information having been v P.C. Wheatley went in search of the prisoner en o ded him near Howley Quay. He had itantdheappoorelihceen, upon him a large quantity of cheese and some bread.— Prisoner said though he was no lawyer or s peaker he knew h e boughtsaa the case was not proved, and he did not think that they the euldiplereosve in prove it LivNeorpoonoelsoan Saturday, him wtakethe hn ct h e e se. whatever H e be suppose 4 would go for nothing.—Tbe prisoner was hcom- mitted to gaol for two mentlis with hard labour. MONDAY DRUNKENNESS AND IMIKORALITY.—EIIen La- imlle (17) and Jane Flynn (16) were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street at half-past eight on the previous night.—The prisoners were so violent that P.S. Spinks and three constables had to be employed to take them to the Bridewell, Lavelle having to be carried. Their conduct there was also disgraceful, and the noise they made was so great that they could be heard half way up Butterrnarket street —Mr. Hunt said he never heard worse language used by two girls before in his life. They prided themselves on the way in which they conducted themselves. —Alderman Davies : They pride themselves on their wickedness ?—Mr. Hunt : Yes, sir.—Mr. Davies said they came to the conclusion on the Bench some time ago to try and put down drunkenness and disorderly conduct on Mon- days by doubling the penalty. They would have to turn back to that sort of thing. Only on the previous day Mr. Rigby was calling his attention to the depravity in the streets on a Monday. It was shameful to see every Monday. Immoral conduct and drunkenness was almost rife in the street.—The prisoners were sentenced to a month's iinprison- cadl. ment with hard labour.—Flynn Thank you.—Lavelle: We A DESIRABLE NAME—Two young men named Martin Burke and Thomas Clynes were charged with being deserters

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1881
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, SEPTEMBER 3, 1881

from Her Majesty's Bth Regiment of Foct stationed at Man chester.—P.C. Corbett on the previous evening met Burke in Winwick-street and asked him for his ,pass. He replied that he had left his pass at Manchester, and lent his belt to a man named Clynes. He said his number was 2,157. In consequence of this statement P.S. Berry went in search of Clynes, and apprehended him in Buttermarket-street. In reply to questions, he said his name was Martin Burke, and his number 2,15?; and/disowned the name of Clynes. He produced a pass to bear out his statement. The prisoners were confronted with each other and both claimed the name of Martin Burke. The sergeant then pulled off Clynes' cap, and found it numbered 2,120; and he confessed he was a deserter, and that the pass belonged to Burke.—Both prisoners were remanded to await a military escort. ASSAULT 035 THE POLICE.—A puddler at the Whitecross wire works named Samuel Bowen was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Horsemarket-street at a quarter-past eleven on the previous night, and also with assaulting P.C.'s Corcorran and Crickett.—At the time named the prisoner was creating a disturbance, and P.C. Corcoran twice removed him from the street and told him to go tome, but he re- turned. On the last occasion he went to the door of the Workmen's Coffee House, and commenced to kick it. The officer then took him into custody, when the prisoner said, "I'll not go until I kill you, or you kill me." Prisoner kicked the officer in a most violent manner, the latter in , self defence knocking.the prisoner to the ground. P.C. Crickett then came to his assistance' and the " snaps " were put upon the prisoner, who had to be carried to the police ' station—Prisoner was fined 20s. and costn or 14 days. THE RESULT OF PLAYING TRUANT FR03.1 SCHOOL. James Marsh (12) and Henry Gorst (1.2) were charged with being vagrants, having been found sleeping in the new market place at 20 minutes past one that morning.—P.C. Corcoran proved the case.—lt appeared the boys had been playing truant from the Parish Church school, and knowing that their parents had heard of their conduct they were afraid to go home.—After being cautioned by the Bench they were discharged. Trtunsney. Before Captain Litton and Alderman Burgess. AN ABSCONDING FATHER.— John Cartwright was charged with having, on the 23rd June, run away and left his three children chargeable to the common fund of the Union, Mr. Garnett, relieving officer, stated that the prisoner's wife applied for relief in June. The case came before the guar- dians who ordered three children into tile house where they had been since. Prisoner went away and left his wife and family unprovided for, and he had been away since. The cost of maintenance amounted to a 15s.—Prisoner said he was out of work at the time he went away, and he found employment at .13olton.—The case was adjourned for two months, to give the prisoner an opportunity of repaying the amount at the rate of 2s. a week. HAWKING BY LADS: EXTRAORDINARY REVELATIONS.— Joseph Gresty (II,) George Cavanagh (14,) and John James Carroll (13,) were charged with stealing from a drawer in the shop of William Lowe, provision dealer. Golborne-street, at half-past 12 on Wednesday afternoon, is. Old. in copper. Mrs. Lowe was leaving the kitchen to go into the shop at the time named on Wednesday, when she was surprised to see the prisoner Gresty not very far from the money drawer, which was wide open. On looking into the drawer she saw the copper was missing, and seized Gresty's hand which was clenched, and in it was Is.old. He was detained, and on the arrival of P.C. Hennessey, was handed over. Cavanagh had been seen outside the shop, and from Gresty's statement , the two other prisoners were apprehended. The three prisoners above named were then charged, together with Thomas forty, James Nolan, William Lester, and Thomas Moran (lads), with stealing from the provision shop of George Taylor, Manchester-road, on Saturday last, six buns, a quantity of sweets, note paper and pens, value is. Tile lads were together on Saturday, between three and four o'clock. They went to Manchester-road where Cavanagh and Nolan went into the prosecutor's shop. Mrs. Taylor heard a noise and came into the shop, and observed one or two of the prisoners leaving the shop, half a dozen or more being outside. On examination she missed the articles named in the charge. The police had received no report of the robbery which came to light when the prisoners were in custody, and they had since admitted having stolen from the stall of George Baden, in the Market, 3 dozen blacking, and 2 dozen matches, and some other articles value Is. 31. —Mr. Hunt said all the prisoners were concerned in the robberies and two or three others which were not completed. Several of them were engaged in selling matches in the streets, and that was doing more to deerade the lade of the town than anything else.—Captain Litton: How do they dispose of them—The Chief Constable: They steal them and hawk them as if they had a legitimate right to do so. On the second charge all the prisoners, except Gresty and Lester, pleaded guilty. Moran had been previously con- victed, and had been before the Bench four times.—Cavanagh, Mr. Hunt stated, went into the market, and upset a stall, and then three or four others came round and stole the goods. He was dreaded by the market people.—The Bench com- mitted Moran and -Cavanagh for one month, and afterwards to a reformatory for 5 years; Lester and Carroll were ordered to be kept in custody until six o'clock that evening, and the other prisoners were ordered six strokes with a birch rod.

- - - WILMINGTON V linvTota.—The return match between these clubs took place on Saturday last. at Huyton, under anything but favourable ciroumstances. Owing to the late heavy rains, the .ground was in a miserably wet condition, and the atten- dance of spectittors was not so largo as usual. The Warring- tonians won the toss and sent in their opponents, a. W. Graham and G. Sowett being privileged to open the score. The bowling was entrusted into the hands of the brothers 0. G. and J. C. Lawton. in the first over of the former, Graham was caught at long-on for a duck," and the succeeding hatsman,`E. Jackson, from wbom something was expected, skied" the seine bowler, and was also caught without scoring. The new comer, P. Eccles, opened his account with a drive to leg for off J. C. Lawton, but immediately afterwards he lost his part- ner, who was dismissed by the same bowler. The condition of things at this pOint, looked rather unhealthy for the home team, three wickets having fallen for a total of five runs. However, matters improved somewhat, when Eccles was partnered by W. Gorst. At 16 the latter lifted O. G. Lawton Over the boundary, for 4, for which he was loudly-cheered. Unfortunately 'he' played the ball on to his wicket before another single had been scored, and his place was filled by H. Eccles, who, how- ever, retired without scoring. W. Wainwright occupied the vacancy, and got C. G. Lawton well away to the boundary for" 4, which he supplemented, shortly after, with& 2, but his career, was short-lived for he was taken at square-leg the next ball.: After scoring a couple, F. Towett gave way to G. Tate. At 35' P. Eccles was caught at short-leg, he having, by careful play,, made nearly one half that number. The next batsman, 0. Reich- ardt, after putting 5 together. stepped out to C. G. Lawton,' and missing the ball was smartly stumped, and W. Moorby, who followed on, received his discharge from the same bowler, the innings closing for a total ofl6 runs, G. Tate being not out with a score of 12 put down to his credit. 0. G. Lawton bowled with great success; in thirteen oven-, of which six were maidens, he obtained nine 'wickets at a cost of 23 runs. After a short interval the visitois went to the wickets, J. C. Lawton and E. England being 'deputed to open the score. The trundling was entrusted into the hands of G. Jowett and H. Eccles, the latter of whom disposed of both batsmen for five runs. G Clarke and R. Tacker then 'came together, and, between them raised the score to 33 before a separation took place, the former being caught at long-leg. 0. O. Lawton filled the vacant wicket, but soon lost his comrade who played the ball on to his wicket after a serviceable innings of 19. Four for 39. Armstrong then became Lawton's vis-a-vis. The latter hit but vigorously and despite the changes in the bowling, the score of the home team was quickly overhauled, the winning hit being made by him amid the plaudits of the Warrington gentlemen. With the ex- ception of T. Lawton, will contributed 11, no other stand was made, the innings closing for a total of 97. The fielding of F. _Jewett, on behalf of Huyton, is worthy of special mention. GRAND CRICKET MATCH AT HUTTON.

MR. A. ECCLES'S ELEVEN V. ROC PEPNEDMENOI. In fine but cold weather, and on a dead wicket, this match was played at Huyton, on Wednesday. A start was effected about twelve o'clock, the home team beginning the defence with E. Roper and J. W. Graham, to the trundling of H. Eccles and C. Martineau, the former taking the first over. Both batsmen were in good form, and gave the visitors plenty of leather hunting, which compelled a change in the bowling at 40, when Lees took the ball from Martineau and G. Hornby from Eccles. The score, however, rapidly rose till it reached 69, when Graham was bowled off his foot, after an excellent innings of 31, which included several good hits. F. A. Jowett then partnered Roper, andj 13 runs having been added, Jacob relieved Lees with the ball, and immediately afterwards H. Eccles again went on in place of Hornby. Soon after Roper gave a " hot " chance to mid-off, but the man at that position failed to hold it, and he acknowledged the let-off by punishing the bowling most unmercifully, so that at 103 it was found necessary to try another bowler, A. Rotherham being selected. Two or three more hits were made, and then the telegraph showed 110,which was onlyaugmented by a single when Jowett was discharged by H. Eccles, who displaced his off stump. W. Wainwright followed, but succumbed to Ruttier- ham's breakers after scoring 3, and he was succeeded by Mar- riott, the professional of the Huyton Club. The score rapidly increased, and at 129 (ten minutes before two o'clock), an ad- journment was made for luncheon. After recommencing Rotherham and Hornby changed ends' but to no purpose, both batsmen continuing to play with care. At 145, however, the desired separation took place, the professional's stumps being removed by Rotherham after a merry 17, :including three 3's. E. Jackson oceneied the vacant wicket, and made matters very lively for the visitors, each of whom had his share of hunting the ball, which was repeatedly driven to the boundary amid the applause of tthe home team. In the meantime Roper had been steadily piling up a score, and at 168 P. Eccles took the leather from Hornby, and, after a single, 11. Eccles, from Rotherham. At 187 Roper had a narrow escape of being caught by the bowler (Hornby). A hit for three by Jackson brought the total to 190, and seven runs later he played on to his wicket. after a hard and rapidly-hit innings of 36, comprising two 4's, four 3's, five 2's, and singles. The partnership was made up by F. Jones. but after breaking his " duck " he was taken at point, the telegraph showing 201 for six wickets. A. Harrison fol- lowed on, and after a couple of singles Roper cut Rotherham for three, completing his 'century" amia loud applause. In I attempting to obtain a short run Harrison retired, and the next batsman, C. ileichardt, after scoring two gave place to W. Bretherton, who, however, returned the ball to the bowler (Rotherham) without scoring. R. S. Eccles was next and last man, but only succeeded in getting a two before his career was ended by Rotherham, Roper carrying out his bat with the splendid score of 115 put down to his credit, or just one run more than half the entire score (229). His score included one 4, twelve 3's, nine- teen 2's, and singles. Notwithstanding that he gave three or four chances, he played excellent cricket, and was enthueias- tically cheered by the spectators on returning to the pavilion. After an interval of a few minutes the visitors commenced theif innings by sending in J. Lees and q. Eccles to the bowlino of r. and ce. 0. laves. Runs came very slowly at first, and at 19 the first-named batsman was dismissed by F. Jones, who in the same over secured the wicket of B. Field, the next man. off his bat. C. Martineau filled the vacancy, and opened his account with two or three hard and well-directed hits, which took the score up to 33, :when he lost his partner, who was succeeded by A. Rotherham. Things now improved consider- ably, both batsmen, for a short time, bitting with freedom. Rotherham got Jones well away to square leg for 6, which was the signal for an Outburst of applause f rem his I comrades. The two carried the scare to 61, when Jones I was again on the spot, and Martineau retired after a well- played 23, comprised six 3's, two 2's. and a single. Rotherham was bowled two runs later, he having put together a capital 17. I A. P. Eccles and G. Hornby. then came together, and an addi- tion of 10 runs having been made F. Jones hastened the dis- missal of the former by knocking out his off stump. Jabcob became Hornby's vis-a-vis, but after "slooging " Eccles for a single he was splendidly caught at long-on by Roper, and the vacancy was occupied by J. Rayner. A change in the bowling at 92, however, compelled his retirement, and his position was taken by E. Draper. The latter and Hornby batted Well. At 108 Marriott succeeded Jones with the ball, and four runs later Roper went on in place of Bretherton. At 114 Hornby "skied" afarriott, but the man at mid on failed to hold it. - Directly after another change in the bowling was made, Eccles and Jones again resuming the ball. Hornby hit Eccles in one over for 4, 3, and a 2 in stv cession in fact, he made at least two-thirds of his score of 55 off Eccles. hitting him no less than five times over the boundary for 4. At 144 "time" was cal'ed, the match resulting in a draw, much in favour of the home team. Score—" MR. A.. EccLEs. s ELEYEI . div.head: BOWLING MATCH AT HUYTON.
div.p: BOWLING MATCH AT HUYTON.

A main at bowls for the silver-plated pint-cup presented to the Ifuyton cricket and bowling club, by Mr. T. B. Fishwick, was played on Saturday afternoon last, on the green at the rear of the tent. The weather though fine was rather cold, and the grounds owing to the late rains was very wet, and anything but agreeable to the players. The attendance of spectators was not so large as could have been wished, especially considering that this was a main for a prize specially presented, without any conditions being attached to it, and which would become the sole property of the gentleman who had the good fortune to win it, but doubt- less the falling off was in a great measure attributable to the fickleness of the weather. Mr. Fishwick thought that it was only fair, and as little as he could do, to make some slight return for the many' years of pleasure and healthy exercise he had enjoyed on the green, and the courtesy and good feeling which had always been manifested towards him by the lumbers. The present took the form of a cup, which, it will be remembered was played for on August 6th, immediately after the main for the president's challenge cup had been completed. It was not Mr. Fish- wick's intention to play for his own cup, but the pressure brought to bear upon him by the other members overcame his scruples, and be consented to play, at the same time remarking that if he won it, he would present another prize. Singularly enough, and notwithstanding, that nearly all the veteran bowlers took part, he succeeded in carrying away the prize amid the applause of those present. Mr. Fishwiek again presented the cup the competition for which came off on Saturday, when he declined to play. The main was played at the original handicap points, the games being nine up. With the exception of Mr. Paris, who secured the cup, all the veteran bowlers came to grief, one of the younger bowlers, Mr. Williams, playing exceedingly well. The following are the scores:— FIRST ROUND. Burnyeat Crook 9 received I beat Wainwright ... 5 received 1 Aldrich Williams Paris Byes :—Turton (owe 1), Busby and Reichardt (received 3 eacl.).

FOURTH ROUND. Paris And won the cup. There was no formal presentation of the cup, and the members continued to play friendly games till dusk.

The Cardiff Licensed Victuallers at the forthcoming licensing session will contend that the Welsh Sunday Closing Act does not come into force until next year. An auction sale of an unusual nature commenced in the Corn Exchange, Kidderminster, on Wednesday. arising out of the recent municipal election. The goods offered were , , those of the unseated candidate, who, it was announced, was obliged to leave his residence on account of the -petition and the writs for penalties against him. The cumulative fines sued for are £5,000. MR. GLADSTONE'S LABOURS.—On Tuesday, Mr. Thorne, secretary to the Wolverhampton Liberal Association, re- ceived a latter from Mr. Gladstone replying to a resolution thanking him for his untiring labours on behalf of Ireland. The Premier says he is much gratified at the approval ex- hibited of his services in the past Session in connection with the affairs of Ireland. He makes allusion to Mrs. Gladstone's recovery, saying she is much obliged by the expression of hope that she would be restored to perfect health. The Welsh Eisteddfod was opened on Tuesday at Merthyr Tydyil. The presidents of the morning meetings are Sir Hugh Owen, Sir Watkin Williams Wynn, M P., Mr. Henry Richard, M.P., and Sir E. J. Reed, K.C.8., M.P.; those of the evening meetings Mr. C. IL James, M.P., Sir Watkin IWilliams Wynn, 1117 P., Rev. J. Griffith (rector of Neath), and Mr. A. J. Williams, of the North Wales circuit. The Eisteddfod on Tuesday passed a resolution expressing sympathy with Mrs. Garfield and the American people in their great trouble, and a hope for the President's speedy , recovery. The Brush electric light, which is making such rapid strides in England, has been utilised at the making , Spa. The start was a highly successful one. The wide : Esplanade was brilliantly illuminated from end te end with seven 2,000 candle-power Brush lights, suspended from prettily-designed iron posts, placed at intervals down the centre. In each of the band-houses a 2,000 candle-power Brush light was hung from the canopy. The large concert- hall was charmingly lighted by a central chandelier, con- sisting of five 2,000 candle-power Brush lights. Altogether sixteen lights were run on the one circuit, and from the one dynamo machine, which was driven by a Robey's semi- portable 12 nominal horse power engine.
