Fifty members of the Emergency Committee have gone to Lough Mask to cut the crops of Captain Boycott. Sir Charles Gavan Duffy has left London on a brief visit to Ireland. Sir Charles, it is believed, will be asked to re- enter political life. . _
Mr. Serjeant O'Hagan, judicial member of the Land Com- mission, was on Monday sworn before the Lord Chancellor as a judge of the High Court of Justice in Ireland.

. _ Mr. Thomas Brennan, late secretary of the Land League, has received formal notice from the Executive that he is "remanded" for a further period of three months to the custody of the Governor of Kilmainhatn gaol. What is called the "Central Committee " of the Fenian Brotherhood in the United States, has sent a communication to the newspapers warning Americans and friends of Ireland against embarking upon any vessel flying the British flag after Thursday next. Many, it is added, may reach their destination, but none, it seems, are safe. Mr. A. M. Sullivan, M.P., has been advised, on account of the state of his health, to resign his seat for the County Meath, and retire from Parliamentary life for a few years. The hon. gentleman has intimated the advice he has received to some of his colleagues, but, in deference to a general opinion, he will not take any final decision until the expiration of the period of quiet ordered by his medical attendants. A large number of people on Monday cut, thrashed, and carted away the corn on the farm at Knockartoo, from which Father Welsh's mother was evicted recently. The police and emergency men in possession were powerless. Miss Parnell, speaking at an Irish demonstration at Glas- gow, on Saturday, and Mr. Parnell, at a meeting at Omagh, in connection with the County Tyrone election, both gave expression to very caarse and offensive epithets regarding the chief members of the Ministry. The Knockermore couty Waterford, Land League on Tuesday passed resolutions expressing satisfaction at the recovery of Mr. A. M. Sullivan and hoping he would be able to frame and pronounce the declaration of Irish Inde- pendence next year in pe old Parliament Rouse on College Green, Dublin. SERIOUS RIOTING AT ROSCREA.—A Parsontown telegram reports serious rioting at Roscrea North Tipperary. The Emergency labourers were attacked by a large mob, whom the police charged. Six or seven constables were injured and a civilian wounded by a bayonet. The windows of the barracks were destroyed. Additional police and military have been summoned.

The speech of Mr. Dillon in Dublin has attraeted much attention, and the Freeman's Journal says it ought to be a tremendous warning to the Government and the land com- mission. The Freeman believes that if the hopes of those who trust in the Act are dashed to the ground, the last state of Ireland will be worse than her first. The landlords will suffer, and the Government will be swept into space. It adds that such a catastrophe can only be averted by the commission bringing about a wholesale, sweeping, and a vast reduction in the rental of Ireland. Impossible rents are the millstone that hangs around the neck of Ireland, and if the commission does not cut the knot that ties it on, the people will do so with a vengeance. THE PROPOSED TESTIMONIAL TO DAVITT.—Mr. Patrick Egan, treasurer of the Land League, has written from Paris with reference to the proposal of presenting Michael Devitt with an estate upon his release from prison. Mr. Egan says:—" The time has not yet come to fittingly honour the brave and noble-minded Devitt. Tlke task which he set be- fore himself was the total abolition of landlordism. That task is only well begun; but let our people maintain steadily and determinedly their spendid organisation and their loyalty to one another, and the time of its complete accomplishment is near at hand. When that time comes the Irish nation will assure honour to Michael Devitt, but not by the pur- chase of an estate that he would not accept. Meanwhile I feel assured the mcst acceptable tribute of grateful people can offer to him, one that will indeed cheer him in his lonely prison cell, is to act fimly on his advice and to hold no term with land thieves." PROPOSED TESTIMONIAL TO MR. GLADSTONE. At a meetiqg held in Belfast on Tuesday evening, under the auspices of the Antrim Tenant Right Assoziation, a com- mittee was appointed to confer with the Tenant Right Asso- ciation in Ulster for the purpose of raising a suitable testi- monial to Mr. Gladstone in recognition of his services on behalf of the farmers of Ireland. MURDEROUS OUTRAGE IN CORK. SEVERAL PERSONS SHOT.

A telegram from Cork, .received on Monday night, de- scribes an extraodinary outrage which occurred at Rach- coole, near Mill-street, county Cork, on the occasion of the marriage of Sir George Colthurst, the chief landlord in the district. The tenants were engaged in rejoicings. They had assembled round the bonfire, and were drinking from some barrels of porter. About eleven o'clock, ten men armed with rifles, revolvers, and pikes, and having their faces blackened, came upon the scene. They formed a a circle round the tenants, who were too much terrified to
move. The word to fire Was given by one of the men; who appeared to be in command, and immediately a volley was discharged amongst the unfortunate people. Several re- . . .
ceived severe shot-wounds in various parts of the body, and two were wounded in their sides with revolver bullets.

The party then rushed in upon the tenants and beat them with sticks. Having driven them off, they quenched the fire with the porter and scattered the embers about the place. They were not followed, and there is no means of identifying any of the party. Severalkof the tenants have been seriously injured, and four are lying in hospital dan- gerously hum

The Wesleyan Methodist Thanksgiving Fund now reaches a total of £301,949 promised; the total amount paid is £247,587. Her Majesty has been pleased to confer the dignity of the Civil Grand Cross of the Most Honourable Order of the Bath on the Speaker of the House of Commons. Mr. E. N. Buxton, chairman of the School Board for Lon- don, opened on Friday night the 239th school built by the Board.

A LADY SENT TO PRISON FOR MARRYING A WARD IN CHANCERY.—Mr, Justice Cave made a very unusual ordet on Wednesday, in a case heard in private. He committed a lady to prison for marrying, in disobedience to an order of the Court, a young gentleman wko is a ward of the Court, the lady herself being an adult. • Tin NEW CHIEF CONSTABLE OF Livarrpoor..—On,Thefil- day, the Liverpool Watch Committee unanimously ap- pointed Captain W. N. Bowyer, head-constable of Leeds, to be Chief-constable of Liverpool, in the place of Major Greig, resigned. There were 74 applications for the office, which is worth £750 per annum. The depositions of a woman named Annison were taken on Wednesday by the Norwich magistrates. The husband, who, it is alleged had attempted to murder his wife, is in custody. The accused had for many years been addicted to drink, which was the result of frequent quarrels. While in a state of intoxication, he took up a knife plunging it into the poor woman's left side, just under the heart. div.head: ST. HELENS TRAAIWAYS COMPANY.
div.p: ST. HELENS TRAAIWAYS COMPANY.

The half-yearly ordinary meeting of the shareholders of this company was held at the Fleece Hotel on Monday. Mr. W. Busby, the chairman, presided, and said that when the directors met half a year ago, they were confident that before August they would not only be able toj say they had completed the laying of the tramway, but that they were earning a revenue. They had, however' been disap- pointed. They had had bad weather to contend with lately, and the capital had not come in as they expected. When they commenced operations they relied upon the greater part of the capital being taken up in the immediate neigh- bourhood of St. Helens; but they had been disappointed in that respect, and they had had to seek capital elsewhere. They had still confidence in the success of the undertaking, and that everything would turn out to their satisfaction. He submitted the following report, and moved its acceptance : "Since the last meeting in February we regret to say that the work of laying the tramways has made but slow pro- gress, owing to a combination of circumstances which we have not been able to avoid. We were most desirous to have the line open for at least some of the summer traffic, but by the time this much to be desired consummation is reached, winter, we fear, will be nearly upon us. We have after much difficulty been able to raise sufficient capital to com- plete our line from Prescot to St. Helens, and we have made a satisfactory agreement as to stables, having obtained a ten years' lease, to be renewed at option, of the stabling and yard of the King's Arms, Prescot, at a reasonable rental. The saving effected by adapting the present buildings to our purpose, instead of erecting entirely new ones will be con- siderable. The contract for the alterations has been let, and the work is proceeding. There is now only about 1,170 yards of tramway lobe laid, and the cars are already sup- plied, so that we may fairlY hope to open the line in a few weeks. There are rails and chairs on the ground sufficient to complete the work, and almost sufficient setts."—Mr. Gesxm said they might be led to infer from the remarks of the Chairman that the tramways had been delayed for want of capital, but the shareholders understood that such was not the case. Sufficient capital had been subscribed to finish between Prescot and St. Helens. There had been great delay for setts and rails, but what guarantee had the shareholders that the delay would now cease? He should not like to throw any reflection upon the company, and say that they were responsible for it, but someone was re- sponsible. He was sorry there were so few shareholders present to ask for a explanation. It was possible things might be as the contractor said, but the contractor was under a

certain amount of supervision, and if he did not adhere to the contract he ought to be made to do so. Why had not this been done? They were now approaching winter.—The CHAIRMAN said the capital was one cause, but that had been removed, and now they had sufficient capital. They lid, however, not sufficient at one time, and it was with great , anxiety and exertion that the Board had been enabled to overcome the difficulty. The weather had been unfavourable for the construction of tramways ; and the action of the Corporation in delaying their sewerage operations until the company were ready to commence had caused delay. There was no denying that the contractor had carried on the operations slowly. When he got half Through the work he commenced at Southport, and the Southport people had as good reason to complain as St. Helens had about the slowness of the work. Those were things the directors could not control. They had agreed with the contractor that he should do the work within a certain time, and the contractor had overrun that time. There was some delay in getting the calls paid up by the subscribers, and on that account the contractor had been re- quested to go on a little slower with the work than he other- wise would have done. But that cause of delay had disap- peared for a considerable time, and the contractor was still very much to blame.—Mr. RILEY said the money could not be called up at once, but only at intervals of two months, and that might occasion some delay.—Mr. GASKIN asked what hold they had on the contractor if he failed to com- plete within a reasonable time? Had the company or the company's officials any control over the contractor, or was the cohtract so broken that the contractor could ride a coach and four through it, and please himself whether he went quickly or slowly? The contractor was patching up one part and going to another, while if he put a good gang of men on he might get done within a reasonable time. People were laughing at them at the way they were going on.—The CHAIRMAN did not think they had so far broken the con- tract as to relieve the contractor from his forfeit, and if the contractor did not do the work within a certain time he must pay the penalty. He had noticed that day that the contractor had not so many men on the ground as he ought to have, and he had told Mr. Beloe to look more strictly after the contractor. There was room for litve times the number of men. The contractor had given sureties for the fulfilment of his contract—Mr. BELOE said that when the contractor had done certain work there hadmot been suffi- cient money to meet the amount of his certificate.—The CHAIRMAN said that was in the former part of the work, but after the sezond issue they had been able to keep up the payments.—Mr. GASKIN said it had been suggested that if the line was continued to near the railway at Shaw-street Bridge it would result in a gain to the company.—The CHAIRMAN said the directors would give the suggestion their serious consideration, and if it was seen to be an ad- vantage they would fall in with it.—The business concluded with a vote of thanks to the Chairman.

div.head: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
div.p: DARESBURY PETTY SESSIONS.
TUESDAY. —Before Mr. Edward Greenall (chairman), rnd Mr. liobeLt rierpoint. BREWSTER SESSIONS.

Superintendent Williamson reported that in the sessional division there were 23 licensed victuallers, 2 beerhouses to sell on or off, and 3 to sell off the premises only—total, 28 and according to last census, 298 persons to each licensed house. Daring the past year no licensed victuallers had been proceeded against. Two beerhouse keepers had been summoned—one was convicted (and had since left the house,) and the case against the other was dismissed. In the past year 28 persons had been proceeded against for drunkenness, as against 27 the previous year—being an increase of one. Of the 28 persons, 27 were convicted, and one discharged on the payment of costs. There was one application by Win. Worrell for a license to sell beer to be consumed off the pre- mises at Whitley Superior.--. The Chairman remarked that it wee a most satisfactory report.—Mr. Slater applied for the transfer of the license of the Stag, Lower Walton. Mr. Wil- son, the former tenant, ran awry from home last April, and the business was carried on some time by his wife, but a short time ago she became insane, and the house was closed. He therefore applied for the transfer of the license to Mr. Maddocks.-The application was granted.—Mr. Moore, on be- half of Mr. William Worrell, applied for a license to sell off the premises at Whitley Superior. The value of the pre- mises was £l5O, and the rateable value £36. Evidence of value having been given, the Overseer of Whitley Superior, on behalf of the ratepayers of the township, asked the bench to withhold the license. It was considered they had already quite sufficient accommodation of this kind. They had two full-licensed houses, and a beerhouse, the latter being with- in five minutes walk of the present applicant's house.—The, Chairman said the magistrates had no option. He quite agreed with the overseer that it was not required; but the Act of Parliament having been 6omplied with they had no alternative but to grant the license.—The Overseer said the gross estimated rental of the house stood at present in the rate book at £ll.—Ultimately the application was adjourned to enable the overseer to bring evidence that the house was not worth £ll a year. DRUNK ON LICENSED PREMISES.—WiIIiam Turnbull, and Samuel Appleton were summoned for having, on the Ist August, been drunk on the licensed premises of Mr. James Powell, Wheat Sheaf, Antrobus, and refused to quit.—P.C. Speed proved the case, and defendants were each fined 15s. and 13s. 6d. costs or one month's imprisonment. UNREGISTERED MILK HOUSE.—William Newton was sum- moned for baying carried on the trade of a milk seller at Appleton without being registered—P.S. Booth said that on the 22nd of July,he visited the defendant's shop at Stockton Heath, and foLnd two mugs containing milk. He saw a per- son in the shop purchasing milk, and defendant's wife was going round hawking milk. The house was not registered CS it was not suitable.—Defendant pleaded ignorance of the requirements of the law, and, as he stated he had only sold milk two days, he was let oil on payment of 4s. 6d. costs. ILLTREATING A HORSE.—James Webster was summoned for having illtreated a horse by allowing the same to work whilst man unfit state, and William Hostage was summoned , for working the same in an unfit state.—P.C. 138, said on 27th July he was on duty at London Bridge, Appleton, and saw the first named defendant's horse drawing a cart. He noticed the horse did not walk properly, and on examining the animal found it suffering from sore shoulders.—P S. Booth said one of the wounds was quite raw and when the collar touched it the horse started with pain.—For the de- fence, Mr. Willett, veterinary surgeon, said he examined the horse and could see nothing but a small wound about the size of a pea.—The Bench were of opinion the case was proved, but as the wound seemed to have been small, Web- ster would simply have to pay the costs 103. 61, the case against Rustage being dismissed.

The first sod of a new park at Aberdeen, a gift of Miss Duthie, was turned on Saturday by that lady. Mr. Henry Savile, well known as ac owner of race horses, expired on Monday, after an illness of a few weeks' dura- tion.

A FORTUNE FOR A WORKHOUSE INMATE.—Betsy Miles, nearly 70 years of age, an inmate of the district union at Rickmansworth, has been removed front thence, consequent upon her having, by the death of a wealthy relative, become entitled to a large fortune, amounting, it is said, to several thousand pounds.

The first sod of the Charnwood Forest Railway, which is intended to connect Nottingham with Birmingham, was turned on Wednesday at Loughborough, Leicestershire, by Lady Alice Packs. daughter of Earl Kimberley. A lun- cheon fullowed, at whieh Major-General Burnaby was the principal speaker.

There Is no medicinal preparation which may be so thoroughly relied upon in the treatment of the above ailments as Hollo- way's Ointment. Rubbed upon the surface of the body, over, or near the affected parts, it disappears under the friction of the hand, penetrating at once to the source of the evil, and thus performs Its healing errand, rapidly, safely, and without pain. In all long standing cases, Holloway's Pills should also be taken, as they purify the Blood and expel all depraved humours from the system. COUGHS, COLDS, SORE THROATS, AND BRONCHITIS. This Ointment is irresistible in the cure of these throat and pectoral complaints, which ashen neglected often end in settled Asthma or consumption. The Ointment well rubbed upon the Chest and Back, night and morning, penetrates the skin and thus absorbed is carried directly to the Lungs, where, ic Immediate contact with the whole mass of circulating Blood, it neutralizes or expels all impurities. By these means all put monary complaints may be cured with rapidity and ease.

DISORDERS OF THE KIDNEYS, STONE, ANDGRAVEL. fore shall be set down as an incorrigible sceptic. I beg to say, notwithstanding, that if the place was not originally either a well or a village bridewell, I do not know what it can have been intended for; certainly not for a tomb. A few yards further down the road an old roofless house is pointed to as the house of Martha and Mary. The next to it, equally in ruins, is said to be the house ef Simon the lepe:! Climbing up the debris, which rises to a level with the walls, we see within the area two women sitting with sieves between their knees sifting grain. Upon the square roofs, as we pass down the village, are a number of women squatting, and evidently making their own remarks upon the odd spectacle we present to their oriental eyes. Little heed they take to the children clamouring mound us with the rudest importunity —children diseased through very filth thrusting their bands in our faces, or holding up the defor- mities and running sores of the babes they carry to excite pity and extort alms. And this in Betkany, the once beautiful Bethany, home of sweetest memories and holiest deeds! How dreadful the curse which devotes a place so honoured by the Saviour to such defilement! How burning the wrath that spares not even Bethany in its outpouring on this once favoured land! How truly the words of Moses are fulfilled in our experience to-day—" The strangers that shall come from a far land shall say, when they see the plagues of that laud and the sickness which the Lord hath laid upon it, 'Wherefore hath the Lord done unto this land ; what meaneth the heat of this great anger ?' " This answer is: "They forsook the covenant of the Lord God of their fathers, and the anger of the Lord was kindled against the land, to bring upon it all the curses that are written in the book of the Lord." Despite all these dark surroundings, how sweet and pleasant it would be if the stranger could feel himself at liberty to ramble about the neighbourhood, and to feast his eyes and his heart on its natural features and soul-moving associations! But no, there is no linger- ing; we must hurry away, the children following a considerable distance as We make our way back to Jerusalem. Not far from Bethany, looking to the left, are the scarcely distinguishable ruins of Bethphage. What a thought, to be near the very place from whence the Saviour sent forward the two disciples to prepare the Pass- over! In a few minutes we come in view of the wide crescent road that sweeps round the gorge at the back of Olivet, and at the same time we obtain a sight, beyond its opposite point, of Jerusalem, embracing about one-third of the city, and as much of the temple area. Then the road falls gently down on one side of the gorge, and rises as gently up the other. I cannot refrain from mentioning the appearance of the roeks as we traversed this semi-circle. Immense blocks of limestone were torn from the mountain side, and lying in the wildest confusion upon the edge of the road. I wondered whether these rocks which had so often looked down upon the Holy One as He passed morning and even- ing to and from Bethany-, and which had echoed to the hosannas of the multitude but a few days before, were THE BETRAYAL. among those that were rent at the crucifixion! of agriculture was not only associated with good seasons, but must NI dependent very much upon the prosperity of the manufacturing interest, and he trusted that means might soon be found by which that interest might in some way recover from the depression which it had long been suffer- ing from. Whatever steps might be taken in that direction, as seemed to be indicated by a growing feeling of public opinion in the manufacturing districts, he thought agricul- turists would only be glad that any measures should be taken I which, without prejudicing in any way the general interests of the community, would restore to the manufacturing dis- tricts that trade which had been languishing for some time. (Hear, hear.) More than that he would not say. He did not think that in that district farmers had need of any pro- tection to enable them to compete in the markes of that and the neighbouring county. Tho Ca/MASAN, in proposing "Success to the Royal Man- chester, Liverpool, and North-Lancashire Agricultural Society," said that notwithstanding the comparatively few entries of cattle, tke show must be considered an absolute success. Speaking to agriculturists, he would remind them that it was all important that they should endeavour to maintain the best and kindest relations between landlord and tenant, such as he believed now existed throughout the length and breadth of this country. In a different profession he had found that notwithstanding the most rigid regulations and bonds of discipline, unless there was a willingness on the part of everyone to work one with another for the general good, they could never carry out any work to perfection. (Hear, hear.) Another question of importance was that of rates and taxes. He thought the school board rate was in many cases unnecessarily heavy, and in this, as in other in- stances, land must be relieved and the farmer must be helped. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the outbreak of disease amongst cattle, the chairman said he knew of one farm on which 22 head of cattle, in consequence of suffering from pleuro- pneumonia, had to be slaughtered within a few months. He remembered a serious outbreak of this disease at the Cape of Good Hope some years ago, when cattle were said to have been largely saved by inoculation, and he suggested that this remedy should by thoroughly inquired into. Mr. J. C. HALE (Knowsley,) whose name was coupled with ' the toast, in replying, sketched the rise of the society from • II its small beginning as the Manchester society to its present I position, which he held to be second to none in the kingdom with the exception of the Royal Agricultural Society. The society had been of great advantage to the agriculture of the country, and he urged that the members should endeavour to increase its utility by extending its list of subscribers. Mr. H. J. TOLLEMACHE„ M.P., gave "The Judges," for whom Mr. W. S. Atkinson responded. Colonel BLACKBURNE, M.P., proposed "The President," and in doing so expressed the hope that those interested in agriculture would follow the suggestion of the chairman, and assist in promoting a good feeling between landlord, tenant, and labour. (Hear, herr.) The CHAIRMAN having acknowledged the toast, "The Mayor of Blackburn and the local committee" was given, and the company separated.

div.head: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
div.p: TRAVELS IN THE EAST.
BY A SOUTH-WEST LANCASHIRE GENTLEMAN. ES BC IA L. No. XIV. JERUSALEM.

Gethsemane ! For years I had pictured to myself a deep and shady solitude through which I might one day have freedom to roam and meditate undisturbed, its ancient olives affording a sombre shelter, underneath which it might be possible to realise more perfectly than ever before the mysteries of that love and the intensity of those sufferings which have given to Gethsemane and Calvary their un- paralleled solemnity of interest. The reality proved bow little of substantial spiritual good is inherent from merely external surroundings, however sacred. Llere, indeed, were the olives, by far the most patriarchal of any we saw in Palestine—grand, hoary relics, under whose shade the Divine sufferer may have passed to and fro on that dreadful betrayal night; but they were exhibited, and the spell was broken. I have been asked whether, having the least pre- tensions to such antiquity and associations, the trees are not worth preserving at any cost. I would say, yes, at any cost but that of placing them under showmen, who, more selfish and grasping than the motley changers of old, do not scruple to make merchandise of the Saviour's groans and tears. To increaso the attraction, and to make it pay the better, they hay built the walls of the garden with niches, in which are placed carved figures in historical groups ill us- trative of the last scenes in the Redeemer's life. Around the immense old olives with their tranksgnarled and hollow, but their branches full of leaves, are flower-beds, beautifully laid out, from which the Franciscan plucks you a flower, and, on receipt of the coveted "backsheesh " in exchange, folds his arms across his breast, and reverently bows you to the door. The exlaibition has become so profitable that the envious Greeks have set up a Garden of Gethsemane of their own a little further up the hill. The position of the place we visited answers in so many respects to the New Testament indices that we cannot have been very far from the spot, il not actually upon it. If, as some think pro- bable, the grand entrance into the city in the Saviour's time was through the Golden Gate, to whiCh a viaduct, spanning the valley of Jehoshaphat from Olivet to Mount Moriah, led, this part of the valley, "across the brook Cedron," would be sufficiently secluded to afford a peaceful retreat, althoughl within the hum of the city's busy life. In penning the following stanzas a few years ago, I almost think I had a more vivid realisation of Gethsemane than I found it possible to gain within its very precincts on this .12th of March :

div.head: WIDNES POLICE COURT.
div.p: WIDNES POLICE COURT.

WEDNESDAL—Bef ore Mr. F. H. Gossage. A Row IN WALMSLEY-STREET.—Wm. Whalley and ;Michael Ward were summoned for having committed a breach of the peace by fighting in Walmsley-street.—P. C. Strickland, said that on Sunday night about a quarter to eleven o'clock, he saw the two defendants fighting in the street, with their coats off. Ward told him that Whalley had set upon him. Michael Ward was also charged with assaulting Mrs. Whalley. Mr. Slater (from the office of Messrs. Robert Davies and Co., Warrington,) appeared for Whalley, and Mr. Husband for Ward.—M. Slater said that Ward was passing along the street late at night, when Mrs. Whalley called out to a neighbour to the effect that she would be too late. Ward then turned round and asked her to whom she was talking, on which she told him to go inside his own house and look after his wife. Ward then ran across the road, and struck her several blows upon the face.—Mrs. Whalley corroborated this statement, and said that the de- fendant told her that she never washed her teeth, and during the row he followed her into her own house and struck her. He was not sober.—Margaret Connolly and John Fox were called to prove the case.—Mr. Husband said that Mrs. Whalley had for some days been in the • habit of using very irritating language, and comparing defendant's house to a wild beasts' show were performances were being held.— Samuel Carter, Warrington-road, said Whalley used very bad language to Ward, and called her house a den.—Patrick Green stated that complainant told defendant it was time for the performance to commence. He denied that defen- dant struck complainant —The Chairman held that an as- sault of some kind had been committed, but it was not of a very serious nature. The summonses would be dismissed on defendants paying costs. Whalley would be bound over in £lO and two sureties of £5 to keep the peace six months, and, in default, be sent to gaol 14 days. AN UNCOMFORTABLE HOME.—Henry Smith, of Gossage- street, was summoned for threatening to assault his; wife.— Complainant said that on the 24th ult, defendant had been working at Liverpool, and owing to his drinking habits she had to go out washing. When she returned she found de- fendant sitting in the entry, an 1 after she had opened the door, she made the remark " Drunk again ! I reckon thou bast lost thy job." Defendant then began to break some of the ironwork belonging to the fire-place. He threatened what he would do to her, when she ran out of the house, and had since been living with a Mrs. Johnson.—Mrs. Brown and Mrs. Johnson were called to prove the case.—Defendant said that frequently when he came home after being at work, he found there was no fire in the house for his children. In fact, she would persist in going out working for other people when she ought to be doing her best to make his own house comfortable. He might have threatened her.— Defendant was ordered to enter into sureties, himself in £lO and two in £5 to keep the peace six months, or be impri- soned 14 days. TROUBLESOME TADS.—Thomas Bradley, Wm. Robinson, Jas. Hedley, and Thos. Bate, boys, were charged with chasing cattle belonging to a farmer named J. Bennett.—Mr. Walker appeared for the complainant, and Mr. Husband for the defence.—Mr. Gossage, after some remarks from Mr. Walker, suggested that the case should be withdrawn on a pledge being made that the lads would not offend in a simi- lar manner in future. This course was accordingly adopted. ANOTHER MATRIMONIAL QUARREL.—John Dolan was brought up in custody charged with assaulting his wife Margaret, on the 19th ult.—She stated that the prisoner went to Runcorn to an improper house in the early part of the day, and on his return to Widnes they had a quarrel, and he struck her on the head with an umbrella. He next told her that if she and the children did not leave the house he would take their lives during the hour. She then ran out of the house in her chemise, and the children followed.—A witness named Mrs. Clarke supported this statement, and the prisoner was ordered to be bound over in £lO and a surety in £5 to keep the peace for six months, or, in default, be imprisoned 14 days.
RUNCORN POLICE COURT.
MoNne.r.—Before Messrs, William Bankes (chairman) and

Alfred Thomas. A DEPARTURE BY MOONLIGHT.—WaIter Williams, Norfolk street, was summoned by Mr. John Johnson for having, on the 11th ult., whilst a fortnightly tenant of a cottage at Clifton, clandestinely and fraudulently removed his goods to avoid payment of £1 2s 8d owing for rent.—Mr. Peter Johnson, son of the complainant, gave evidence proving the case.—Defendant said he had been out of work for about eight weeks, and was, therefore, in pecuniary difficulties when he removed the goods.—He was ordered to pay the amount of rent and the costs Ils 6d. AN UNGALLANT YOUNG MAN.—William Peck, son of Mr. Peck, cab proprietor, was summoned for having, on the Bth inst., used violent and abusive language, calculated to cause a breach of the peace, to Miss Alicia Rhodes, daughter of the landlady of the Egerton Arms. As defendant had not ap- peared to a summons, he was now brought up on a warrant. —Complainant said that the young man had been to see her that .horning and asked her to forgive him.—The Bench expressed a wish to hear something of the case, and the young lady then said that defendant, who was in drink at •the time, came to the house and used very strong language; in fact, " he called her anything but a lady."—The Chair- man said that defendant bad pleaded guilty to having com- mitted the offence with which he was charged, and he would he fined 5s and 18s costs. STREET FIGHTERS. Joseph Hirst. John Brown, and Mar- garet Bramby were convicted, on the evidence of P.C.'s Hibbert and Baker, of having, on the night of the 27th ult., fought in Fryer-street.—Each defendant was hound over in £lO and two sureties of £5 to keep the peace, or, in default, be sent to gaol 14 days. THE CHARGE OF EMBEZZLEMENT AGAINST A DRAPER'S TRAVELLER.—Joseph Clough, a young man employed as a country traveller and general assistant by Mr. Randle, of Bridge-street, was brought un on remand charged with ern- Ihezzling the sums of 355, 21s, and 30s, the moneys of his employer. A considerable number of young men, who had been acquainted with the prisoner, were present in court, and the Rev. Henry Valentine (Wesleyan minister) was also in attendance, and was affected even to teals by the position of the prisoner, who preserved a remarkably cool demeanour. —The prosecutor said the prisoner had been in his employ from the lot March as a country traveller and assistant in the shop. Prisoner, on the 17th ult., went to Dunham-on- the-Hill and Alvanlev—what was called the Kingsley round—and he gave him .E 1 in silver for change. He ought to have returned on the following Friday evening, in order to account for any money he had received on the journey, but he did not do so. The first time he next saw Clough was on Thursday last, when he appeared before the local Bench. In consequence of what he heard he took out a warrant against the prisoner on the 23rd ult. He (witness) had a customer named Miss Edwards, who lived at Alvan- ley, and two named respectively Miss Booth and Mrs. Booth, at Dunham-on-the-Hill. In the book produced prisoner was instructed to enter any same he received.—Miss Margaret Edwards, of Alvanlev, said that on the 18th ult. she paid I Clough an account of £1 15s for drapery sunplied. She produced the receipt—Miss Kate Booth, Dunham-on-the- , Hill, stated that she had paid him £1 10s 54 on account of her mother, and received from him the receipts produced.— Mrs. Ann Both, mother of the last witness, said she lived at Dunham-on-the-Hill, and paid the prisoner £1 Is on account upon the 18th ult.—Sergeant Morris gave evidence to the effect that on the 24th ult. he received the prisoner in custody from the Dover police, and in his possession was £3 8s 4d. Prisoner, on being charged, said he did not know the amount he had embezzled.—The prosecutor, addressing the Bench, said: I wish to plead on behalf of the prisoner, who has been a friend of mine for ten or eleven years, and I engaged him on account of our previous friendship. He has always, I believe, borne an excellent character, and had he, instead of running away to Dover, communicated with me, I should certainly have forgiven him the offence with which he now stands charged. I feel very sorry that his foolish conduct has led him to this pass, and I am sure that the mental punishment he has undergone since his arrest has been quite sufficient for him, even if he received no other. I therefore beg of you to deal with him as leniently as you can—The Chairman asked the prisoner if he had any reason to urge why punishment should not be passed upon him.— Clough said he had not. He might. however, say that he attributed what had taken place to the excessive quantity of drink which he took on the day before he absconded.—The Chairman (to the prisoner): This being your first offence, and your former master having spoken so favourably of Tour previous character, we shall deal .leniently with you. We have the power to commit you for six mosiths, and we trust that even the punishment we shall give you will be sufficient warning to conduct yourself better in future. You will be committed to Knutsford one month.—At the conclu- sion of the case, the prosecutor, the Rev. H. Valentine. and a host of acquaintances went. up to the prisener to shake hands with him previous to his removal to the cells. A WARNING TO POOR. BATE DEFAULTERS.—Mr. W. Sutton, assistant overseer, summoned 81 people for non- payment of poor rates. Orders were made for payment im- mediately in most of the cases, and of the rest in a few days.

DEATH FROM DELIRIUM TREMENS AT WARRINGTON.— At the Three Pigeons, Dallam-lane, on Wednesdiy an in- quest was held by Mr. Driffield, coroner, on the body of Bernard Fearnon, who died suddenly on Sunday last. De- ceased, who had lodged with a Mrs. Dukes for about eleven weeks, was a labourer at Bewsey Forge, and an army pen- sioner. He had not been working for the last five or six weeks. He had a large abscess on one knee, but commenced drinking then staying out all day and sometimes at nights. On Friday, the 2&h ult., deceased stayed in all day, but talked of getting back to wo'rk saying he was breaking him- self with the d rink. On Saturday he was in part of the day, but after being out said he had had an odd glass, and com Mained of being ve7 poorley. He spoke very sensibly but - looked very wild and trembed very much. On Sunday about eleven o'clock he came down stairs and put on his boots and cap saying he was going out. The landlady bagged the deceased to lie down and f he did so. She afterwards sen. 0r _ a doctor, but he could not be seen. After a time she hear a noise upstairs, and running up found deceased laid on the .:. room floor. She called up the lodgers and went down soiri On her return the lodgers had laid him partially on the She went down again and one of the lodgers ioltoved h er and told her be was dead. Deceased took little food drinking and told the landlady he could not take De- ceased, who. was about 45 years of age, had been a teetotaller for twelve months, and was a hard drinker at timer. The jury returned a verdict that the deceased died. ;11 ,rOlll,l pear, from an attack of delirium tt:ernens NN: .. et following a prolonged spell of di inklng, i necessary and proper food.

NO VISITOR TO SOUTHPORT SHOULD MISS SEEING THE BOTANIC GARDENS, CHURCHTOWN, SOUTHPORT. Acknowledged to be one of the most charming spots In the North of England. SPLENDID GROUNDS AND SHRUBBERIES. The Unique Fernery, with its Mirrors, Grottoes Waterfalls, Fountain, and Fishpools, forms a lovely Pantomimic Fairy Scene. THE GRAND CONSERVATORY, With its mass of rich ever-varying Bloom, and large central Fountain, is indeed a "thing of beauty." Fine Ranges of VINERIES AND PLANT HOUSES Excellent MUSEUM of Natural History, Geology, Coins, Medals, and Curiosities. (The Natural History Section contains a complete Entomological Collection of Southport.) Spacious and well-appointed first and second-class public and private Refreshment Rooms. Admission t€ the Gardens (in- cluding Conservatory. Fernery, and Museum), 4d; children under 12 years of age, 2d each. Street tramway cars run between the Botanic Gardens, Southport. and Birkdale, every seven minutes in summer.

MEETING OF THE SENSES. • 'Twas a wonderful meeting, as you will declare, When we say that the seven human senses were there; And old father Reason was placed in the chair, Which he took with a cool and deliberate air; And, looking to see if all members were there, He called upon Speech to stand up and declare The object they had in assembling there. (This is all very true, and 'twas quite debonnair.) "The question," said Speech, "is all over the town. Why Lewis's Tea has obtained such renown V And our business to-night, my dear friends, is to try To get at the ' wherefore' and find out the 'why.'" Then Hearing gets up, and his thorax he clears, And as Rumour was tongues, so was Hearing all ears; But he rose, and with voice like a bell's he exclaimed "I can tell you why Lewis's Tea is so famed. I know what I hear, and I hear It each minute, The people enjoy the aroma that's in it; Though only a florin a pound they may pay, 'Tie tne cheapest and best, and that's what they all say," "Well done l" said the Nose, "For I always can tell When 'tis Lewis's Tea—yes, the moment I smell; For who should know better, I cannot suppose, That any knows better than I, Mr. Nose' " Hear, hear Very true !" said the sharp Mr. Sight, " 'Tie the comfort of man, it is woman's delight; And Lewis's beautiful Two-shilling Tea Is as pure and as perfect as any can be." Said Feeling," My evidence may not be much, But I almost can tell it directly It ugh." "Any yet after all," shouted Taste, as he stood, "I think you'll admit that my judgment is good; In Lewis's Tea I can always delight, For its strength is immense, and its flavour is right." So the Chairman rose up. "My dear brethren, said he, "The matter is perfectly simple to me. The secret Is this, as it seems you agree, That Lewis's sell us the best of all Tea. Though only two shillings a pound, do you see ?"
